nodes.body:
**Decisions**

- The scope wording was agreed in chat on 2026-10-19, and is written into CLAUDE.md as a new section, "What this project is".
- The sentence on the threat to plan for (scanning bots and worms, not a targeted attack) came from the same chat, after the wording was agreed. It's in the security bullet.
- The security exception covers only issues for security problems set aside for later. Raising a security problem in a PR is fine, since it gets fixed or accepted before the PR merges. Agreed in chat after the first CI review.
- The set-aside rule, with its security exception, is kept only in CLAUDE.md, since it applies in chat too. DEVELOPMENT.md section 9 points to it.

**Set aside:** nothing.

**Config changes needed:** none.

The new security exception (line 5) and this section disagree. Line 5 says a security problem goes to Joe in chat first, and gets written down only once he approves. This section tells reviewers to report security problems, and the CI reviewer reports by posting inline comments on the PR. This repo is public, and the CI reviewer has no chat. So a security problem found in CI is posted in public before Joe decides, which is what line 5 is meant to stop. One fix is to say here how a reviewer reports a security problem, for example as a comment that names the file and asks Joe to look, without spelling out the attack.

This rule does not hold for the CI workflow this PR also changes. `.github/workflows/code-review.yml` uses floating major tags (`actions/checkout@v7`, `actions/setup-node@v7`, `actions/upload-artifact@v7`), `node-version: 24`, and installs `bubblewrap` and `socat` from apt without versions. Each run can pick up a newer release. If a new release changes how the reviewer behaves, the change cannot be traced to a PR. Either pin those, or say here that the CI runner actions and packages are not covered.

The CI log this cites will expire. GitHub deletes run logs after the repo retention period (90 days by default), so the evidence is gone well before the project ends. Quote the log line instead: `Ignoring 5 permissions.allow entries from .claude/settings.json: this workspace has not been trusted.`

This sentence is now in two places, word for word: here and in CLAUDE.md line 5. The set-aside rule was already in both, and now the security exception is too. When one copy changes, the other has to change with it, or Claude Code and the CI reviewer get different rules. Keep the rule in one file, and have the other point to it.

Review guidance is now in two places in this file: this section, and the "When reviewing a PR" bullet under "Pull requests" (line 40). A reader who finds one can miss the other. Putting that bullet under this heading keeps all the review rules together.

The new security exception conflicts with the decisions-comment rule. Line 40 here and DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 (line 100) say the PR comment lists "what was set aside, and where it was written down". A security problem set aside during a task is exactly that, so following section 7 puts a description of the hole in a public PR comment, which this exception is meant to prevent. Say here (or in section 7) that a set-aside security problem is left out of the decisions comment and raised with Joe in chat.

The reason given for allowing security problems in a PR, "since it gets fixed or accepted before the PR merges", does not hold for the accepted ones. PR comments stay public after the merge, so a hole Joe accepts stays described on the PR just as it would in an open issue. It also does not cover a reviewer finding a problem in existing code the PR does not touch (the review recipe looks at unchanged lines in touched functions), which the PR will not fix either. If the intent is that PR exposure is acceptable, the sentence should say that, rather than rest on a reason that is false for those cases.

The exception leaves a set-aside security problem with nowhere to be written down. The rule just before it says to write set-aside things down right away, but the exception forbids an issue until Joe approves and names no other place. If Claude Code sets one aside in a session and Joe does not answer before the session ends, nothing records it and it is lost. Name where it goes meanwhile, such as telling Joe in chat right away and opening the issue only once he approves.

This understates what the token can do. `pull-requests: write` is granted for the whole repo, not just the PR under review, so a reviewer steered by injected text in the code can comment on, edit (title and body), or close any open PR in the repo. Since this comment is what the risk was accepted on, it should say "any PR in the repo" rather than "the PR".

This conflicts with line 21. Line 21 says a serious security hole in a locked version gets patched, but this bullet tells reviewers not to report version updates. A reviewer who notices a locked package or action with a known serious hole is told both to report it (a security problem) and not to (a version update). Add "except for a serious security hole" to the version-update clause.

## Decisions

All agreed with Joe in chat on 2026-10-19, and written into code review design section 3.1 unless it says otherwise.

- **Each finding gets one label, the first in the table that fits.** D1 and D2 come first, so a false claim, or one that only disagrees with the design, isn't posted, whatever else it says.
- **F2 to F4 carry their own condition, "in normal use".** A finding that fails it gets the matching NF label, and is a note. F5's condition is the threat model in CLAUDE.md, and NF5 is a security hole outside it. F1 and F6 have no NF label, since normal use doesn't apply to them.
- **Normal use** covers a failure the code is meant to handle, such as an outside service not answering in time. It doesn't cover an unlikely input, a setting no one would choose, or timing so narrow that two things have to line up in a particular order. Code that's written but not called yet is judged as if it were called the way the design says.
- **F3 is text an agent reads that's false.** The test is whether an agent that believes it would do the wrong thing. Unclear or repeated text is N3.
- **F6: a wrong design doc is above the bar.** This answers open question 2 on #75. A design choice that causes wrong behavior in normal use is F6. Otherwise a finding that only disagrees with the design is D2.
- **F1** counts what a design section asks for as part of the task, when a "Do" item points to that section. **F2** defines "wrong" as different from the design docs and the task, or where they say nothing, from what a user would plainly expect.
- **A wrong code comment is N5,** a note.
- **Section 3.1 cites no PRs and no real cases,** so the labelers don't go looking for them. The rest of section 3 keeps its examples. "Add a check" moved to section 3.7, since it says how to fix a finding, not which label it gets.
- **No cap on notes** (section 4.2). The cap of 3 had no written reason. Rounds are already capped at three.

nodes.body:
## Decisions

All agreed with Joe in chat on 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-20, while checking the first labeling run against his own calls, and written into code review design section 3.1 unless it says otherwise.

- **V1, first in the table: the label depends on a fact the reviewer can't check from the repo,** such as how an outside service answers, and that fact decides whether it's a fix. It applies only when the fact is outside the repo, settling it needs a real call or run the reviewer can't make, and the answer changes whether it's a fix. It's posted as a third kind, "check" (section 4.2). The fix loop leaves it alone, and Joe has it checked and relabeled in a Claude Code session, not in CI.
- **D2 needs the design to be settled on the point.** When another issue covers it, such as with an open question, D2 doesn't fit, and the finding gets the next label that fits.
- **D2 needs a check of what the user would see.** Before choosing D2, the labeler says what the user would see if the code ran as designed. If that's wrong in normal use, the label is F6.
- **D3: work the task asks for, handed to another issue.** A code comment where the work belongs names the issue. The issue is open, isn't the PR's own, and its description says what the work is. The reviewer reads it to check. If any part is missing, the label is F1. The PR's own open questions don't count, since that issue closes when the PR merges. Work the task doesn't ask for, such as a test or a cleanup, keeps its usual label.
- **A plausible mistake by a road trip agent is normal use.** Plausible means a slip models make in practice, such as a wrong input name or the same ID twice, not input the model has no reason to produce.
- **F3 and N3 are about the road trip agents,** the coordinator and its workers, not the agents that build or review the code.
- **F4 defines lost and corrupted.** Lost is gone. Corrupted is saved wrong, so the stored data needs repair. A load that fails on stored data that's fine is F2.
- **F7: a wrong test is a fix.** It passes with the code broken, or fails when the code is right. A wrong test gives false confidence, which is worse than none. A missing test stays N2.
- **N6: a design doc problem no builder would act on** is a note. It pairs with F6 the way N3 pairs with F3.

## Set aside

- **How the fix loop and the reviewer keep track of V1 findings.** Joe suggested the PR description, but DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 keeps that to the task and the "Done when" results. Added to #75's open questions, to settle once the loop runs.
- **Whether the "Code review" workflow can read issues,** which D3 needs. Already in #75's open questions.
- **Labeling the corpus again with this rubric,** with Joe not labeling this time. Added to #75's "Do". It's planned for a new session.

## Config changes

None.

Added in be11a88, agreed in chat on 2026-10-20:

- **Section 4.6:** neither the reviewer nor the fixer gets WebFetch or WebSearch. A finding whose label hangs on an outside fact gets V1, not a guess from the web.
- **Section 4.1:** our reviewer can run node, to test a claim. V1 says the reviewer runs code when running it would settle the label, and the labelers needed node for 32-2 and 34-1.

Blocking the web tools doesn't stop a program such as `node` from reaching the web. Limiting the network for the agents' commands is #82, which #75 now waits on.

Added in 6203c93, agreed in chat on 2026-10-20 after the #82 spike:

- **Section 4.6:** each agent's commands run in Claude Code's sandbox, with only `github.com` and `api.github.com` reachable. The settings are passed with `--settings`, since CI ignores `.claude/settings.json`. #82's CI runs showed other sites refused, and `git`, `gh`, and `npm run check` still working.
- **Section 4.1:** our reviewer runs `node` to test claims that need no outside access. A claim that only an outside service can settle gets V1.
- Sandboxed commands can read the checkout's GitHub token. That's accepted, since the fixer's token is a GitHub App token limited to this repo.

Changed in 5f68b31, agreed in chat on 2026-10-20 after round 2 of the labeling:

- **D3 no longer needs the work to be task work.** Work handed to an issue that names it is D3 either way, since the issue tracks it. Round 2's labeler a gave 44r4-1 N3 because phase 13a's task didn't ask for the work, though phase 22's Do item named it.
- **The issue has to name this work, not just work near it.** In K2, both labelers took phase 16's "turned back into links on load" as covering `load()` loading places. That was added to phase 16 only after the review, so K2 is F1.
- Put-off work that no issue tracks is unchanged: task work is F1, and other work keeps its usual label.

Changed in ca69da5, agreed in chat on 2026-10-20 after round 2 of the labeling. These come from Joe's round 2 labels, read by category (V, D, F, N):

- **A D label fits only when it clearly fits.** A D finding is never seen again, so when unsure, keep going down the table. A wrong note costs only a posted comment.
- **D1:** the failure has to be impossible with the code as it stands. True only for an unlikely input is NF, and so is a failure that only code not yet written would prevent.
- **D2:** the design has to speak to the point itself, not just through a general rule. When it does, D2 comes before the NF labels, even when the harm is outside normal use.
- **F3:** false text is a specific claim an agent could act on, including a wrong reason for an error. A vague error that doesn't point the agent the wrong way is N3.
- **F7:** a test is wrong when it can't catch a break in the very thing it targets. A test that checks the real thing but misses a case or a path is N2.

The rubric's examples avoid the corpus's own cases, so they don't give away the answer key.

## Decisions

Joe was away while this was built, so each choice below was made without asking. #75 says "Settled in: chat", so the design text in this PR is a proposal. Each item says where it's written.

### How it runs

- **The prompt is a project skill, `.claude/skills/review-pr/SKILL.md`.** The workflow runs `/review-pr <number>`. It has `disable-model-invocation: true`, so it never starts on its own in a coding session. You can run it locally with `/review-pr 83`. It returns the findings and posts nothing. Written in code review design sections 2 and 4.1.
- **The workflow posts the findings, not the reviewer.** The reviewer returns JSON, which `claude -p --json-schema` checks before the run ends. The next step posts it with code in `src/code-review/`. So a wrong post traces to code, and the reviewer needs no command that writes. Written in section 2.
- **The posting code is TypeScript in `src/`, with tests.** That way it's linted, type-checked, and tested like the rest. It also means this PR changes `src/`, so the new reviewer reviewed this PR. It isn't part of the app's build.
- **The reviewer gives only the label.** The code works out the kind from it: V1 is "check", D is not posted, F is "fix", and N or NF is "note". Written in section 4.1.
- **A finding on a line outside the diff goes on its file.** GitHub refuses an inline comment on a line outside the diff. A finding on a file outside the diff, such as a design doc the PR didn't change, goes in one review body. The reviewer's step 2 reads review bodies too. Written in sections 2 and 4.2.
- **`gh` is narrowed to `gh pr view`, `gh pr diff`, `gh issue view`, and `gh api`.** It was all of `gh` before. `gh api` can still post, and that's left as it is, since the job's token could already comment.
- **The job runs `npm ci` before the reviewer starts.** Then `node` can use the repo's packages, such as Zod, and `node --import tsx` can import the repo's TypeScript. The skill tells the reviewer how.
- **The schema is written in its own step.** That step runs the PR's code, so it's kept apart from the step that holds the Claude token.
- **The scrub and the `/proc` block stay on,** next to the sandbox. The sandbox limits the network, not what a command can read.
- **No `--effort` flag.** The stock review ran at the model's default, and "high" was its review level, which our prompt is built from. Written in section 4.1.

### What the prompt does beyond section 4.1

- **It adds a fourth angle: the task, the docs, and the tests.** Section 4.1 lists only the 3 bug angles. Those read code, so nothing would look for F1, F3, F6, or F7 on purpose. The stock review never found a doc that didn't match the code (research doc, section 8.3). Written in section 4.1. Cut it if you'd rather match the stock prompt more closely.
- **It checks each finding before labeling it.** The stock prompt has no check step. D1, a false claim, needs one. A false claim is still returned as D1, not dropped, so you can check it in `not-posted.md`.
- **It has no cap on the number of findings.** It first kept the stock cap of 10. Joe dropped it on 2026-10-21, since a finding cut by the cap isn't posted or listed anywhere. Look at it again after a few PRs. Written in section 4.1.
- **It may read an issue's body, never its comments.** That includes the PR's own issue. Section 4.3 forbids only the comments. The body's settled open questions name decisions, but those are in the design docs too.

### Comment text

- **Each comment shows the label's reason too:** "**Fix (F2)**", then the finding, then "**Why F2:** ...". Section 4.2 asked only for the kind and label. The reason lets you check a label without rerunning anything. Written in section 4.2.
- **`not-posted.md` quotes the finding under each line.** The design's example gave only the reason. Without the finding, you can't tell what was dropped. Written in section 4.2.

### Docs

- **DEVELOPMENT.md section 7** now names our reviewer and its three marks, and points to code review design section 3 for handling findings.
- **CLAUDE.md isn't changed.** Its "When reviewing" rules still fit.

### Changed after the first runs

- **The prompt says to run commands without `cd`** (8746524). In run 1, one command was refused: a `cd`, then `grep` on a relative path. Claude Code refuses that while a `Read()` deny rule is set, and ours blocks `/proc`. The reviewer recovered, but #77 may fail a run on any refused command.
- **The prompt says to take each line number from the file** (5482f4f). In run 2, the reviewer gave line 600 of a file with about 130 lines. It had taken the number from its saved copy of the diff. The posting code still put the finding on the file, as it should.
- **Run 3 had one refused command: `npx`,** which wasn't allowed. The reviewer switched to `node --import tsx` on its own. Joe then allowed `npx vitest` and `npx tsx` on 2026-10-21 (8c29418). They add nothing `node` can't already do, and the sandbox stops `npx` from downloading a package. Written in sections 2 and 4.1.
- **`npx vitest` was taken back out the same day** (64afc87). Run 4 used it to rerun the PR's tests, which the "Check and deploy" workflow already runs, so it only spent tokens. The prompt now says not to run the tests. `npx tsx` stays. Written in sections 2 and 4.1.
- **The prompt says to run checks inline, and not to write files** (8dd1148). It used to say to write scratch files under `$TMPDIR`. In run 4, Claude Code refused a command that sent output to `"$TMPDIR/v.txt"`, and another with `${PIPESTATUS[0]}`, since it can't check either before the command runs. The prompt now names both.
- **The prompt no longer has text that only undid the stock prompt** (517689e). The reviewer never sees the stock prompt, so that text did nothing useful. It dropped "A review with no findings is a normal result. There's no minimum," which pulled against "report when in doubt." It also dropped a reason that held only when every finding was fixed, and the `$TMPDIR` example from the earlier scratch-file wording.
- **The Agent tool is blocked** (517689e). The reviewer has no use for subagents, so the workflow blocks the tool instead of the prompt asking it not to.
- **Code review design section 4.1 now says what the reviewer does,** not how it differs from the stock prompt (517689e).
- **The rubric is now its own doc, `design/review-rubric.md`** (4c97305). In all four runs, the reviewer read the whole of `code-review.md`, which puts the real cases the rubric leaves out in front of it. Section 3.1 is now a pointer, so links to it still work. The skill no longer points to section 4.4 either. Step 6.2 already says what to do with the "Set aside" list. `design/README.md` lists the new doc. Its entry for code review now says it's for changing the workflow or the reviewer, or fixing findings. Check the transcripts of the next few PRs to see whether the reviewer still opens `code-review.md` on a PR that doesn't touch it.
- **Section 4.2 now says why the next review doesn't see the D labels** (b8e152a). It labels a dropped finding again on its own, so it's a second check on a label only you would otherwise see. Counting findings that flip between rounds is now an open question on #86.
- **The reviewer always reads `DEVELOPMENT.md`** (0dea9e7). The prompt said to read it only when the PR changes code, but the workflow reviews only PRs that change `src/` or `web/`.
- **Angle A now says its bug kinds are examples** (928f26e). It used to read "Look for" and a list, which could read as the whole search. It now ends with "A bug of any other kind counts the same."
- **Section 4.6 now says `gh pr view` and `gh issue view` work** through the sandbox. Run 1 showed it.

## Set aside

- **The fix count as a job output** (section 4.6) is left for #77, which builds the fix job that reads it.
- **Who records each finding's outcome** (section 4.8), before the loop exists. Added to #77's open questions.
- **Failing a review whose commands were all blocked** is already in #77's open questions.

## Security: tested, not a hole

**With `node` allowed, could a command read the Claude token from another process?** Tested 2026-10-21 in a throwaway CI run ([run](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/actions/runs/39592935001)), set up like the review job. No:

- Inside the sandbox, a `node` script run by the agent saw only 3 processes: the sandbox's own init, its shell, and itself. Claude Code's process and the runner's weren't visible. The sandbox gives commands their own process namespace.
- None of the environments it could read had the token. The scrub kept it out of the shell's.
- A control run of the same script outside the sandbox, with a dummy token, found the token in 3 processes. So the script does detect it when it can.

The branch and the probe workflow were deleted after the run.

Replies to the review findings. Joe judged both before anything was changed.

> **Note (N6)** on `design/code-review.md:31`: Section 2 says the reviewer "can read code and run `node`, but not change anything or post", and that its tools are "the `gh` commands that read the PR and its issues". The workflow allows `Bash(gh api:*)`, and `gh api` can send any request, not only reads. [...] So `gh api -X POST ...`, or a `fetch` from `node -e` to api.github.com, would post a comment from inside the sandbox. Only the skill's prompt stops the reviewer from posting.

The finding is right, and N6 fits. The line in section 2 overstates the limit. The tools can post. Only the prompt stops it. The fix would be one sentence in section 2: "It's told not to post, but `gh api` and `node` could, since the job's token can comment." Fixed in 928f26e. It's a note, but section 2 is on lines this PR already changes (code review design section 3.2). Section 2 now says the prompt tells the reviewer not to post, and that `gh api` and `node` could still post with the job's token.

> **Check (V1)** on `src/code-review/post-to-github.ts` (posted as "Line 600"): `postFindings` moves a finding down to a file comment, and then into the review body, only when GitHub refuses with status 422. [...] To check: [...] POST [...] for a line outside the diff. Then POST with `commit_id`, `subject_type: "file"`, and a `path` the PR doesn't change. Note the status of each. If either answer isn't 422, that fallback is broken.

I checked it. Both requests get 422. The first is in run 2's own log, since this finding's line was outside the diff. I sent the second one on this PR, for `README.md`, and GitHub refused it with "pull_request_review_thread.path could not be resolved". By the finding's own reasoning, that means there's no finding. Its line number, 600, was wrong. The file has about 130 lines. The prompt now says to take line numbers from the file (5482f4f).

**Note (N6)**

Section 2 says the reviewer "can read code and run `node`, but not change anything or post", and that its tools are "the `gh` commands that read the PR and its issues". The workflow allows `Bash(gh api:*)`, and `gh api` can send any request, not only reads. The job token has `pull-requests: write`, and `GH_TOKEN` is in the reviewer's environment. So `gh api -X POST repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/<n>/comments ...`, or a `fetch` from `node -e` to api.github.com, would post a comment from inside the sandbox. Only the skill's prompt stops the reviewer from posting. The tools don't. The workflow's own comment (code-review.yml lines 94-97) says this token can comment on, edit, or close the PR, so the design doc and the workflow disagree.

**Why N6:** The doc doesn't match the code, but the workflow comment states the real limit and calls the risk accepted, so no builder would build the wrong thing from it. That makes it N6, not F6. The risk itself was already accepted, so this isn't a new security finding (F5 or NF5).

Line 600.

**Check (V1)**

`postFindings` moves a finding down to a file comment, and then into the review body, only when GitHub refuses with status 422. Any other status makes `gitHubPost` throw, which stops the posting step, so the rest of the findings are never posted. The two fallbacks depend on GitHub answering 422 in two cases. One is a line comment on a line outside the diff. The other is a `subject_type: "file"` comment on a file the PR doesn't change. The tests use a fake that always answers that way. This PR's first run posted only one finding, and it went on its line, so neither fallback has run against GitHub yet. Reviews often find problems in design docs the PR doesn't touch, which takes the second path. To check: on a test PR, POST to `repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/<n>/comments` with `commit_id`, `path`, `line`, and `side: RIGHT` for a line outside the diff. Then POST with `commit_id`, `subject_type: "file"`, and a `path` the PR doesn't change. Note the status of each. If either answer isn't 422, that fallback is broken.

**Why V1:** Whether it's a fix depends on how GitHub's API answers two requests the code hasn't sent for real yet. The reviewer can only reach GitHub with read commands, and nothing in the repo shows the status. If either answer isn't 422, findings on design docs outside the diff are lost in normal use, which is F2. If both are 422, there's no finding.

DEVELOPMENT.md section 4 says schemas for outside data, including tool inputs, go in `*.schema.ts` files. Nothing checks it, and two files break it: `src/tools/trip-brief-tools.ts` (the `update_trip_brief` input) and `src/persistence/trip-repository.ts` (the Postgres lock error).

## Do

- Add a lint rule that bans importing Zod for use outside `*.schema.ts` files, while still allowing type imports and tests.
- Move both schemas into `*.schema.ts` files.
- This changes `eslint.config.*`, which Joe approved on 2026-10-18.

## Done when

- `npm run check` passes, and a Zod import for use in a file that isn't a `*.schema.ts` file or a test fails the lint.

Closes #72

## Results

- **`npm run check` passes:** yes. 64 test files, 501 tests.
- **A Zod import for use outside a schema file or test fails the lint:** yes. Checked by hand with throwaway files, not committed:
  - `import { z } from "zod"` in `src/` and in `web/src/`: fails.
  - `import { z } from "zod/mini"`: fails.
  - `import type { z } from "zod"` and `import { type z } from "zod"`: pass.
  - `import { z } from "zod"` in a `*.schema.ts` file and in a `*.test.ts` file: pass.
- **Checked by hand:** `npx tsx src/code-review/print-findings-schema.ts`, which the "Code review" workflow runs, prints the same JSON as on `main`.

nodes.body:
## Decisions

- **A third file broke the rule.** `src/code-review/print-findings-schema.ts` called `z.toJSONSchema()`. That call moved into `findingsJsonSchema()` in `review-result.schema.ts`, and the script now only prints its result. The script keeps its name, so the "Code review" workflow doesn't change.
- **The `read_trip_brief` input moved too.** It's an empty `z.strictObject({})`, now `READ_TRIP_BRIEF_INPUT`, next to `UPDATE_TRIP_BRIEF_INPUT` in `src/tools/trip-brief-input.schema.ts`. The lock error schema is in `src/persistence/postgres-error.schema.ts`.
- **The rule is `@typescript-eslint/no-restricted-imports`,** with `allowTypeImports`. It covers `zod` and any `zod/*` path, such as `zod/mini`. It's off for `*.schema.ts` and `*.test.ts` files. Fakes (`*.fake.ts`) aren't exempt. None import Zod today.
- **No design doc change.** DEVELOPMENT.md section 4 already says where schemas go.

## Set aside

Nothing.

## Config changes

`eslint.config.mjs`, as approved in #72 on 2026-10-18.

body:
## Do

- Add the Google Weather client, the Open-Meteo client, and `look_up_stay_weather`, which picks the source from the stay's dates.

## Done when

- Tests use saved responses, including Open-Meteo's spent-limit reply.
- A real call for a stay within 7 days returns a forecast.
- A real call for a stay in October 2027 returns seasonal averages, labeled "Typical for this time of year, based on 2016–2025."
- A forecast that leaves out a date returns an error.

Closes #63

## Results

- **Saved responses:** done. Google's Moab, Honolulu, and Leadville forecasts and Open-Meteo's 10 years of Moab data and a January in Leadville were saved from real calls on 2026-10-21. The spent-limit reply is in `src/open-meteo/saved-responses/spent-limit.json`, and tests cover it at the client and through the tool. `npm run check` passes (527 tests).
- **Real call, stay within 7 days:** done. With the Moab trip moved to start on October 23, 2026, `look_up_stay_weather` returned Google's forecast for October 23 to 26, with the stay's two activities.
- **Real call, October 2027:** done. The Moab stay on October 10 to 13, 2027 returned seasonal averages from Open-Meteo, labeled "Typical for this time of year, based on 2016–2025."
- **Forecast that leaves out a date:** done. The tool returns an error that names the missing date, and doesn't call Open-Meteo. Tested at the client and through the tool.

Checked by hand: the two real calls above, run through the tool with the real clients against the Moab example trip.

nodes.body:
## Decisions

- **Google's first forecast day isn't always today** (the issue's open question, settled in chat on 2026-10-21). Before 7 a.m. local time, it's yesterday. The client asks for 10 days and picks each date by its `displayDate`. Written into Google design section 3.
- **The tool and the saved label use one rule.** `StaysService.weatherFor()` decides forecast or seasonal averages. `stay_weather` picks its source by it, and `setWeatherText()` labels the text by it, so they can't disagree.
- **The spent-limit saved response is the Open-Meteo design's example** (section 2.4), not one captured live. Capturing one would take hundreds of calls in a minute. A real Open-Meteo error reply (a bad request, HTTP 400) has the same `error` and `reason` shape. The client checks the body for `error` whatever the status.
- **A rain day is 0.039 in or more,** not 0.04. Open-Meteo gives 1 mm as 0.039 in, so 0.04 would miss exactly 1 mm. A snow day is 0.39 in (1 cm). The Open-Meteo design 2.3 says "0.04 in (1 mm)". I left the doc alone, since the intent is 1 mm.
- **A wrong-kind ID gets its own error,** such as "day_… is a day ID, not a stay ID." (tool design section 4). It's in `src/tools/id-kind.ts`, for later tools to reuse.
- **An activity whose time isn't known yet** shows "time not known yet". That happens when its day's leg isn't routed.

## Set aside

- The weather server isn't connected to an agent yet. #64 does that, with the weather worker.

## Config changes

- None.

More decisions, settled in chat on 2026-10-21:

- **The tool is now `look_up_stay_weather`,** so its name starts with a verb like the other tools. Not `get_stay_weather`, since next to `set_stay_weather` it would read as getting the saved text.
- **Each forecast line names what the chance is of,** such as "40% chance of snow," from Google's precipitation type. This fixes the review's finding on `weather-tools.ts` line 104. A real Leadville forecast is saved as the test. On one day its text says "Light rain" and its type says snow.
- **The stale sentence in Google design section 3 is fixed,** per the review's finding there.
- **The tool description no longer says "The tool picks which from the stay's dates, and the reply says which it is."** The sentences before it already say when it's a forecast, and the reply's own label says which it is.
- **The finding on a window that crosses New Year is left as is.** It's below the bar.

One more decision, settled in chat on 2026-10-21:

- **Rain days are counted from Open-Meteo's `rain_sum`, not `precipitation_sum`.** This fixes the second review's finding on Open-Meteo design 2.3. `precipitation_sum` counts snow as its water, so a snowy stay showed rain days. A saved January in Leadville is the test. Every wet day there was snow, and it now gives 0% rain days and 28% snow days.

Set aside, settled in chat on 2026-10-21: the third review's finding on tool design 2.5, which still says the forecast gives "chances of rain", is left as is. It's below the bar, since the row points to Google design section 3, which has the right rule.

**Check (V1)**

`forecastLines` always calls Google's `daytimeForecast.precipitation.probability.percent` a "% chance of rain". The schema in `weather-forecast.schema.ts` (line 41) drops `probability.type`. The saved responses all have `type: "RAIN"`, but Google's precipitation type can also be `SNOW`, `RAIN_AND_SNOW`, and so on. Example: for a stay in a Colorado mountain town in December, Google could send `{type: "SNOW", percent: 60}`. The tool would then reply "Light snow. 60% chance of rain", and the weather worker could give rain-gear advice instead of snow-gear advice. To check: call `forecast/days:lookup` for a place where snow is forecast, such as Leadville, CO or a town in Alaska in winter, and look at `daytimeForecast.precipitation.probability.type`. If it can be anything other than RAIN, the reply should name the type, or say "precipitation".

**Why V1:** Whether the tool's reply is false depends on what Google sends for a snowy day, and nothing in the repo shows that. If Google does send SNOW, the false reply happens on a normal winter trip and is F3. If not, the finding goes away.

**Note (NF2)**

`seasonalAverages` shifts each year's window from the stay's first year. So when a stay's window crosses New Year, the last year's request ends in the current year. Example: on January 3, 2027, a stay on December 27 to 30, 2027 gives a 2026 request for 2026-12-20 to 2027-01-06. That end date is after today, and the archive doesn't have the last few days yet. Open-Meteo would leave those days empty or refuse the request. A refusal makes the tool return "Seasonal averages are unavailable right now" every time until about mid-January. The data used also falls partly outside the "2016–2025" range the label names.

**Why NF2:** It needs a late-December stay planned in the first week or so of January, which isn't normal use, so it's NF2, not F2. The claim holds as the code is written, so it isn't D1.

**Note (N6)**

Google design section 3 still says "The tool checks the dates before calling" about the 10-day limit. The client now always asks for exactly `FORECAST_DAYS_ASKED` = 10 days and does no such check. It never asks for more than 10, so the sentence describes a check that doesn't exist.

**Why N6:** The doc doesn't match the code, but the same section says to ask for 10 days. No builder would add a wrong check because of it, so it's N6, not F6.

**Note (N6)**

Tool design 2.5 still says the forecast returns "chances of rain and thunderstorms". This PR changed `forecastLines` in `src/tools/weather-tools.ts` to name the type of the chance from Google's `precipitation.probability.type`. Google design section 3 was updated to say so too. So for Leadville on October 24, 2026, the tool now replies "40% chance of snow", while the tools.md row says the chance is always of rain. The row should say "chances of precipitation, named by type (rain, snow, or both), and thunderstorms", or just point to Google design section 3.

**Why N6:** The doc no longer matches the code. But the row links to Google design section 3, which spells out the type, so no builder would go back to a rain-only line. That makes it N6, not F6. The finding is true, so it isn't D1, and no other issue covers it, so it isn't D2 or D3.

These findings are on files this PR doesn't change, so they can't be inline comments.

### `design/data-sources/open-meteo.md:47`

**Fix (F6)**

Open-Meteo design 2.3 calls the share of days with at least 0.04 in of `precipitation_sum` the "Chance of rain". The tool follows it, and `averagesLines` in `src/tools/weather-tools.ts` (line 117) prints it as "Days with rain". But `precipitation_sum` includes snowfall as its water equivalent, so every snow day also counts as a rain day. Example: for a stay in Leadville, CO in January, nearly all precipitation falls as snow. The reply would then say something like "Days with rain: 30%. Days with snow: 28%." The weather worker, believing it, would plan rain gear and warn about rain on days that only snow. This PR already fixed the same rain-versus-snow mix-up on the Google forecast side. The fix is to name this share as precipitation (rain or snow), both in design 2.3 and in the tool's line, such as "Days with rain or snow".

**Why F6:** The code does what the design says, but the design's choice gives the agent false text on a normal winter mountain trip, so the rubric makes it F6, not D2. It isn't D1, since `precipitation_sum` counts snowfall as written.

title: Weather data

body:
## Task

From #76. This PR does steps 1 to 3. The replays, steps 4 to 7, and the "Done when" items about them, come in a second PR. #76 stays open until that one merges. Agreed in chat on 2026-10-22.

### Do

Joe runs the fixer by hand, as a subagent of a Claude Code session on his machine, to see how it works and tune its prompt. It gets tested on two PRs' rounds:

- **PR #44,** the trip server. Its findings came from the stock review, and were labeled with the rubric in #75. Rounds 1 to 3 had findings above the bar. Round 4 had none, so the fixer doesn't run on it.
- **PR #90,** weather data. Its findings came from our reviewer, as it posts them today. Round 1's one check (V1), rain vs snow, was checked and counts as an F3, the way Joe relabels a check (code review design 4.2). Round 2 had one F6. Round 3 had only a note, so the fixer doesn't run on it.

1. **Write the decisions above into code review design 3.2, 3.3, 3.6, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, and 4.8.** Done when the docs say the fixer reads the decisions comment, acts only on findings marked "fix", fixes no notes, and returns JSON that code checks and posts on each finding's thread, and that code keeps the summary.
2. **Write the fixer as the `fix-pr` skill, in `.claude/skills/fix-pr/SKILL.md`,** as code review design 4.5 describes. It reads the review rubric, and what code prints: the PR description, the decisions comment, the findings marked "fix", and the earlier rounds' replies. It checks each finding first (3.5), and a fix comes with a test (3.4). It writes what it defers into issues' open questions, runs `npm run check`, makes one commit, and returns a reply for each finding as JSON (3.6). Done when the skill is written and the review skill's layout is followed where it fits.
3. **Write the code around the fixer,** in `src/code-review/`: what prints its input, the check of its answer, and what posts the replies, resolves the threads, and updates the summary (code review design 3.6, 4.4, and 4.5). Done when its tests pass, and the posting is checked by hand on a replay's draft.
4. **Build each round's inputs.** Each round is replayed from the commit its review saw, not from the fixer's last result. Then each round is tested on its own, and it lines up with what was done by hand. Done when there's a `review.json` for each of these rounds, in the format `src/code-review/review-result.schema.ts` checks:

   | Round | Commit the review saw | Fixed by hand in | Findings from |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | #44 round 1 | `8d3d3a1` | `9a68517` | `scratch/code-review-eval/labeling/items/44r1.json` |
   | #44 round 2 | `9a68517` | `3035d77` | `.../items/44r2.json` |
   | #44 round 3 | `3035d77` | `ae79839` | `.../items/44r3.json` |
   | #90 round 1 | `829efb1` | `3c9b58a` | Run 39631417046's `review-transcript-1` artifact |
   | #90 round 2 | `3c9b58a` | `67338a4` | Run 39653578216's `review-transcript-1` artifact |

   - #44's base is `8fe14f4`. Its items have only the claim and the place, so give each one the label the labeling rounds settled on, from the last round that labeled it (`scratch/code-review-eval/labeling/`, on Joe's machine). Write a `labelReason` for each.
   - #90's artifacts are deleted after 30 days, on about 2026-11-20. Download them first. In round 1, change the V1's label to F3.
5. **Replay each round, and compare.** For each round, push a branch at the round's base commit and one at the reviewed commit, named `replay/<pr>-base` and `replay/<pr>-round-<n>`. Open a draft PR from one to the other, with the original PR's description, and copy its decisions comment onto it. Post the round's findings on it with `post-findings.ts`, as the reviewer app (#92). Run the fixer as a subagent in a worktree of that branch. It commits in the worktree, and doesn't write to GitHub. Where it would write into an issue, its reply says what it would write. Then post its answer with the fixer app's token (#92). The skill, the rubric, and the fixer's code in `src/code-review/` aren't in the old commits, so point the subagent at this branch's copies. Run `npm ci` in each worktree, since the packages differ by commit. Done when each round has the fixer's commit and reply on its draft, next to the hand fix.
6. **Tune the prompt, and replay again** where the fixer went wrong. Done when Joe agrees the results are good enough to try on a live PR.
7. **Close the draft PRs, and delete the replay branches.**

### Done when

- For each round in the table, this PR shows the fixer's result next to what was done by hand: each finding, what the fixer did with it, and its turns, time, and cost.
- `npm run check` passes.

Part of #76

## Results so far

Steps 1 to 3 are done. Steps 4 to 7, the replays, come in a second PR.

- **Step 1:** Code review design 3.2, 3.3, 3.6, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, and 4.8 now say the fixer reads the decisions comment, acts only on findings marked "fix", fixes no notes, and returns JSON that code checks and posts on each finding's thread. Section 4.4 says code keeps the summary.
- **Step 2:** The skill is `.claude/skills/fix-pr/SKILL.md`. It follows the `review-pr` skill's layout: numbered steps, the commands to run, and an output section.
- **Step 3:** The code is in `src/code-review/`. `fix-input.ts` prints the fixer's input, `check-fix.ts` checks its answer, and `post-fix.ts` does the writes as the fixer's app. Its tests pass. The posting was checked by hand on #96, a throwaway replay draft of #90 round 1:
  - **Round 1:** the reviewer's app posted the findings, with the V1 relabeled F3. `fix-input.ts` printed the F3 and none of the notes. `check-fix.ts` refused a bad answer, with what was wrong. A hand-written "needs attention" answer was posted on the F3's thread, and the summary listed it.
  - **Round 2:** after a reply as Joe, a new head, and round 2's F6 posted in a review body, `fix-input.ts` printed the F6, and the F3 with both replies and the note that the fixer may take it. A hand-written answer, with a commit made as the fixer, fixed the F3 and deferred the F6 to #77. `post-fix.ts` pushed the commit, replied on the F3's thread and resolved it, posted the F6's reply as a tagged conversation comment, and updated the summary to list only the F6, with a checkbox. The notes' threads were left alone.
  - #96 is closed, and its branches deleted.
- **The CI review** ran three rounds. Round 1's F2 and F6, and round 2's F2, were fixed. Round 2's N6 was left as is, and round 3's F6 was deferred to #77, both agreed in chat.
- **Steps 4 to 7:** in a second PR. #76's body says where they stand.

## Decisions

All settled in chat on 2026-10-21, and struck out in #76's open questions.

**Written into code review design:**

- The fixer reads the decisions comment: 4.5.
- The fixer acts only on findings marked "fix", and fixes no notes, even on lines it's changing: 3.2 and 4.2. Section 3.2's example is now the N3 that was fixed by hand on PR #44 round 1, and wouldn't be under this rule.
- A finding is "deferred" only when it holds up and is above the bar, an open issue already plans work on the same code that the fix fits better, and nothing breaks in normal use while it waits. The fixer adds the work to that issue's open questions, and never opens an issue. "Deferred" keeps it apart from CLAUDE.md's "set aside": 3.8.
- A finding the fixer won't fix is "not fixed", below the bar or wrong. One Joe has to decide on "needs attention", including a fix too big for the PR that no open issue plans: 3.6.
- Each finding gets a reply on its own thread, starting with a marker for its outcome. A finding in a review body gets a conversation comment of its own: 3.6.
- The reviewer gets its earlier findings from code, without the replies: 4.3. That's built in #93.
- Code keeps one summary comment of what's deferred and what needs attention. It resolves the threads that are fixed or not fixed. Joe resolves the rest, or ticks a box for a finding in a review body: 4.4.
- The fixer returns JSON, which code checks and then posts. It pushes nothing and posts nothing on the PR itself. Its only writes to GitHub are to issues' open questions: 4.5.
- The "Set aside" list in the PR description is dropped, so CLAUDE.md and DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 are back to what's on `main`.

**In the skill only:**

- The skill carries code review design section 3's rules itself, and reads only the rubric and DEVELOPMENT.md. Joe agreed the skill implements those rules, like code, and changes when they do.
- A test comes with a fix that changes what code does. A fix to text only needs none. A fixed test (F7) is checked by breaking the thing it targets for a moment.

**In step 3's code, 2026-10-22:**

- Code tells the reviewer's findings, the fixer's replies, and Joe's replies apart by who posted them, using the apps from #92. A reply counts as the fixer's only when it starts with a marker. Written into code review design 4.5.
- Each finding's ID is its comment's, as `comment-<id>`, or for one in a review body, `review-<id>-<n>`, its place there. A reply to a review-body finding is tagged with that ID on a hidden line, so code can find it again.
- Joe replies to a review-body finding in a conversation comment that names its ID, since there's no thread to reply on. The fixer's reply shows the ID, and says to do that. Changed 2026-10-22 after the first review's F2, which found that Joe's reply was otherwise never read. Written into code review design 3.6 and 4.5.
- In the loop, Joe can ask for a fix only on a finding that needs attention. A finding that wasn't fixed has its thread resolved, so he fixes it himself, or asks in chat. Written into code review design 3.3, after the first review's F6.
- A ticked line in the summary stays, ticked, instead of being dropped. Dropping it would lose the only record that Joe handled it, and the next update would add it back unticked. Code review design 4.4 changed to match.
- `fix-input.ts` also stops when the fixer already replied on this round's findings, so a second run can't post twice.
- The check of the answer also refuses changes left uncommitted, and a commit that isn't one commit on top of the PR's head.
- Code review design 4.5 said the fixer can open issues. It now says it edits one only to defer a finding's work to it.
- The CI review posts as `github-actions[bot]` until #93, so `fix-input.ts` won't see its findings until then. #77's first live run already waits on #93.

**After the second review, 2026-10-22:**

- Joe can ask for a fix on a finding from the review of the PR's head too, once the fixer has marked it "needs attention" and pushed nothing. Before, code only read his reply on findings from earlier reviews. Fixed after the second review's F2. Written into code review design 4.5 and the skill's step 2.
- The second review's N6, that design 4.5's list of when the fixer stops leaves out the case where Joe replied, is left as is. Agreed in chat: the next bullet and the skill already say it.
- CLAUDE.md now says to read DEVELOPMENT.md before reviewing code too, not only before writing or changing it. Joe asked for it in chat, to see whether the reviewer then reads DEVELOPMENT.md. It has skipped it on every PR so far (#87).

**Set aside:**

- The third review's F6, that nothing in CI starts the fixer after Joe replies "fix it": deferred to #77's open questions, agreed in chat on 2026-10-22.

- Each agent gets its own GitHub App: #92.
- The reviewer reads its earlier findings from code: #93.
- How the fix job keeps the fixer away from the config files: #77's open questions.

**Config changes:** none.

> **Fix (F6)**
>
> Section 4.5 (line 197) says that when Joe replies "fix it" on a finding that needs attention, "the next fixer fixes it". [...] Nothing in the workflow ever runs the fixer "again" because of Joe's reply. [...] #77 builds the fix job from sections 4.6 and 4.7, so it would build this trigger as written.

([finding](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/91#discussion_r4349315316))

**Deferred to #77,** agreed with Joe in chat on 2026-10-22. The finding holds: the code reads Joe's reply, but nothing in the workflow starts a fixer that would. What starts the fix job is #77's work, and nothing breaks while it waits, since there's no fix job in CI yet. It's in #77's open questions.

**Fix (F2)**

`findingsFromReview()` only links a conversation comment to a review-body finding when the comment has the hidden tag `<!-- fix-loop: review-<id>-<n> -->`. Only code writes that tag. Joe can't see it in the rendered comment, and "Quote reply" doesn't copy it. So when a review-body finding gets "Needs attention" and Joe writes a conversation comment such as "Fix the F6 on design/x.md:47", the comment is never added to the finding's `replies`. `isAskable()` stays false, and the next round's `fix-input.ts` doesn't print Joe's comment anywhere. If the fixer tries to act on it anyway, `check-fix.ts` refuses the entry because the ID isn't in `allowed`. Joe's instruction is dropped without any message. Inline findings don't have this problem, because Joe's reply goes on their thread. A concrete case is #90 round 2, where the F6 was posted in a review body.

**Why F2:** Design 4.5 says the next fixer fixes a needs-attention finding when Joe replies and asks for it, and the app silently ignores that request for review-body findings, which happen in normal use (#90 round 2). This is wrong behavior, not just a doc gap, so F2 fits before F6, and no open issue or design point covers it, so no D label fits.

**Fix (F6)**

Section 3.3 still says the fixer "lists it for Joe in the PR comment, quoting the finding, with a short reason. Joe can still ask for it to be fixed." That's the old rule, and the rewritten sections contradict it. Section 3.6 says that when findings are handled by hand, no replies are posted, and that in the loop each finding gets a reply on its own thread instead of one quoting comment. Section 4.4 says not-fixed findings stay only in their threads and are resolved. Section 4.5 and `isAskable()` only let Joe ask for a fix on a finding that "needs attention", not on one that was below the bar. Section 3 says it applies both to work by hand and to the loop. So someone handling findings by hand, or building #77 or #93 from 3.3, would post a quoting PR comment and expect Joe to be able to get a below-the-bar finding fixed. The rest of the doc says neither of those happens.

**Why F6:** This doc was changed in this PR, and it now contradicts itself on where replies go and on what Joe can ask the fixer to fix. A builder would act on either version, so this is F6 and not N6. F1 doesn't fit because the task's item 1 asked for sections 3.2, 3.3, 3.6, and the others to be updated, and the main 3.3 update was made in its second paragraph.

**Fix (F2)**

`fixRound()` only looks for Joe's "fix it" replies among `earlier` findings, the ones reviewed at a commit other than the PR's head (`askable: earlier.filter(isAskable)`). If a finding from the review of the current head needs attention, Joe's reply to it is never picked up. `stopReason()` makes it worse: once the fixer has replied on this round's findings, it returns "The fixer already replied on this round's …". Here is a concrete case. The review of head H marks one F5 "fix". The fixer can't fix it in the PR, so it answers `needs_attention` with `commit: null`. Nothing is pushed, so the head stays H and the loop stops. Joe replies on the thread, "Fix it here, changing X is fine." When `fix-input.ts` runs again, it prints `Stop: The fixer already replied on this round's comment-…`, and the fixer never sees Joe's reply. `check-fix.ts` would also refuse an entry for that ID, because it isn't in `round.askable`. Joe's request is only acted on if some other commit is pushed first. A round where every finding needs attention is exactly when nothing gets pushed.

**Why F2:** Design 3.3 and 4.5 say Joe can ask for a fix on a finding that needs attention, and the next fixer fixes it. Here the code drops that request in a normal case: a round where nothing was fixed. The claim matches the code, so D1 doesn't fit. The design doesn't say that only findings from earlier commits can be asked about, and no issue covers this, so D2 and D3 don't fit. F1 doesn't fit either, because the task's items are done. The failure is in how they behave.

**Note (N6)**

Section 4.5 says the fixer "stops when the checked-out commit isn't the PR's head, when there's no finding marked \"fix\", or when `npm run check` already failed". The code doesn't stop in one case that sentence covers. `stopReason()` in `fix-input-text.ts` goes on when this round has no finding marked "fix" but `round.askable` isn't empty, meaning Joe has replied to an earlier finding that needs attention. The skill's step 2 and the bullet "It reads Joe's replies too" match the code. Only this sentence leaves the case out.

**Why N6:** The doc doesn't match the code on one stop condition. The next bullet in the same section and the skill already describe the askable case, so a builder wouldn't build the wrong thing from this sentence. That makes it N6 and not F6. The claim matches the code, so no D label fits.

Line 207.

**Fix (F6)**

Section 4.5 (line 197) says that when Joe replies "fix it" on a finding that needs attention, "the next fixer fixes it". It says this holds "for a finding from the review of the PR's head too, when the fixer pushed nothing after it and runs again." But section 4.6 says the fix job runs only when the review job's count of findings marked "fix" is above zero. It also says a run starts only on a push ("The loop goes on only because the fixer pushes. No push means no new run"). Nothing in the workflow ever runs the fixer "again" because of Joe's reply. Here is a concrete case. The review of head H marks one F5 "fix". The fixer answers `needs_attention`, with `commit: null`, so nothing is pushed and the loop stops. Joe replies on the thread, "Fix it here." A reply isn't a push, so no run starts. Joe could push a commit to start one. But review 2 won't post the F5 again, since section 4.4 says the reviewer doesn't post a finding again once it needs attention. So review 2 likely marks nothing "fix", and the fix job is skipped. The `askable` path in `fixRound()` and `stopReason()` is never reached in CI, and Joe's request is dropped without a word. #77 builds the fix job from sections 4.6 and 4.7, so it would build this trigger as written.

**Why F6:** The doc contradicts itself. Section 4.5 promises that Joe's "fix it" reply is acted on, and section 4.6's trigger means it never is. A builder of #77 would follow 4.6, and Joe's request would be lost in a normal case: a round where the fixer pushes nothing. No D label fits. The claim matches the doc, the design isn't settled on this, and #77's body doesn't name this work.

Closes #92

## Do

Each agent that writes on a PR gets its own GitHub App, so its comments and commits show under its own name, and code can tell them apart by author. Agreed 2026-10-21 in chat, while working on #76. An app for a future implementer agent is left for later.

2. **Store each app's ID and private key.** For CI, as repo secrets. For local runs, the key file stays on Joe's machine in a folder outside the repo, and `.env` holds the ID and the file's path.
3. **Write a script that makes a token from an app's ID and key,** for local runs. A token lasts an hour. It also gives the bot's noreply address, for a commit's author.

## Do

## Done when

- Tests use saved responses, including Open-Meteo's spent-limit reply.
- A real call for a stay within 7 days returns a forecast.
- A real call for a stay in October 2027 returns seasonal averages, labeled "Typical for this time of year, based on 2016–2025."
- A forecast that leaves out a date returns an error.

Closes #63

## Results

- **Saved responses:** done. Google's Moab, Honolulu, and Leadville forecasts and Open-Meteo's 10 years of Moab data and a January in Leadville were saved from real calls on 2026-10-21. The spent-limit reply is in `src/open-meteo/saved-responses/spent-limit.json`, and tests cover it at the client and through the tool. `npm run check` passes (527 tests).
- **Real call, stay within 7 days:** done. With the Moab trip moved to start on October 23, 2026, `look_up_stay_weather` returned Google's forecast for October 23 to 26, with the stay's two activities.
- **Real call, October 2027:** done. The Moab stay on October 10 to 13, 2027 returned seasonal averages from Open-Meteo, labeled "Typical for this time of year, based on 2016–2025."
- **Forecast that leaves out a date:** done. The tool returns an error that names the missing date, and doesn't call Open-Meteo. Tested at the client and through the tool.

## Decisions

- **Google's first forecast day isn't always today** (the issue's open question, settled in chat on 2026-10-21). Before 7 a.m. local time, it's yesterday. The client asks for 10 days and picks each date by its `displayDate`. Written into Google design section 3.
- **The tool and the saved label use one rule.** `StaysService.weatherFor()` decides forecast or seasonal averages. `stay_weather` picks its source by it, and `setWeatherText()` labels the text by it, so they can't disagree.
- **The spent-limit saved response is the Open-Meteo design's example** (section 2.4), not one captured live. Capturing one would take hundreds of calls in a minute. A real Open-Meteo error reply (a bad request, HTTP 400) has the same `error` and `reason` shape. The client checks the body for `error` whatever the status.
- **A rain day is 0.039 in or more,** not 0.04. Open-Meteo gives 1 mm as 0.039 in, so 0.04 would miss exactly 1 mm. A snow day is 0.39 in (1 cm). The Open-Meteo design 2.3 says "0.04 in (1 mm)". I left the doc alone, since the intent is 1 mm.
- **A wrong-kind ID gets its own error,** such as "day_… is a day ID, not a stay ID." (tool design section 4). It's in `src/tools/id-kind.ts`, for later tools to reuse.
- **An activity whose time isn't known yet** shows "time not known yet". That happens when its day's leg isn't routed.

## Set aside

- The weather server isn't connected to an agent yet. #64 does that, with the weather worker.

## Config changes

- None.

<!-- fix-loop: summary -->

## Fix loop: deferred, and needs attention

Code updates this comment after each fix round. Resolve a finding's thread once it's handled. A finding in a review body has no thread, so tick its box instead.

**Deferred**

- [ ] Open-Meteo design 2.3 calls the share of days with at least 0.04 in of `precipitation_sum` the "Cha… (`design/data-sources/open-meteo.md:47`): [finding](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/96#pullrequestreview-5615011373), [reply](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/96#issuecomment-6342009175), #77 <!-- fix-loop: review-5615011373-1 -->

**Needs attention**

None.

**Deferred:** #77.

> On `design/data-sources/open-meteo.md:47`, in [the review](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/96#pullrequestreview-5615011373):
>
> Open-Meteo design 2.3 calls the share of days with at least 0.04 in of `precipitation_sum` the "Chance of rain". The tool follows it, and `averagesLines` in `src/tools/weather-tools.ts` (line 117) prints it as "Days with rain". But `precipitation_sum` includes snowfall as its water equivalent, so every snow day also counts as a rain day. Example: for a stay in Leadville, CO in January, nearly all precipitation falls as snow. The reply would then say something like "Days with rain: 30%. Days with snow: 28%." The weather worker, believing it, would plan rain gear and warn about rain on days that only snow. This PR already fixed the same rain-versus-snow mix-up on the Google forecast side. The fix is to name this share as precipitation (rain or snow), both in design 2.3 and in the tool's line, such as "Days with rain or snow".

Hand check of the posting code: written by hand. Deferred to show the summary's checkbox.

<!-- fix-loop: review-5615011373-1 -->

Hand check done for #76 step 3: fix-input.ts printed both rounds' input, check-fix.ts refused a bad answer, and post-fix.ts pushed as the fixer, replied with markers on a thread and on a review-body finding, resolved the fixed thread, and kept the summary.

**Fix (F3)**

`forecastLines` always calls Google's `daytimeForecast.precipitation.probability.percent` a "% chance of rain". The schema in `weather-forecast.schema.ts` (line 41) drops `probability.type`. The saved responses all have `type: "RAIN"`, but Google's precipitation type can also be `SNOW`, `RAIN_AND_SNOW`, and so on. Example: for a stay in a Colorado mountain town in December, Google could send `{type: "SNOW", percent: 60}`. The tool would then reply "Light snow. 60% chance of rain", and the weather worker could give rain-gear advice instead of snow-gear advice. To check: call `forecast/days:lookup` for a place where snow is forecast, such as Leadville, CO or a town in Alaska in winter, and look at `daytimeForecast.precipitation.probability.type`. If it can be anything other than RAIN, the reply should name the type, or say "precipitation".

**Why F3:** Whether the tool's reply is false depends on what Google sends for a snowy day, and nothing in the repo shows that. If Google does send SNOW, the false reply happens on a normal winter trip and is F3. If not, the finding goes away.

**Needs attention.**

Hand check of the posting code: this answer was written by hand, not by the fixer. Whether Google sends SNOW can't be settled from the repo, so Joe has to check it.
Hand check: a reply as Joe. Fix it anyway.

**Fixed** in ecd357295ce90198528359e03a89a4363ccac866.

Hand check of the posting code: written by hand. Nothing was really fixed.

**Note (NF2)**

`seasonalAverages` shifts each year's window from the stay's first year. So when a stay's window crosses New Year, the last year's request ends in the current year. Example: on January 3, 2027, a stay on December 27 to 30, 2027 gives a 2026 request for 2026-12-20 to 2027-01-06. That end date is after today, and the archive doesn't have the last few days yet. Open-Meteo would leave those days empty or refuse the request. A refusal makes the tool return "Seasonal averages are unavailable right now" every time until about mid-January. The data used also falls partly outside the "2016–2025" range the label names.

**Why NF2:** It needs a late-December stay planned in the first week or so of January, which isn't normal use, so it's NF2, not F2. The claim holds as the code is written, so it isn't D1.

**Note (N6)**

Google design section 3 still says "The tool checks the dates before calling" about the 10-day limit. The client now always asks for exactly `FORECAST_DAYS_ASKED` = 10 days and does no such check. It never asks for more than 10, so the sentence describes a check that doesn't exist.

**Why N6:** The doc doesn't match the code, but the same section says to ask for 10 days. No builder would add a wrong check because of it, so it's N6, not F6.

These findings are on files this PR doesn't change, so they can't be inline comments.

### `design/data-sources/open-meteo.md:47`

**Fix (F6)**

Open-Meteo design 2.3 calls the share of days with at least 0.04 in of `precipitation_sum` the "Chance of rain". The tool follows it, and `averagesLines` in `src/tools/weather-tools.ts` (line 117) prints it as "Days with rain". But `precipitation_sum` includes snowfall as its water equivalent, so every snow day also counts as a rain day. Example: for a stay in Leadville, CO in January, nearly all precipitation falls as snow. The reply would then say something like "Days with rain: 30%. Days with snow: 28%." The weather worker, believing it, would plan rain gear and warn about rain on days that only snow. This PR already fixed the same rain-versus-snow mix-up on the Google forecast side. The fix is to name this share as precipitation (rain or snow), both in design 2.3 and in the tool's line, such as "Days with rain or snow".

**Why F6:** The code does what the design says, but the design's choice gives the agent false text on a normal winter mountain trip, so the rubric makes it F6, not D2. It isn't D1, since `precipitation_sum` counts snowfall as written.

## Task

## Decisions

Phase 13a is settled in the PR, so each of these is a proposal. Approving the PR agrees to them.

1. **Each trip brief item goes by its name in the domain model**, such as `tripLengthInDays` and `mealPreferencesText`. The rule errors already name items that way ("The trip brief's focus can't be empty"), so the error matches the input. Written into tool design section 2.1.
2. **The usual start time is a clock time, in and out**, such as "7:30 a.m.". Tool design section 2.1 already says tool times are clock times. "07:30" is refused by the schema. Written into tool design section 2.1.
3. **`read_trip_brief` returns one line per item, as `name: value`**, with "not set" for an empty item. This is also in tool design section 2.1.
4. **Every input of `update_trip_brief` is optional.** That goes against the "no optional inputs" principle, but tool design section 2.1 says items not given are left alone, so it follows the design. An update with no items is refused.
5. **A refused write starts with "Nothing was saved."**, then the rule's message. Technical spec 5.2 tells the coordinator a refused update saved nothing, so the error says it in words. The busy-trip error already says so, and is passed on as it is.
6. **Only errors the agent can act on become a readable reply:** a broken rule, a busy trip, or a failed Google call. Any other error, such as a lost database connection, is thrown, and the Agent SDK reports it as a failed call. That keeps bugs from looking like normal refusals.
7. **The reply after a write is "Saved the trip brief." plus the check results.** Each result is one line, such as "- New warning: ...", "- Already known warning, approved: ...", or "- Gone: ...". When nothing is new or gone, it says "No new or gone check results." The check-results code is shared, so phase 22's writes can use it. Phase 22 adds the leg changes to the reply, as its "Do" already says.
8. **The server sets `alwaysLoad: true`.** Otherwise Claude Code can hide MCP tools behind a tool search when an agent has many tools. The coordinator will have 24.
9. **The code is in `src/tools/`.** `trip-access.ts` makes the app's `TripWriter`, with a `RoutesClient` from `env.googleMapsServerKey` and the global `fetch`, and the `TripReader`. Nothing calls it yet. Phase 13c's dev script will.

## Set aside

Nothing.

## Config changes that seem needed

None.

## Note on the schema

A schema error, such as a usual start time of "07:30", comes back as the Agent SDK's own MCP validation error. It includes our message, but wrapped in JSON (see the example in the description). It's readable, so I left it.

<!-- fix-loop: summary -->

## Fix loop: deferred, and needs attention

Code updates this comment after each fix round. Resolve a finding's thread once it's handled. A finding in a review body has no thread, so tick its box instead.

**Deferred**

None.

**Needs attention**

None.

**Replay of #44 round 1, for #76 step 5.** The branches are #44's base, `8fe14f4`, and the commit round 1's review saw, `8d3d3a1`. The description is #44's as it was when that review ran. The findings are #44 round 1's, with the labels the labeling rounds settled on (#75).

| | The fixer | By hand, in `9a68517` |
|---|---|---|
| F2: a misnamed item is dropped | Fixed in `883816d`: `update_trip_brief` takes a strict schema, so the call is refused and the error names the key. Test through an MCP client in `trip-server.test.ts`. | Fixed the same way, with a shared `strictTool()` helper in a new file, `src/tools/strict-tool.ts`. |
| The two N3 notes, on the limit errors and the schema's lower bound | Left alone, as the fix loop says | Changed too |
| Turns, time, cost | 63 turns, 5.5 minutes, $1.77 at API prices | |

The fixer ran with `claude -p`, Opus 5.5 at `high`, in a fresh config folder. Its commit had Claude Code's "Co-Authored-By" line, which was taken out before the push.

**Fix (F2)**

A misnamed item is silently dropped, and the reply still says "Saved the trip brief." The SDK builds a plain `z.object` from this shape, which strips unknown keys, and the JSON Schema in the PR has no `additionalProperties: false`. Example: an update with `focus: "Utah"` and `tripLength: 5` saves only the focus, then replies "Saved the trip brief." The model believes the length was saved too. If every key is misnamed, the reply is "Give at least one trip brief item to change.", which does not say why. Tool design section 4 says "the tool never guesses". Refuse unknown keys, for example with a strict object schema if `tool()` accepts one, so the error names the key.

**Why F2:** A misnamed input, such as `tripLength` for `tripLengthInDays`, is a slip a model makes in normal use. The update then saves part of what was asked and says it saved the brief, which is wrong behavior. No design doc speaks to unknown keys, so it isn't D2, and the claim holds, so it isn't D1.

**Fixed** in 883816db1173dcf5d84d545a950f0c330686ec67.

Confirmed through an MCP client connected to the real trip server: `{ focus: "Utah", tripLength: 5 }` saved only the focus and replied "Saved the trip brief." `updateTripBriefTool()` now hands the server `UPDATE_TRIP_BRIEF_SCHEMA`, a `z.strictObject` of the item shape, instead of building the tool with `tool()`. `tool()` takes only a raw shape, and the server turns a shape into a plain object, which drops unknown keys. Now the server refuses the call before the handler runs, and the error names the key (`Unrecognized key: "tripLength"`). The JSON Schema in `tools/list` now has `additionalProperties: false`, and every item's description is still there. The handler parses its args again with the same schema to get the item types, since `createSdkMcpServer` types a hand-built tool's args as `Record<string, unknown>`. The test is "refuses an item name it doesn't know, names it, and saves nothing" in `src/tools/trip-server.test.ts`. It calls `update_trip_brief` through an MCP client from `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, a peer dependency of the Agent SDK, so no package was added. It failed before the fix with `isError` undefined. The tool tests in `trip-brief-tools.test.ts` now parse with `UPDATE_TRIP_BRIEF_SCHEMA`, so they check the same schema the server uses.

**Note (N3)**

This description, and the new design line ("an error that names an item matches the input"), say the error names the item that was refused. The two limit errors do not: `TripBriefService` says "A trip is at most 14 days long..." and "Comfortable driving is at most 12 hours a day...", not `tripLengthInDays` or `comfortableDrivingInHours`. When several items are given, the model has to guess which input the error is about. Either name the item in those messages, or change the description to match.

**Why N3:** The two limit errors use plain words, not the input names, but each still points to one item and gives the limit. An agent that believes the description wouldn't do the wrong thing, so it's N3, not F3.

**Note (N4)**

`touchedIds` holds only the itinerary, and `result.legChanges` is never read. Tool design 2.1 says the reply to a write gives the new drive time of each re-routed leg, and counts "the days in the leg changes" as touched. A brief change re-routes nothing today, so nothing is wrong yet. But each writing tool will have to repeat this, and the next one could easily forget the leg days. A shared reply builder that takes the whole `WriteResult` and adds the leg days itself would cover every tool.

**Why N4:** A trip brief change re-routes no legs, so nothing is wrong in today's replies. The finding is advice about writing tools that don't exist yet, so it's N4.

**Note (N3)**

Without a `.min(1)`, `z.int()` puts `"minimum": -9007199254740991, "maximum": 9007199254740991` in the JSON Schema the model sees (shown in the PR). That says nothing true about a trip length, and costs tokens on every turn, since the tool is always loaded. `.min(1)`, or `.positive()`, would give the real lower bound. The domain rule still runs.

**Why N3:** The safe-integer bounds are true of the schema, and the field's description already says "A whole number, at least 1." The domain rule refuses anything below 1 with a clear error. The schema text is noisy, not false, so it's N3, not F3.

**Note (N2)**

`tripAccessFor` has no caller and no test. Phase 13a says to give `update_trip_brief` a `TripWriter` whose `routeFinder` is a `RoutesClient` made from `env.googleMapsServerKey` and the global `fetch`. Only this function does that, and nothing runs it, so a wrong argument (for example, the wrong key) would go unnoticed until phase 13c. A small test that builds it from a fake pool and env, or wiring it in now, would cover it.

**Why N2:** The wiring in `tripAccessFor` matches the env schema, the `RoutesClient` options, and phase 13a's Do. Phase 13a's Done when doesn't ask for a test of it. A missing test for working code is N2.

**Note (N1)**

`MINUTES_IN_HOUR` and `NOON_HOUR` are defined again here, the same as in `src/domain/check-text.ts`. The 12-hour mapping is now split: `clockText` writes it in `check-text.ts`, and `timeOfDayFromClockText` reads it here. `clockTextOf` also works out minutes since midnight by hand, which `TimeOfDay` already does privately (`#minutesSinceMidnight`). Keeping the parser next to `clockText` would keep both directions of the a.m./p.m. rule in one file.

**Why N1:** Both directions of the a.m./p.m. rule are correct. The finding is about repeated constants and where the parser lives, so it's N1.
