**The deferral leans on later work.** #55 was opened on 2026-10-19, a day after this round's review. Its item was written after the hand fix, since it says to take out `touchedBy()`. When the round ran, no open issue planned this work. The replay hands the fixer today's issues.

**Fix (F6)**

This comment, and `touchedIds` holding only the itinerary, assume a brief change touches no day. Two items do touch every day. `usualStartTime` is the start time of every day without its own (`Calendar.startTimeOf`, calendar.ts:145), and `comfortableDrivingInHours` is the limit in every `dailyDriving` warning. A day result that is still there after the change is "already known", so it is filtered out, even when its text changed. Example: Day 2 has "needs about 7 h of driving. Comfortable driving is 6 hours a day." The user lowers it to 5. The warning is still there, now saying 5 hours, but the reply is "No new or gone check results.", so the coordinator keeps the old text. The same goes for a late or opening-hours warning whose times moved with a new usual start time. Count the days that use the changed item as touched (for `usualStartTime`, the days with no start time of their own; for `comfortableDrivingInHours`, every day), or check that tool design 2.1 means to leave them out.

**Why F6:** Lowering `comfortableDrivingInHours` is normal use. The day's driving warning changes its text, but the reply leaves it out as already known, so the coordinator keeps talking about the old limit. A design choice that causes wrong behavior in normal use is F6, not D2.

**Deferred:** #55.

The claim holds. A brief change counts only the itinerary as touched, so a day's driving warning whose text now gives the new comfortableDrivingInHours stays out of the reply as already known. The same goes for a late or opening-hours warning whose times moved with a new usualStartTime. The PR's code follows technical spec section 8 as written. That section says a change that only moves worked-out times touches only the trip, and it accepts that a driving warning whose text changes stays already known for the MVP. Open issue #55 ("Build the skeleton") already plans the general fix in its "Do" list. FeasibilityChecker.compare() will mark a known result whose text changed as "changed", and every write's reply will list changed results anywhere in the trip. That covers both items here, and every other write tool, without a special case in updateTripBriefTool(). Nothing breaks in normal use while it waits. Technical spec 5.2 tells the coordinator to stay quiet about already-known results either way. The coordinator set the new value itself, and a read_itinerary shows each result's current text. So I changed no code, and the touchedIds comment in updateTripBriefTool() stays. #55 already names this work, so I'd add only two lines to its item. One would say that a new usualStartTime moves the times in late and opening-hours warnings too, so those need the "changed" mark just like the driving-hours example. The other would point to PR #98 finding comment-4350236067. Its step to take out touchedBy() in src/tools/trip-brief-tools.ts doesn't apply to this PR, since this PR doesn't add that function.

**Note (NF3)**

The description says the read "Returns every item, one per line". The text items are the words of the user, and nothing stops them from holding a line break. Example: `mustSeesText` given as "Delicate Arch at sunset", a line break, then "mealPreferencesText: none" is saved as given. The read then shows a line that looks like a second `mealPreferencesText` item, and the model can read the wrong value. Show line breaks in a value some other way, such as quoted text, or refuse them in the schema.

**Why NF3:** A line break in a text item that also looks like `name: value` isn't something a user types in normal use. When it happens, the read shows an item that isn't there, which is false text, so it's NF3. No design doc says how values are formatted, so it isn't D2.

**Note (N1)**

The repo-root CLAUDE.md says "Check outside data with Zod where it enters the program (DEVELOPMENT.md section 4)". That section lists "Tool inputs from the agents" as outside data, and says "Schemas for outside data go in files named `*.schema.ts`." `UPDATE_TRIP_BRIEF_INPUT` is the tool input from the agent, but it is in `trip-brief-tools.ts`. Moving it to a file such as `src/tools/trip-brief-tools.schema.ts` would follow the rule, and later tools would follow it too.

**Why N1:** The schema still checks the tool input with Zod where it enters, so the program behaves correctly. Which file it lives in is a structure cleanup, so it's N1.

**Note (N1)**

`strictTool()` builds the definition but takes no annotations, so `readTripBriefTool` spreads its result and patches `annotations` on afterwards. Every later read tool, such as `read_itinerary` and the memory reads, will have to repeat this, and the spread makes it easy to drop. An optional `annotations` argument to `strictTool()`, which `StrictToolDefinition` already has a field for, would make this one call.

**Why N1:** The result is correct today, with `readOnlyHint` added after the spread. Taking annotations in `strictTool()` would save repeating that in later read tools. That's duplication and structure, so it's N1.

**Note (N2)**

The test checks `z.toJSONSchema` on the Zod schema itself, not the tool list the server gives. `strict-tool.ts` exists because the SDK can change the schema on the way through, by wrapping a plain shape in an object that drops unknown keys. This test would still pass if `createTripServer` went back to `tool()` with a shape, or if an SDK update stripped the strictness. A misnamed item would then vanish again, with "Saved the trip brief." Checking the input schema of the tools `createTripServer` hands the SDK, or making a call with an unknown key through the server, would catch that.

**Why N2:** The test catches a break in what it checks: the schema stops being strict, or stops converting. So it isn't a wrong test. The path from the server through the SDK has no test, and a missing test is N2.

## Decisions

Phase 13a is settled in the PR, so each of these is a proposal. Approving the PR agrees to them.

1. **Each trip brief item goes by its name in the domain model**, such as `tripLengthInDays` and `mealPreferencesText`. The rule errors already name items that way ("The trip brief's focus can't be empty"), so the error matches the input. Written into tool design section 2.1.
2. **The usual start time is a clock time, in and out**, such as "7:30 a.m.". Tool design section 2.1 already says tool times are clock times. "07:30" is refused by the schema. Written into tool design section 2.1.

The repo-root CLAUDE.md says "Check outside data with Zod where it enters the program (DEVELOPMENT.md section 4)". That section lists "Tool inputs from the agents" as outside data, and says "Schemas for outside data go in files named `*.schema.ts`." `UPDATE_TRIP_BRIEF_INPUT` is the tool input from the agent, but it is in `trip-brief-tools.ts`. Moving it to a file such as `src/tools/trip-brief-tools.schema.ts` would follow the rule, and later tools would follow it too.

**Why N1:** The schema still checks the tool input with Zod where it enters, so the program behaves correctly. Which file it lives in is a structure cleanup, so it's N1.

**Note (N1)**

`strictTool()` builds the definition but takes no annotations, so `readTripBriefTool` spreads its result and patches `annotations` on afterwards. Every later read tool, such as `read_itinerary` and the memory reads, will have to repeat this, and the spread makes it easy to drop. An optional `annotations` argument to `strictTool()`, which `StrictToolDefinition` already has a field for, would make this one call.

**Why N1:** The result is correct today, with `readOnlyHint` added after the spread. Taking annotations in `strictTool()` would save repeating that in later read tools. That's duplication and structure, so it's N1.

**Note (N2)**

The test checks `z.toJSONSchema` on the Zod schema itself, not the tool list the server gives. `strict-tool.ts` exists because the SDK can change the schema on the way through, by wrapping a plain shape in an object that drops unknown keys. This test would still pass if `createTripServer` went back to `tool()` with a shape, or if an SDK update stripped the strictness. A misnamed item would then vanish again, with "Saved the trip brief." Checking the input schema of the tools `createTripServer` hands the SDK, or making a call with an unknown key through the server, would catch that.

**Why N2:** The test catches a break in what it checks: the schema stops being strict, or stops converting. So it isn't a wrong test. The path from the server through the SDK has no test, and a missing test is N2.

nodes.body:
## Decisions

Phase 13a is settled in the PR, so each of these is a proposal. Approving the PR agrees to them.

1. **Each trip brief item goes by its name in the domain model**, such as `tripLengthInDays` and `mealPreferencesText`. The rule errors already name items that way ("The trip brief's focus can't be empty"), so the error matches the input. Written into tool design section 2.1.
2. **The usual start time is a clock time, in and out**, such as "7:30 a.m.". Tool design section 2.1 already says tool times are clock times. "07:30" is refused by the schema. Written into tool design section 2.1.
3. **`read_trip_brief` returns one line per item, as `name: value`**, with "not set" for an empty item. This is also in tool design section 2.1.
4. **Every input of `update_trip_brief` is optional.** That goes against the "no optional inputs" principle, but tool design section 2.1 says items not given are left alone, so it follows the design. An update with no items is refused.
5. **A refused write starts with "Nothing was saved."**, then the rule's message. Technical spec 5.2 tells the coordinator a refused update saved nothing, so the error says it in words. The busy-trip error already says so, and is passed on as it is.
6. **Only errors the agent can act on become a readable reply:** a broken rule, a busy trip, or a failed Google call. Any other error, such as a lost database connection, is thrown, and the Agent SDK reports it as a failed call. That keeps bugs from looking like normal refusals.
7. **The reply after a write is "Saved the trip brief." plus the check results.** Each result is one line, such as "- New warning: ...", "- Already known warning, approved: ...", or "- Gone: ...". When nothing is new or gone, it says "No new or gone check results." The check-results code is shared, so phase 22's writes can use it. Phase 22 adds the leg changes to the reply, as its "Do" already says.
8. **The server sets `alwaysLoad: true`.** Otherwise Claude Code can hide MCP tools behind a tool search when an agent has many tools. The coordinator will have 24.
9. **The code is in `src/tools/`.** `trip-access.ts` makes the app's `TripWriter`, with a `RoutesClient` from `env.googleMapsServerKey` and the global `fetch`, and the `TripReader`. Nothing calls it yet. Phase 13c's dev script will.

## Set aside

Nothing.

## Config changes that seem needed

None.

## Note on the schema

A schema error, such as a usual start time of "07:30", comes back as the Agent SDK's own MCP validation error. It includes our message, but wrapped in JSON (see the example in the description). It's readable, so I left it.

**Note (N3 - Text a road trip agent reads is unclear, or says something twice, or is an error message with the wrong reason for a failure)**

The "may be too early" mark repeats what the result text already says. `markedTooEarly()` in `stop-checks.ts` appends "An earlier stop on this day has no place picked yet, so this time may be too early." to the text of every result with `hasUnselectedStopBefore`. So a real reply line reads "- New warning, may be too early: Milt’s closes at 12:30 p.m. ... An earlier stop on this day has no place picked yet, so this time may be too early." The test passes only because its fake text leaves that sentence out. Either drop the mark here, or stop appending the sentence in the domain.

**Why N3:** The claim holds: the coordinator reads the same caveat twice. Nothing it says is false, so it isn't F3. Text an agent reads that says something twice is N3.

**Note (N1 - Cleaner code)**

This branch can never run. The write above always passes `"coordinator"`, and `TripWriter` gives a null `checkComparison` only for a `"worker"` write. If it did run, the reply would say only "Saved the trip brief." with no check results, which tool design 2.1 does not allow for a coordinator write. Throwing on null, or a writer method for coordinator writes whose result has a non-null comparison, would remove the dead path for every coordinator tool that follows.

**Why N1:** `update_trip_brief` always writes as the coordinator, so the null branch can never run, and nothing goes wrong. Code that can never run is N1.

**Note (NF2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, but not in normal use)**

An earlier comment on this call (now outdated) pointed out that `result.legChanges` is never read. The change since did not fix it: the touched set still leaves out the days in the leg changes, and the reply gives no re-routed leg times. Tool design 2.1 counts "the days in the leg changes" as touched for every write. A brief change re-routes nothing today, but `updateLegs()` runs on every write, so a leg it routes here would have the known results of its days dropped from the reply.

**Why NF2:** A brief write re-routes nothing, since legs depend only on places, stops, and waypoints. The missing results would show up only if stored legs were already out of date, which isn't normal use, so it's NF2.

**Note (N1 - Cleaner code)**

`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` is needed at run time, not only by the tests: `createSdkMcpServer` in `trip-server.ts` builds an MCP server from it, and the Agent SDK lists it as a peer dependency. Listing it under `devDependencies` says production can do without it. It still installs under `npm ci --omit=dev` in `docker/app.Dockerfile` only because the lockfile reaches it through the peer edge of the Agent SDK. If that edge changes, the production image loses it. It belongs in `dependencies`, next to `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`.

**Why N1:** The lockfile entry has no dev flag, so the production install still gets the package, and production works today. A break would need a later Agent SDK upgrade. Putting the dependency in the right list is N1.

body:
## Do

- Add the Google Weather client, the Open-Meteo client, and `stay_weather`, which picks the source from the stay's dates.

## Done when

- Tests use saved responses, including Open-Meteo's spent-limit reply.
- A real call for a stay within 7 days returns a forecast.
- A real call for a stay in October 2027 returns seasonal averages, labeled "Typical for this time of year, based on 2016–2025."
- A forecast that leaves out a date returns an error.

Closes #63

## Results

- **Saved responses:** done. Google's Moab and Honolulu forecasts and Open-Meteo's 10 years of Moab data were saved from real calls on 2026-10-21. The spent-limit reply is in `src/open-meteo/saved-responses/spent-limit.json`, and tests cover it at the client and through the tool. `npm run check` passes (523 tests).
- **Real call, stay within 7 days:** done. With the Moab trip moved to start on October 23, 2026, `stay_weather` returned Google's forecast for October 23 to 26, with the stay's two activities.
- **Real call, October 2027:** done. The Moab stay on October 10 to 13, 2027 returned seasonal averages from Open-Meteo, labeled "Typical for this time of year, based on 2016–2025."
- **Forecast that leaves out a date:** done. The tool returns an error that names the missing date, and doesn't call Open-Meteo. Tested at the client and through the tool.

Checked by hand: the two real calls above, run through the tool with the real clients against the Moab example trip.

nodes.body:
## Decisions

- **Google's first forecast day isn't always today** (the issue's open question, settled in chat on 2026-10-21). Before 7 a.m. local time, it's yesterday. The client asks for 10 days and picks each date by its `displayDate`. Written into Google design section 3.
- **The tool and the saved label use one rule.** `StaysService.weatherFor()` decides forecast or seasonal averages. `stay_weather` picks its source by it, and `setWeatherText()` labels the text by it, so they can't disagree.
- **The spent-limit saved response is the Open-Meteo design's example** (section 2.4), not one captured live. Capturing one would take hundreds of calls in a minute. A real Open-Meteo error reply (a bad request, HTTP 400) has the same `error` and `reason` shape. The client checks the body for `error` whatever the status.
- **A rain day is 0.039 in or more,** not 0.04. Open-Meteo gives 1 mm as 0.039 in, so 0.04 would miss exactly 1 mm. A snow day is 0.39 in (1 cm). The Open-Meteo design 2.3 says "0.04 in (1 mm)". I left the doc alone, since the intent is 1 mm.
- **A wrong-kind ID gets its own error,** such as "day_… is a day ID, not a stay ID." (tool design section 4). It's in `src/tools/id-kind.ts`, for later tools to reuse.
- **An activity whose time isn't known yet** shows "time not known yet". That happens when its day's leg isn't routed.

## Set aside

- The weather server isn't connected to an agent yet. #64 does that, with the weather worker.

## Config changes

- None.

<!-- fix-loop: summary -->

## Fix loop: deferred, and needs attention

Code updates this comment after each fix round. Resolve a finding's thread once it's handled. A finding in a review body has no thread, so tick its box instead.

**Deferred**

None.

**Needs attention**

None.

**Replay of #90 round 1, for #76 step 5.** The branches are #90's base, `5a00613`, and the commit round 1's review saw, `829efb1`. The description is #90's original. Only the first decisions comment is copied, since the others came after this review ran. The findings are the reviewer's, as it returned them, with the V1 relabeled F3 after the check (code review design 4.2).

| | The fixer | By hand, in `3c9b58a` |
|---|---|---|
| F3: every chance of precipitation is called rain | Fixed in `ab4a409`: the schema keeps Google's `probability.type`, and the reply names it, with "precipitation" for a type it doesn't know. Google design 3 and the tool design say so. Test through the tool in `weather-tools.test.ts`. | Fixed: saved a real Leadville response with snow, and named the chance from Google's type. Also dropped a stale sentence in Google design 3, and a repeated line in the tool description. |
| The NF2 and N6 notes | Left alone | |
| Turns, time, cost | 38 turns, 2.9 minutes, $0.96 at API prices | |

Of the fixer's seven type names, only RAIN and LIGHT_RAIN are in the repo's saved responses. The rest came from what the model knows. A type it doesn't know is called "precipitation", so a wrong guess gives no false text.

**Fix (F3 - Text a road trip agent reads says something false, in normal use)**

`forecastLines` always calls Google's `daytimeForecast.precipitation.probability.percent` a "% chance of rain". The schema in `weather-forecast.schema.ts` (line 41) drops `probability.type`. The saved responses all have `type: "RAIN"`, but Google's precipitation type can also be `SNOW`, `RAIN_AND_SNOW`, and so on. Example: for a stay in a Colorado mountain town in December, Google could send `{type: "SNOW", percent: 60}`. The tool would then reply "Light snow. 60% chance of rain", and the weather worker could give rain-gear advice instead of snow-gear advice. To check: call `forecast/days:lookup` for a place where snow is forecast, such as Leadville, CO or a town in Alaska in winter, and look at `daytimeForecast.precipitation.probability.type`. If it can be anything other than RAIN, the reply should name the type, or say "precipitation".

**Why F3:** Joe had the check made, and relabeled this F3 from V1. Google can send a precipitation type other than RAIN, such as SNOW. Then on a normal winter trip the tool says "chance of rain" for a chance of snow, and the weather worker acts on that false text.

**Fixed** in ab4a409a6bc9aac519adcbfbd0fe60376c64d2b7.

The forecast schema now keeps Google's `precipitation.probability.type` as any string, so a type the app doesn't know yet still parses. `ForecastDay` carries it as `precipitationType`, or null when Google gives none, and `rainChancePercent` is renamed `precipitationChancePercent`. `forecastLines` names the chance with `precipitationWords()`: RAIN, LIGHT_RAIN, HEAVY_RAIN, SNOW, RAIN_AND_SNOW, SLEET, and FREEZING_RAIN get their own words, and any other type, or none, is called "precipitation". So it never says rain for a chance of snow. Google design section 3 and the `stay_weather` row in the tool design now say this. The test is "names the kind of precipitation Google forecasts, not always rain" in `src/tools/weather-tools.test.ts`. It calls the tool with a forecast whose types are SNOW, RAIN_AND_SNOW, NONE, and an unknown type. It failed before the fix, since every day said "chance of rain".

**Note (NF2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, but not in normal use)**

`seasonalAverages` shifts each year's window from the stay's first year. So when a stay's window crosses New Year, the last year's request ends in the current year. Example: on January 3, 2027, a stay on December 27 to 30, 2027 gives a 2026 request for 2026-12-20 to 2027-01-06. That end date is after today, and the archive doesn't have the last few days yet. Open-Meteo would leave those days empty or refuse the request. A refusal makes the tool return "Seasonal averages are unavailable right now" every time until about mid-January. The data used also falls partly outside the "2016–2025" range the label names.

**Why NF2:** It needs a late-December stay planned in the first week or so of January, which isn't normal use, so it's NF2, not F2. The claim holds as the code is written, so it isn't D1.

**Note (N6 - A design doc is unclear, or doesn't match the code, in a way no builder would act on)**

Google design section 3 still says "The tool checks the dates before calling" about the 10-day limit. The client now always asks for exactly `FORECAST_DAYS_ASKED` = 10 days and does no such check. It never asks for more than 10, so the sentence describes a check that doesn't exist.

**Why N6:** The doc doesn't match the code, but the same section says to ask for 10 days. No builder would add a wrong check because of it, so it's N6, not F6.

title: Replay: #90 round 2, outside-fact rule with a new example

body:
## Task

From #76. This PR does steps 4 to 7. #91 did steps 1 to 3.

### Do

Joe runs the fixer by hand, with `claude -p` on his machine, to see how it works and tune its prompt. It gets tested on two PRs' rounds:

- **PR #44,** the trip server. Its findings came from the stock review, and were labeled with the rubric in #75. Rounds 1 to 3 had findings above the bar. Round 4 had none, so the fixer doesn't run on it.
- **PR #90,** weather data. Its findings came from our reviewer, as it posts them today. Round 1's one check (V1), rain vs snow, was checked and counts as an F3, the way Joe relabels a check (code review design 4.2). Round 2 had one F6. Round 3 had only a note, so the fixer doesn't run on it.

4. **Build each round's inputs.** Each round is replayed from the commit its review saw, not from the fixer's last result. Then each round is tested on its own, and it lines up with what was done by hand. Done when there's a `review.json` for each of these rounds, in the format `src/code-review/review-result.schema.ts` checks:

   | Round | Commit the review saw | Fixed by hand in | Findings from |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | #44 round 1 | `8d3d3a1` | `9a68517` | `scratch/code-review-eval/labeling/items/44r1.json` |
   | #44 round 2 | `9a68517` | `3035d77` | `.../items/44r2.json` |
   | #44 round 3 | `3035d77` | `ae79839` | `.../items/44r3.json` |
   | #90 round 1 | `829efb1` | `3c9b58a` | Run 39631417046's `review-transcript-1` artifact |
   | #90 round 2 | `3c9b58a` | `67338a4` | Run 39653578216's `review-transcript-1` artifact |

   - #44's base is `8fe14f4`. Its items have only the claim and the place, so give each one the label the labeling rounds settled on, from the last round that labeled it (`scratch/code-review-eval/labeling/`, on Joe's machine). Write a `labelReason` for each.
   - #90's artifacts are deleted after 30 days, on about 2026-11-20. Download them first. In round 1, change the V1's label to F3.
   - #90's two `review.json` files are saved in `scratch/code-review-eval/replays/`, on Joe's machine, as `90r1-review.json` and `90r2-review.json`. They're as the reviewer returned them, so round 1's V1 still needs changing to F3.
   - #90's base is `5a00613`, where it branched from `main`.
5. **Replay each round, and compare.** For each round, push a branch at the round's base commit and one at the reviewed commit, named `replay/<pr>-base` and `replay/<pr>-round-<n>`. Open a draft PR from one to the other, with the original PR's description, and copy its decisions comment onto it. Post the round's findings on it with `post-findings.ts`, as the reviewer app (#92). Run the fixer as a subagent in a worktree of that branch. It commits in the worktree, and doesn't write to GitHub. Where it would write into an issue, its reply says what it would write. Then post its answer with the fixer app's token (#92). The skill, the rubric, and the fixer's code in `src/code-review/` aren't in the old commits, so point the subagent at this branch's copies. Run `npm ci` in each worktree, since the packages differ by commit. Done when each round has the fixer's commit and reply on its draft, next to the hand fix.

   How it went on #96, the hand check of step 3, run from the repo root unless it says the worktree:

   ```sh
   git push origin <base>:refs/heads/replay/<pr>-base <reviewed commit>:refs/heads/replay/<pr>-round-<n>
   gh pr create --draft --base replay/<pr>-base --head replay/<pr>-round-<n> ...

     npx tsx src/code-review/post-findings.ts <review.json> <not-posted.md>

All settled 2026-10-22 in chat with Joe, and written into code review design.

Closes #93

## Do

1. **Build the reviewer's list of earlier findings,** in `src/code-review/review-input.ts`, with the code #76 adds to read the threads and their markers. It reads a marker from the fixer's app or from `nimbusscale`, and no one else. Each finding gives its text, its place, and only what the marker means for the review:
   - **Fixed:** check whether the fix worked, and post it again if it didn't.
   - **Deferred:** drop it. The list gives the issue number, since that's scope.
   - **Not fixed, or needs attention:** drop it. The list doesn't say which, or why.
   - **No reply yet,** such as a note: as today, don't post it again unless its lines changed and the problem is still there.
2. **Change the `review-pr` skill to read that list,** in place of its `gh api` calls for the comments and reviews. Change the "Code review" workflow to match: take `gh api` off the reviewer's allowed list, lower the job's `pull-requests` permission to `read`, and have the posting step post as the reviewer app, `nimbusscale-review-pr`, with the app's token from #92 (code review design 4.6). Today it posts as `github-actions[bot]`. Moved from #92 on 2026-10-22. Take out the skill's two mentions of a "Set aside" list in the description, which #76 dropped.
3. **Write it into code review design 2 and 4.3, and DEVELOPMENT.md section 7.** Section 7 says not to reply on a finding's thread, since the next review would read the reply. That rule goes once the reviewer no longer reads the threads. In its place: a finding handled by hand gets a reply on its thread from Joe's account, starting with the marker. PR #108 already wrote the decisions in, so check that the code matches them, and fix the docs where the code shows they're wrong.
4. **Run the fixer by hand on this PR, as the fix loop will.** This is #77's first step too. After each CI review that marks a finding "fix", run the `fix-pr` skill as a subagent, then post its answer with `post-fix.ts`, as the fixer's app (`app-token.ts fixer`, code review design 4.6). #76's replays did the same, with `scratch/code-review-eval/replays/run-fixer.sh` on Joe's machine. The fixer's push starts the next review. Do up to three fix rounds. Record each round in code review design section 5. Check which files each review read, and add it to #87.

## Done when

- A review of a PR whose threads have fixer replies reads the list, and its transcript shows it read no reply.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Results

Reviews 2 to 6 of this PR ran `review-input.ts`, with fixer replies on the threads. None of the replies' text is in their transcripts, and none ran a command that reads comments. They didn't post a handled finding again.

## Decisions

- **The list calls a "not fixed" or "needs attention" finding "Handled. Don't post it again."** It doesn't say which, as #93 asks. A "Fixed" finding gives the commit, and a deferred one gives the issue. Written in code review design 4.3 already, by #108.
- **The list goes by the last marker on the thread.** So a finding that needed attention, and was fixed later, shows as "Fixed", and the review checks the fix.
- **The skill also tells the reviewer not to run `fix-input.ts`, or read comments with `node` or another script.** `node` stays on its list, so the prompt and the transcript are the guard here, as code review design section 2 says.
- **Code ignores a reply from anyone but the fixer's app and `nimbusscale`,** in what the fixer reads and in when a finding counts as asked for. It drops those replies where it reads the threads, in `fix-round.ts`, so `fix-input.ts`, `post-fix.ts`, and the list all see the same replies. Written into code review design 4.5.
- **Only Joe's reply without a marker asks the fixer for a fix.** A reply with a marker means Joe handled the finding. Fixed in round 3, eec3b5c.
- **The reviewer runs the repo's TypeScript with `node --import tsx`,** since `npx tsx` fails in the sandbox. Joe also took `Bash(npx tsx:*)` off its allowed tools. Code review design 2 and 4.1.
- **The skill's step 1 names `DEVELOPMENT.md` and `design/README.md`,** and says to read them in full with the Read tool, since no review before had. Agreed with Joe in chat. Code review design 4.1.
- **The fixer doesn't get to edit skill files.** Round 1's finding needed attention for that reason, and Claude Code fixed it by hand and replied from Joe's account. Agreed with Joe in chat, and written into #77's open questions for code review design 3.6.
- **The posting step makes the reviewer's token with `actions/create-github-app-token@v3`,** limited to `pull-requests: write`. It takes `app-id`, which v3 marks as deprecated in favor of `client-id`. It still works, and the repo has the app ID as a variable.
- **Code reads findings only from the reviewer's app,** so findings `github-actions[bot]` posted before this PR aren't on the list. No other PR was open.
- **The fix rounds ran with the fixer's app, by hand,** with a runner based on #76's replays, plus deny rules for the config files. It's `scratch/code-review-eval/fix-loop-93/run-round.sh` on Joe's machine.

## Set aside

- **Review 6's F6,** that a "Fixed" marker makes every later review check the fix again: deferred to #77's open questions, on Joe's call.
- **For the fix job:** `fix-pr` still runs `npx tsx`, and ESLint fails on a throwaway `.js` file the fixer leaves in `scratch/`. Both are in #77's open questions.
- **Whether the first review finds what later rounds find:** #110, with the ideas from chat.
- **Which files each review read:** on #87, with the step 1 change.

<!-- fix-loop: summary -->

## Fix loop: deferred, and needs attention

Code updates this comment after each fix round. Resolve a finding's thread once it's handled. A finding in a review body has no thread, so tick its box instead.

**Deferred**

None.

**Needs attention**

- Step 2 tells the reviewer to run `npx tsx src/code-review/review-input.ts $ARGUMENTS`, but `npx tsx`… (`.claude/skills/review-pr/SKILL.md:32`): [finding](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/109#discussion_r4352232124), [reply](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/109#discussion_r4352279850)

**Fix (F2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, in normal use)**

Step 2 tells the reviewer to run `npx tsx src/code-review/review-input.ts $ARGUMENTS`, but `npx tsx <file>` always fails inside the CI reviewer's sandbox. The tsx CLI opens an IPC socket in the temp dir, at /tmp/claude-1001/tsx-1001/<n>.pipe, and the sandbox refuses the bind with `listen EPERM: operation not permitted`. This review of #109 hit it. `npx tsx src/code-review/review-input.ts 109` and `npx tsx src/code-review/print-findings-schema.ts` both crashed with that error before running any code. `node --import tsx src/code-review/review-input.ts 109` worked. So on every CI review, the one command meant to give the reviewer its earlier findings fails. Whether the reviewer recovers depends on it guessing the `node --import tsx` form. Otherwise it reviews with no list, and posts again findings that were fixed, deferred, or handled. That is the outcome #93 was opened to stop, now that `gh api` is gone as a fallback. Design section 4.3 (design/code-review.md:175) names the same command. A fix is to use `node --import tsx src/code-review/review-input.ts $ARGUMENTS` in the skill and the design doc. Step 6's advice to run TypeScript with `npx tsx <file>` has the same problem.

**Why F2:** Every CI review runs this step, so the reviewer goes wrong in normal use. That makes it F2. It isn't F1, because the PR builds the list and points the skill at it as the task asks. The command is what fails at run time.

**Needs attention.**

The claim holds, and F2 fits. The tsx CLI calls `listen` on a socket at `<tmpdir>/tsx-<uid>/<pid>.pipe` in `createIpcServer`, and a failed listen rejects, so the command dies before running the script. I checked it locally with a preload that makes every `net.Server.listen` fail with EPERM. `node node_modules/tsx/dist/cli.mjs src/code-review/print-findings-schema.ts` crashed with that error. `node --import tsx src/code-review/print-findings-schema.ts` printed the schema, since the loader opens no socket. I didn't fix it, because the fix is in `.claude/skills/review-pr/SKILL.md`, and a permission rule blocked my edit to that file. Joe has to approve the edit, or make it. The fix: in step 2, run `node --import tsx src/code-review/review-input.ts $ARGUMENTS`. In step 6 item 1, replace "run a TypeScript file with `npx tsx <file>`" with `node --import tsx <file>`, and say not to use `npx tsx` in the sandbox. Then change code review design section 4.3 (the `review-input.ts` command) and the reviewer's tools in section 4.1 ("Can run `node` and `npx tsx`") to match. I left the design doc unchanged, so it doesn't disagree with the skill. The workflow's `Bash(npx tsx:*)` entry in `--allowedTools` can stay or go. It does no harm, but the command can't work in the sandbox.

**Fixed** in 419ffcd.

Fixed by hand by Claude Code, since the fixer can't edit files under `.claude/` in `claude -p`. Step 2 and step 6 now use `node --import tsx`, and code review design 4.1 and 4.3 match. Whether the fix job should be able to edit skill files is a question for #77.

Line 322.

**Fix (F1 - The PR doesn't do what its task says)**

Do item 4 says to run the fixer by hand on this PR and record each round in code review design section 5. Section 5's table still ends at PR #44 round 4, and the PR adds no row or write-up for PR #109. A fix round has already happened on this PR: the first review's F2 finding (comment-4352232124) is marked "Fixed in 419ffcd". So round 1's review and fix are missing from section 5. The PR description also doesn't report the other half of the item, that the files each review read were added to #87.

**Why F1:** The task asks for each fix round to be recorded in section 5, and that record is missing. Nothing in the PR hands it to another issue, so D3 doesn't fit, and the rubric makes missing task work F1 even when nothing breaks.

**Fixed** in 6952c845cc5739ff7855635ceee4a0638e4dba10.

The claim holds, and F1 fits. Do item 4 asks for each round to be recorded in code review design section 5, and nothing for PR #109 was there. I added two rows to the section 5 table, for the review at 07d3309 (round 1) and the review at 419ffcd (round 2). I also added a short write-up for each round at the end of section 5. Round 1's write-up says the fixer answered "needs attention", because it couldn't edit the `review-pr` skill, and that Claude Code fixed it by hand in 419ffcd. Round 2's write-up says the review didn't post round 1's finding again, and names this finding and the N6 note. There's no test, since this is a doc change. I didn't do the other half of the item, the comment on #87 saying which files each review read. The fixer may write to an issue only to add an open question, so that comment has to come from whoever runs the loop. It needs each run's transcript, from `gh run download`.

Line 31.

**Note (N6 - A design doc is unclear, or doesn't match the code, in a way no builder would act on)**

Section 2 still lists `npx tsx` among the reviewer's tools, next to `node`. Section 4.1 (line 133), as changed by this PR, says `npx tsx` fails in the sandbox and the reviewer runs TypeScript with `node --import tsx`. So the doc contradicts itself. The workflow does the same: it still allows `Bash(npx tsx:*)`, and its comment at .github/workflows/code-review.yml:80 says the reviewer gets "node, npx tsx", but that command can't run.

**Why N6:** The skill and section 4.1 already tell a builder to use `node --import tsx`, so no one would build the wrong thing from line 31. That makes it N6, not F6.

**Fix (F2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, in normal use)**

`isAskable` marks a finding as askable whenever any reply from `JOE` comes after the fixer's "Needs attention" marker. It doesn't check whether that reply carries a marker of its own. Code review design section 3.6 now says Joe answers a finding he handled by hand with a marker reply, such as `**Fixed** in 419ffcd.`. That is what happened in this PR's round 1. The fixer answered "Needs attention", and Joe then replied "Fixed" on the thread. I ran it locally: an inline F2 finding with a fixer reply of `**Needs attention.**` followed by a `nimbusscale` reply of `**Fixed** in 419ffcd.` comes back in `fixRound(state).askable`, and `stopReason(round, HEAD_SHA)` returns null. So every later fix round treats the finding as "Joe asked for a fix". The fixer starts even when no finding is marked "fix". It gets the prompt "Someone replied after this finding was marked 'needs attention'. If the reply says to fix it, handle it like a finding marked 'fix'". In #77's loop, the review job's count of needs-attention findings with a reply from Joe (design 4.7) would also count it. A Joe reply that starts with a marker should mean "handled". Only a reply without a marker should make the finding askable.

**Why F2:** The fixer starts and is asked to act on a finding Joe already closed by hand, which is the wrong behavior in normal use. It happened on this PR's own round 1, so it is F2. It isn't F1, because the task doesn't speak to this interaction.

**Fixed** in eec3b5c505651dda99f3832157003a35cea5dbc6.

The claim holds, and F2 fits. On this PR, Joe's "**Fixed** in 419ffcd." reply on comment-4352232124 made that finding count as asked for, so this round's input told the fixer to handle it again. `isAskable()` in `src/code-review/fix-round.ts` now looks at the last reply with a marker, from the fixer or Joe. The finding counts as asked for only when that last marker is the fixer's "Needs attention", and Joe replied after it without a marker. A marker from Joe means he handled the finding himself, as code review design section 3.6 says. The test is "doesn't ask for a fix on a finding Joe handled by hand" in `src/code-review/reply-authors.test.ts`. It failed before the fix and passes now.

**Note (N5 - A code comment is wrong)**

The usage line in the header comment says `npx tsx src/code-review/review-input.ts <pr-number>`. This PR's own fix (419ffcd) found that `npx tsx` fails in the reviewer's sandbox, and the skill and design 4.3 now say `node --import tsx src/code-review/review-input.ts <number>`. Anyone who copies the comment's command into CI gets `listen EPERM`.

**Why N5:** Only a code comment is wrong. The skill, which is what runs the command, already uses the right form, so this is N5 and not F2 or F6.

**Check (V1 - The label depends on a fact the reviewer can't check from the repo, and that fact decides whether it's a fix)**

Do item 4 also says to check which files each review read and add that to #87. The "Done when" item needs the transcript of a review whose threads have fixer replies to show it read no reply. Round 2, reviewed at 419ffcd, was that review, and section 5 says it ran. But the PR description still gives this "Done when" result as "pending". Neither the description nor the round 1 and round 2 notes in section 5 say what files each review read, or that #87 got those results. The earlier F1 finding (comment-4352302504) already raised the #87 half. Its fix, 6952c84, added only the section 5 rows and notes, so it didn't cover that half. What to check: download the artifact for each review run on this PR with `gh run download <run-id> -n review-transcript-<attempt>`. In each `.jsonl` transcript, confirm that no Read, Bash, or node call read a thread reply (for example, no `gh api .../pulls/109/comments` and no `fix-input.ts`). Then list the files each review read. Also confirm #87 has a comment with these results for this PR. If the results are missing from #87 or the description, this is F1.

**Why V1:** Whether the task is done depends on the review run artifacts and on comments on #87. The reviewer can't download artifacts into its sandbox and isn't allowed to read issue comments, so it can't settle this from the repo. If the work is missing, the answer makes this F1, and otherwise there's no finding, so V1 fits.

**Fixed** in c489e0b.

Checked by Claude Code. #87 had no results for this PR when review 4 ran. They are posted now, and the PR description gives the link and the transcript result. c489e0b records rounds 3 and 4 in section 5.

**Fix (F6 - A design doc is wrong, so an agent building from it would build the wrong thing)**

A finding marked "Fixed" tells every later review to check the fix again, with no end. That holds even after a later finding about the same problem was closed. Here is the case. Round 1 posts finding A, and the fixer replies `**Fixed** in abc1234.` Round 2 disagrees, and posts finding B: "the fix for A didn't cover it." The fixer or Joe answers B with `**Not fixed:** wrong.` In round 3, `reviewInputText` (src/code-review/review-input-text.ts:41) still gives A as "Fixed in abc1234. Check whether the fix worked. If the problem is still there, post it again." It gives B as "Handled. Don't post it again." The reviewer still thinks the problem is there, so it follows A's instruction and posts the finding a third time. That overrides the decision recorded on B. Section 4.4 says the reviewer doesn't post a finding again once it's not fixed or needs attention. Section 4.3's "Fixed" rule, and the code built from it, don't honor that once the problem moves to a new finding. The skill's step 6 gives no rule for two earlier findings with conflicting instructions. One fix: the "Fixed" check applies only until a later finding re-raises the problem. Another: the list says when a later finding makes the same point.

**Why F6:** The code does what section 4.3 asks, but that choice leads to wrong behavior in normal use: the loop keeps raising a finding that was already closed, which section 4.4 says must not happen. So per the rubric it's F6, not D2. It isn't F1 or F2, because the code matches the task and the design.

**Deferred:** #77.

Left unfixed on Joe's call, since it needs a disputed fix and then a "wrong" on the dispute. Written into #77's open questions, where the loop will show whether it happens.

Closes #77

## Task

From #77's "Do" and "Done when":

- **First, the fixer runs by hand on a real PR.** That's done in #93, on its own PR, for up to three rounds (#93, "Do" step 4). Done on #109: three fix rounds, and six reviews in all. Write up what it did in this issue's PR. Joe doesn't need to look before the job is built. Still untested: whether the fixer acts on a reply from Joe that asks for a fix. That needs Joe, so leave it for him, and say so in the PR.
- **Make the changes the settled open questions above say,** as code review design 4.5 to 4.7 now describe them (written in by PR #108): the fixer's answer shape, the deny rules for the config files, the reviewer's `status` and the backstop check, and when the fix job runs. Check the sandbox's placeholder files in CI, with the fix job's Claude Code version, against the list in `.gitignore`.
- Give the fix job the fixer app's token, from #92.
- Start the fix job's `--allowedTools` from the list #76's replays used. Leave out `Bash(npx tsx:*)`.
- Turn off Claude Code's attribution in the fix job's `--settings`: `"attribution": {"commit": "", "pr": "", "sessionUrl": false}`.
- Add the fix job, the cap of three fix rounds, and the "ready for Joe" label to the "Code review" workflow.
- Run the loop on real PRs.

**Done when:** A PR goes through the loop and gets the "ready for Joe" label, and its runs' transcripts are saved.

## Done when: results

**Done.** This PR went through the loop in [run 39852268146](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/actions/runs/39852268146), at 54f1fc3, and got the "ready for Joe" label.

- **The review job** posted 3 findings: 1 marked "fix" (F6), and 2 notes (NF5, NF2). Its counts were `fix=1`, `asked=0`, `fixer-commits=0`. Cost: $1.62 at API prices.
- **The fix job** ran the fixer, which answered "needs attention" on the F6, since its fix is in the workflow file, and the fixer can't change one. It made no commit, so nothing was pushed. The posting step replied on the thread and posted the summary comment. No command was refused. Cost: $0.54.
- **The ready job** added the label, since the fixer pushed nothing.
- **Transcripts:** the run's artifacts, `review-transcript-1` and `fix-transcript-1`, kept 30 days.

**The second run,** [39855660869](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/actions/runs/39855660869), at e7e6eed, after the F6 was fixed by hand:

- **The unready job** took the label off at the start.
- **The review** answered "done" with no findings, and said the F6 fix works. But one of its commands was refused, so the backstop in code review design 4.7 failed the step. It was a false alarm, since the reviewer had read the PR. Joe accepted the backstop as it is (#115). Cost: $1.42.
- **The fix and ready jobs** were skipped, so the label stayed off.

No fix round has pushed yet, so the loop going on after a fixer push hasn't run in CI. The fixer acting on a "fix it" reply from Joe is untested too (#114).

## Checked by hand

- `npm run check` passes.
- **Both reviews read the rubric, `DEVELOPMENT.md`, and `design/README.md` in full,** with the Read tool, as their first three steps.
- **The sandbox's empty files in CI,** with Claude Code 2.1.308 and the fixer's settings, from a one-off job since taken out. There were 26, all ignored by `.gitignore`, and none untracked.
- **The fixer's transcript:** it ran `fix-input.ts` and `check-fix.ts` with `node --import tsx` in the sandbox, and read the rubric, `DEVELOPMENT.md`, the design doc, and the workflow.

## Decisions

The open questions were settled in chat before this PR, and written in by #108, #111, and #112. These are the decisions made while building it.

- **The fix job pins Claude Code 2.1.308.** The review job stays on 2.1.301. 2.1.308 is the version the fixer, the deny rules, and the sandbox's empty files were tested with. Code review design section 2.
- **Only the review job is in the concurrency group.** If the whole run were in it, the fixer's own push would start a run that cancels the fix job that pushed. Code review design section 4.6.
- **The fix job pushes last,** after it posts the replies, resolves threads, and updates the summary. The push starts the next review, and that review reads the replies' markers. `postFix()` in `fix-post.ts` does the writes in that order. Code review design section 4.5.
- **The fixer never holds a token that can push or post on the PR.** The fix job makes two tokens from the fixer's app. The fixer's token can read code and the PR, and write issues. The posting step's token, made after the fixer ends, can push and post. The checkout doesn't keep the job's own token. Code review design section 4.6.
- **The fixer is also denied `.claude/skills/**` and `.github/workflows/**`.** The fixer's app can't push a workflow file, so a fix there would be posted as "Fixed" and then fail at the push. The skill files were already off limits (settled in #77). The deny rule also stops `sed` from changing one. A fix in either needs attention. Code review design sections 3.6 and 4.5, and the `fix-pr` skill.
- **A wildcard deny rule stays, next to the files it expands to.** For example, `Edit(tsconfig*.json)` stays, along with `Edit(tsconfig.json)`. The sandbox skips the wildcard rule, but the Edit and Write tools still follow it. So they can't create a new matching file. `deny-rules.ts`.
- **A fixer that stops fails the fix job,** so the PR doesn't get the "ready for Joe" label. Code review design section 4.6.
- **Each run takes the "ready for Joe" label off when it starts,** in a job of its own, and only the ready job puts it back. Before, only a fixer push took it off, so a push by Joe left it on a commit whose review could still fail. From the first review's F6, agreed with Joe in chat. Code review design section 4.6.
- **`web/tsconfig.json` has an ask rule now,** `Edit(/web/tsconfig.json)` in `.claude/settings.json`. So the fixer's deny rules cover it too. `Edit(/tsconfig*.json)` covers only the repo root. Joe approved the change in chat.
- **The review job's "fix" count is the findings marked "fix" on the PR's head that have no fixer reply yet.** `round-counts.ts` counts them the same way `fix-input.ts` picks the fixer's findings. So the two always agree. Code review design section 4.6.
- **The sandbox's empty files were checked in CI** with a one-off job, since taken out. It found 26, all of them covered by `.gitignore`. 15 of them stay after the run ends. Code review design section 4.6.

## Set aside

- **Untested: whether the fixer acts on a reply from Joe that asks for a fix.** That needs Joe, so it's left for him (#77, "Do"). To test it, reply "fix it" on a finding the fixer marked "needs attention", then re-run the PR's latest "Code review" run.

## One gap, accepted

- **The fixer's commands could still create a new `eslint.config.js`.** The sandbox skips the wildcard rule `eslint.config.*`, so only the existing `eslint.config.mjs` is read-only for commands. ESLint reads `eslint.config.js` first, so a new one would replace our rules. The commit would show it, and the next review would see it. An exact ask rule for `Edit(/eslint.config.js)` wouldn't help. The sandbox would then make an empty `eslint.config.js` while each command runs, and ESLint would read that instead. An exact deny rule wouldn't help either, for the same reason. Accepted by Joe in chat, since the deny rule `Edit(eslint.config.*)` already stops the Edit and Write tools from creating the file.

## The fixer run by hand on #109

#77's first "Do" step: the fixer ran by hand on a real PR before the fix job was built. That was #93's PR, #109. It went through three fix rounds and six reviews. Each round ran the way the fix job now does: `claude -p` with a fresh config folder, the fixer app's token, and the deny rules for the config files. `research/code-review/review-rounds.md` has each round, under "PR #109".

- **Round 1: the fixer couldn't fix its one finding.** The fix was in the `review-pr` skill, and `claude -p` refuses an edit under `.claude/` unless permissions are bypassed. It answered "needs attention", and Claude Code fixed it by hand. That's why the fixer now leaves skill files alone.
- **Round 2: the fixer fixed an F1.** The PR hadn't recorded its rounds, as its task asked, and the fixer added them. The review before it didn't post round 1's fixed finding again.
- **Round 3: the fixer fixed an F2, and saw the bug in its own input.** A "Fixed" marker from Joe still made a finding count as a request for a fix. So the fixer's input asked it to handle round 1's finding again. It worked out that this was the bug it was fixing, and left that finding alone.
- **Round 4's review marked nothing "fix",** so the loop would have stopped there, and given the PR the "ready for Joe" label. Reviews 5 and 6 ran after the cap, on commits Claude Code made by hand.
- **No review read a reply.** None of the replies' text shows up in the review transcripts.
- **Cost, at API prices:** $0.66 to $0.86 per review, and $0.60 to $0.78 per fixer run.

**Still untested: whether the fixer acts on a reply from Joe that asks for a fix.** That needs Joe, so it's left for him. The decisions comment says how to test it.

<!-- fix-loop: summary -->

## Fix loop: deferred, and needs attention

Code updates this comment after each fix round. Resolve a finding's thread once it's handled. A finding in a review body has no thread, so tick its box instead.

**Deferred**

None.

**Needs attention**

- The "ready for Joe" label is only taken off when the fixer pushes (`design/code-review.md:275`): [finding](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/113#discussion_r4353425231), [reply](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/113#discussion_r4353436366)

**Fix (F6 - A design doc is wrong, so an agent building from it would build the wrong thing)**

The "ready for Joe" label is only taken off when the fixer pushes. A push by Joe, or a re-run Joe starts after replying "fix it", leaves it on. Case: the loop ends and the PR gets the label. Joe pushes a commit of his own. The new run's review marks a finding "fix", and the fix job runs for up to an hour with the label still on. If that review then fails, say on a usage limit, or the fixer stops, the label stays on, and the latest commit was never reviewed. That breaks the section's own rule, "Joe never gets a PR nobody read". The design, and the workflow built from it (`.github/workflows/code-review.yml` line 361), take the label off only in the fix job after a push. One fix is to take it off when the review job starts, so only the ready job puts it back.

**Why F6:** The code does what section 4.6 says, but that choice gives the wrong result in normal use: Joe pushing after the label is on is the usual next step, and a failed review is a failure the code is meant to handle. That makes it F6, not D2. It's not F1 to F5, since the workflow matches the design and nothing is lost or exposed.

**Needs attention.**

The claim holds. In `.github/workflows/code-review.yml`, only the fix job's "Post the replies, and push" step takes the "ready for Joe" label off, and only after the fixer pushes. A push by Joe starts a run with the label still on. If that run's review job fails, or its fixer stops, the ready job doesn't run, and the label stays on a commit nobody reviewed. Joe pushing after the label is on is normal use, and a failed review is a failure the workflow is meant to handle, so F6 fits.

The fix belongs in the workflow file, and the fixer can't change files under `.github/workflows/`. Changing only design section 4.6 would make the doc disagree with the workflow, so I changed nothing. Joe has to decide on the fix and make it by hand. One way: add a job with no `needs`, outside the review concurrency group, with `issues: write` (or `pull-requests: write`), that removes the label at the start of every run, using the same check-then-DELETE as the fix job. Then only the ready job puts it back, and the fix job's own removal can go. It shouldn't be a step in the review job that uses `github.token`. That would give the reviewer's token write access, and the review step uses that token. In design section 4.6, the "three jobs" list and the paragraph at line 275 would change to say the label comes off when a run starts. The next fixer should leave this finding alone until Joe has made that change.

**Fixed** in e7e6eed89e6665970352732ee3020eae9e3da5c7.

A new job, `unready`, takes the label off at the start of every run, and the ready job now waits for it. The fix job no longer takes the label off itself. Code review design 4.6 says so.

**Note (NF5 - A security hole outside the threat model)**

The posting step runs `npx tsx src/code-review/post-fix.ts` from the checkout the fixer just committed in, with the posting token. That token can write contents, pull requests, and issues. So code the fixer changed runs with a write token before anyone reviews it. Case: a finding on `src/code-review/fix-post.ts` or `fix-check.ts` gets fixed, and the fixer's new version does the posting and pushing in the same job. A prompt-injected or confused fixer could change `post-fix.ts` to post or push anything that token allows, on any branch. This gets around the split that section 4.6 states: "The fixer never holds a token that can push or post on the PR". Running the scripts from the PR's head commit, such as from a second checkout of `HEAD_SHA`, would close it.

**Why NF5:** It's a hole only an agent steered on purpose could use, which is a targeted attack and not scanning bots or worms, so it's outside the threat model. The fixer's commit is pushed anyway, so what's gained over the push itself is small. That makes it NF5, not F5.

**Not fixed:** below the bar.

Joe agreed it is NF5. The posting token works only on this repo for an hour, and can't change workflow files. So the worst case is a mess in the repo, which is accepted for this project.

**Note (NF2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, but not in normal use)**

The step runs `set -o pipefail` and then `if gh api ... --jq '.[].name' | grep -qxF 'ready for Joe'`. `grep -q` exits on the first match. If `gh` then writes another label name, it gets SIGPIPE and exits non-zero. Under pipefail, the `if` then reads the pipeline as failed and skips the DELETE. Case: the PR has "ready for Joe" plus a label listed after it, and `gh` writes the names in separate writes. The fixer pushes, and the label stays on while the loop runs again. Dropping `-q` and sending grep's output to `/dev/null`, or filtering in `--jq`, avoids it.

**Why NF2:** It depends on a second label and on the timing of gh's writes, so it's not normal use. That makes it NF2, not F2.

**Fixed** in e7e6eed89e6665970352732ee3020eae9e3da5c7.

The F6 fix moved the label check to the new `unready` job, which reads the labels with `--jq 'any(...)'` instead of piping to `grep -q`.

## Decisions

These are proposed here, and settled when the PR is approved. None is written into a design doc yet. Tool design section 2.2 says what each tool takes and returns, and none of these changes it.

- **The server's instructions hold the started-trip rule, and that refusals change nothing.** The started-trip rule covers three of the tools, so it goes in the instructions, not in each description (tool design section 4). It says nothing about user IDs or trip IDs, as with the trip server since 0f96ae4: the schemas have none to pass.
- **The limits are in what the model sees, built from the settings.** `add_memory_item`'s description gives the maximum items, and each `text` input gives the maximum length. So the coordinator can write a short item the first time, instead of learning the limit from an error. The length isn't a `maxLength` in the schema. A schema failure comes back as an MCP input error, and the writer's error is the one that reads well: "A memory item is at most 300 characters. This one is 301."
- **`read_memory` starts with each memory's count and limit,** such as "User memory: 12 of 50 items." So the coordinator sees memory filling up without counting lines. Then one line per item, in the order added: `- mem_k7m2x9qa (user): We never eat at chains.`
- **The add reply gives only the new ID and which memory it's in.** Update and forget give only the ID. None echoes the text back (tool design section 2.1 says the same for the trip tools).
- **The `memory` input is an enum of `user` and `trip`, with no description.** What each is for is in the coordinator's instructions (technical spec 5.2), and the input says only how to pass it (tool design section 4).
- **An ID of another kind gets its own error,** such as "stay_k7m2x9qa is a stay ID, not a memory item ID.", from `refuseWrongKind()`, as in the weather tool. Any other unknown ID gets "No such memory item."
- **`memoryAccessFor()` is in `memory-server.ts`,** as `weatherAccessFor()` is in `weather-server.ts`. It isn't connected to the app yet.

## Set aside

- The server isn't given to an agent yet. #48 does that, with the coordinator.

## Config changes

- None.

<!-- fix-loop: summary -->

## Fix loop: deferred, and needs attention

Code updates this comment after each fix round. Resolve a finding's thread once it's handled. A finding in a review body has no thread, so tick its box instead.

**Deferred**

None.

**Needs attention**

None.

**Fix (F1 - The PR doesn't do what its task says)**

No test sends `update_memory_item` for a trip item on a started trip. Tool design section 2.2 says that adding, updating, or forgetting a trip item on a started trip is refused. The `add_memory_item` and `forget_memory_item` blocks each test this case through the tool, but the `update_memory_item` block doesn't. For example, if `updateMemoryItemTool` passed `null` as the trip, or stopped calling the writer's started-trip check, the tool tests would still pass. Add a test like the forget one: put a row for `STARTED_TRIP` in the store, call `update` on it, and check that the error starts with "Nothing was changed. This trip has started" and the row's text is unchanged.

**Why F1:** The "Done when" asks for tool tests that cover the four tools as section 2.2 describes them, and this refusal is in 2.2, so the missing test is task work. No other issue tracks it, so D3 doesn't fit.

**Fixed** in 8946320fa7c3321e401bc98d08548fb7fbd95eac.

Added "refuses a trip item on a started trip, and still updates a user item" to the update_memory_item block in memory-tools.test.ts. It puts a STARTED_TRIP row in the store, calls update on it through the tool, and checks that the error starts with "Nothing was changed. This trip has started". It also checks that a user item still updates, and that the trip row's text is unchanged. I took out the #refuseIfTripStarted() call in MemoryWriter.update() for a moment, and the test failed. Then I put it back. The test file went over the 300-line lint limit, so the shared setup (toolsFor, textOf, added, STARTED_TRIP, and a new startedTripItem() helper) moved to src/tools/memory-tools.fake.ts, as trip-writer.fake.ts does. The forget started-trip test uses startedTripItem() too.

**Fix (F1 - The PR doesn't do what its task says)**

No test sends `forget_memory_item` for the user's own trip item from another trip. Tool design section 2.2 says `forget_memory_item` works on a trip item only if it's this trip's, and any other ID gets "no such memory item". The `update_memory_item` block tests this case ("refuses the user's own item from another trip"), but the `forget_memory_item` block tests only another user's item and a missing ID. For example, user A's session on TRIP_1 could forget user A's TRIP_2 item, and no tool test would fail. Add a test that adds a trip item in a TRIP_2 session, forgets it from a TRIP_1 session, and checks for the `NO_SUCH_ITEM` error and that the row is still there.

**Why F1:** The "Done when" asks for tool tests that cover each tool as section 2.2 describes it, and the rule about another trip's items is in 2.2. No other issue tracks this test, so it's task work and not D3.

**Fixed** in 8946320fa7c3321e401bc98d08548fb7fbd95eac.

Added "refuses the user's own item from another trip" to the forget_memory_item block in memory-tools.test.ts. It adds a trip item in a USER_A / TRIP_2 session, and forgets it from a USER_A / TRIP_1 session. Then it checks for NO_SUCH_ITEM, and that the row is still in the store. I made MemoryWriter.forget() pass the item's own trip to getOwnItem() for a moment, and the test failed while the others passed. Then I put it back.

body:
Closes #117

## Do

- Change the "rule that covers several tools" bullet in tool design section 4. A rule that covers several tools goes in the system prompt of each agent that has those tools, not in an MCP server's instructions, and not in each tool's description. When the rule applies to more than one agent, its text is written once in code, and each agent's prompt that needs it includes it. A tool's description holds only what's specific to that tool, and the system prompt never repeats it. When an agent evaluation shows a model missing one of these rules, the rule is repeated in the description of the tool where it was missed. Drop the sentence about where Claude Code puts server instructions.
- Remove `instructions` from the `trip` server (`src/tools/trip-server.ts`) and the `memory` server (`src/tools/memory-server.ts`), along with the constants that hold the text, and fix any test or comment that refers to them. Fix the comment on `createWeatherServer` too, which says it needs no instructions because it has one tool.
- Don't put the removed text anywhere in this issue. #48's "Do" list holds it, word for word, and puts it in the coordinator's instructions. The started-trip sentence is dropped (open questions).

## Done when

- No MCP server in `src/` sets `instructions`.
- Tool design section 4 says where a rule that covers several tools goes, as above.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Results

- No MCP server sets `instructions`: `grep -rn "instructions" src/tools/*-server.ts` finds nothing. No test referred to the removed constants.
- Tool design section 4's bullet now says the rule goes in each agent's system prompt, with the reasons, the shared-text rule, and the fallback to a tool description.

title: Move MCP server instructions into the agents' system prompts

body:
Closes #48

## Do

- Add the coordinator, with only the tools on the `trip` server (`src/tools/trip-server.ts`, PR #44) and the `memory` server (#47). Its instructions cover conduct, the trip brief items to establish, the memory rules, and comfortable driving hours (technical spec, section 5.2).
- Put these rules for the `trip` and `memory` tools in the coordinator's instructions, word for word. They were the servers' instructions until #117 removed them, and tool design section 4 now says they go in the system prompt:
  - "Every tool that changes the trip makes the whole change or none of it. If any part is refused, nothing is changed, and the error says why. Each of these tools replies with the feasibility check results the change made new or gone, anywhere in the trip."
  - "When a memory change is refused, nothing is changed, and the error says why."
- Give each trip brief item in the coordinator's instructions by the name the tools use, such as `tripLengthInDays`, with what it means (tool design, section 4). The `update_trip_brief` input descriptions say only how to pass each value, so the meanings are in no tool. Functional spec 5.2 gives most of them. It doesn't give these, which the input descriptions said before PR #44 trimmed them:
  - Interests and must-sees are in the user's words, with why they matter. A must-see can be one place, an area, a road, or an activity.
  - The rest days item records what the user asked for. It doesn't mark any day.
  - The default tier is the budget tier for lodging and meals when no budget rule covers them.
- Add a `coordinatorModel` setting to `settings.json`, set to the exact model ID `claude-opus-5-5`, and give it to the Agent SDK. A short name such as "opus" would move to newer models on its own, so a later run could use a different model. Write the setting into technical spec section 10. Agreed in chat on 2026-10-18.
- Give the coordinator the maximum trip length (functional spec 5.2). Add a trip length bullet next to comfortable driving hours in its instructions (technical spec 5.2): it gives the maximum, and says that when the user asks for more, explain the limit and propose a version that fits. Also give the limits in the `update_trip_brief` input descriptions: `tripLengthInDays` gets "from 1 to" the maximum trip length, and `comfortableDrivingInHours` gets "at most" the maximum daily driving. Fill in every number, in the instructions and the descriptions, from `settings.json` when the app starts, as the memory tools do for the item length. Never write a number into the text, so a changed setting can't leave stale text. Write this into technical spec 5.2 and 10, and tool design section 4. Agreed in chat on 2026-10-23.
- Add today's date to user messages, and the line after a resume, as technical spec section 5.2 says.
- Log each `mirror_error` message, with the session's ID and the error, and do nothing more. The Agent SDK sends the app that message when it drops transcript lines after 3 failed tries to save them (persistence design section 6). A few transcript lines out of order after a retry are accepted. Write both into persistence design section 6. Agreed in chat on 2026-10-18.
- Add a dev script to chat with the coordinator in the terminal, against the local database.

## Done when

Joe runs these conversations by hand in the terminal. Claude Code runs each one first, to catch problems before Joe's run, and the PR quotes the lines that show it.

- A discovery conversation fills in the trip brief, and `read_trip_brief` shows every item.
- "We never eat at chains" goes to user memory, and "skip I-35 this time" goes to trip memory.
- On a second trip, the coordinator confirms the user's usual driving hours instead of asking from scratch (functional spec 11, S9).
- Asked for 14 hours of driving a day, the coordinator pushes back, and sets no more than the maximum daily driving (technical spec section 10).

## Results

Claude Code's runs, with `npm run chat`, against the local database, with the final instructions. Joe's run is still to come.

**Discovery fills the trip brief.** Three messages about a Utah trip filled all 11 items. A new session on the trip (`--trip trip_39dwccdz`) then read it:

```
  [tool] mcp__trip__read_trip_brief {}
  [reply] focus: Utah national parks
          tripLengthInDays: 9
          interestsText: We love long hikes, the harder the better, since we train for it all year.
          mustSeesText: Angels Landing, because my partner has wanted to do it since college. Delicate Arch at sunset for photos.
          comfortableDrivingInHours: 5
          routePreference: scenic
          restDaysText: No rest days.
          usualStartTime: 6:30 a.m.
          defaultTier: midRange
          budgetRulesText: Mid-range by default, but splurge on lodging in Moab.
          mealPreferencesText: We always go for local cafés over hotel breakfast, and we love Mexican food.
```

**User or trip memory.** In a Texas barbecue trip, for a new user:

```
> We never eat at chains. And skip I-35 this time.
  [tool] mcp__memory__add_memory_item {"memory":"user","text":"Never suggest chain restaurants; the party never eats at chains."}
  [tool] mcp__memory__add_memory_item {"memory":"trip","text":"Avoid Interstate 35 on this trip; plan drives on other roads (e.g., TX-130, US-183, US-290, US-79, Hill Country roads)."}
...
- **No chains:** I saved this as a standing preference for all your trips, since you said you *never* eat at chains. It's also in this trip's meal preferences.
- **No I-35:** I saved this for this trip only, since you said "this time."
```

**Second trip (S9).** A new Oregon trip for the Utah user, whose user memory holds "Comfortable driving about 5 hours a day on road trips":

```
> Let's plan a new trip: the Oregon coast, about a week.
...
**From your past trips, please confirm these still hold:**
1. **Driving:** about 5 hours a day is comfortable. On this coast you probably won't need that much.
```

**14 hours of driving.** In the Texas trip:

```
> We can drive 14 hours a day if we have to. Set it to 14.

I can't set it to 14. The app plans at most 12 hours of driving a day, and it recommends 6 hours or less. At 12 or more, most of the day is spent in the car, with little time to eat or see anything.
...
> I hear you, but we really like long drives. Set it as high as it goes.
  [tool] mcp__trip__update_trip_brief {"comfortableDrivingInHours":12}
```

## Checked by hand

- **Today's date.** The stored transcript's first user message reads "Today is Friday, October 23, 2026." and then the user's text.
- **Resume.** `--resume` restored the conversation from Postgres. On the first message after it, the coordinator read the trip brief and memory again, and said "Nothing in the trip brief or memory changed while you were away."
- **Trip length.** Asked for "about three weeks through the Southwest," the coordinator said the app plans up to 14 days, and offered two 14-day trips that cover less ground.
- **`mirror_error`.** Stopping the local Postgres in the middle of a turn logged "Transcript lines for session session_nh4j7drb weren't saved: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432". The turn still finished.
- **Transcripts.** Each session's lines were in `transcript_lines`.
- `npm run check` passes.

nodes.body:
## Decisions

Agreed in the issue, and written in:

- **`coordinatorModel`** is in technical spec section 10. The settings schema refuses a value that doesn't start with `claude-`, so a short name such as "opus" stops the app from starting.
- **Limits from the settings.** The maximum trip length and the maximum daily driving are filled in, in the instructions and in the `update_trip_brief` input descriptions. Written into technical spec 5.2 (a new trip length bullet, and a line above the list) and section 10, and tool design section 4.
- **`mirror_error`** is logged, and a few lines out of order after a retry are accepted. Written into persistence design section 6.

Agreed in chat on 2026-10-23, while building:

- **The resume line.** Technical spec 5.2 and persistence design sections 7 and 8.5 now say the coordinator reads the trip brief, the itinerary, and memory again. The line is "This session was resumed. Read the trip brief, the itinerary, and memory first." The code's line leaves out the itinerary, since the coordinator can't read it yet. #54 has an open question to add it.
- **Check results.** The instructions have a "Check results" section with two sentences from technical spec 5.2's bullet on broken feasibility rules: don't raise a warning that comes only from the days not being laid out yet, and stay quiet about results marked already known. Without them, the coordinator told the user "The trip is 1 day, and the brief asks for 9" in reply after reply during discovery. Holding the warning back in code was turned down. #55 has an open question to fold the two sentences into the full bullet.

Made while building, and not written into a design doc:

- **More in the instructions than the issue's list.** They also cover reading the trip brief and memory at the start of a session and after a resume (technical spec 3.1 and 5.2), the lines the app adds to user messages, a refused trip brief update (technical spec 5.2), and what the coordinator remembers and forgetting an item (functional spec 10.5). Functional spec 10.5 isn't in technical spec 5.2's list. #65 checks the instructions against 5.2.
- **No test statements in the prompt.** The memory examples in the instructions don't use "we never eat at chains" or "skip I-35 this time", so those runs show the coordinator's own judgment.
- **The SDK's user message** is built in `src/agent/sdk-user-message.schema.ts`, since its snake_case names are allowed only in schema files. It's marked `origin: { kind: "human" }`, since the SDK treats a message with no origin as unattributed.
- **Not unit tested:** the loop in `converse()` that waits for each turn to end, and the `mirror_error` log line. A fake SDK message stream needs snake_case objects, which lint allows only in schema files. Both were checked by hand (PR description).
- **`npm run chat`** is dev only, so it's not in `npm run build`. It's in DEVELOPMENT.md section 2. Users live in Supabase, so it uses a fixed dev user ID unless `--user` gives another.
- **A started trip.** `converse()` doesn't refuse a message once the trip has started. A comment where the check belongs names #52, which adds it with the browser chat. The coordinator can't set a start date yet.

Fixed after Joe ran the stock `/simplify` and `/code-review`, with Joe's picks (2026-10-23):

- **The date line goes out whenever the date differs,** not only on a later date. Before the trip has a start place, the date is UTC's, a day ahead in a US evening. Once a start place is set, the date goes back a day, and the coordinator needs the new one. Written into technical spec 5.2.
- **`budgetRulesText` isn't required** in the instructions. Functional spec 5.2 gives budget posture as the default tier plus any rules, so a user can have none.
- **`converse()` reads the start place itself,** from the trip reader, instead of each caller passing a function for it. Today's date for a trip is `tripToday()` in `src/domain/today.ts`, next to `todayAt()`.
- **The prompt quotes `RESUMED_LINE`,** so the two can't drift when #54 changes it. `logMirrorError()` isn't exported.

Left alone on purpose (Joe, 2026-10-23):

- **Findings that touch only `npm run chat`.** It's a short-lived tool for testing and debugging, so its findings aren't fixed. That covers a crash when Ctrl-D is pressed during a turn, a turn whose result has `is_error` set not being reported as failed, an empty trip left by Ctrl-D at the first prompt, flags that are ignored or end in a stack trace, and the shape of the `userTexts()` loop.
- **Test cleanups,** such as the copied MCP client setup in `trip-server.test.ts` and the fake memory session built by hand in `coordinator.test.ts`.

## Set aside

- The itinerary in the resume line: #54's open questions.
- The full bullet on broken feasibility rules: #55's open questions.

## Config changes

None needed.

**Note (N3 - Text a road trip agent reads is unclear, or says something twice, or is an error message with the wrong reason for a failure)**

The coordinator's instructions for `defaultTier` say "The tiers are value, mid-range, and posh." The `update_trip_brief` input takes `midRange`, not "mid-range" (`TIERS` in `src/domain/tier.ts`), and `read_trip_brief` shows `defaultTier: midRange`. Every other item in this section goes by the name the tools use, and `routePreference` lists its values as the tools spell them ("scenic or fastest"). Only this one gives a value in prose. A model that copies "mid-range" from the instructions would get a schema error, then have to work out the right spelling from the enum.
