body:
## Do

**Decided by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat:**

- **What counts as grounded.** A fact in a reply is grounded if it came from any of these:
  - a tool result, from this turn or an earlier turn in the session. This includes trip tool results, such as `read_itinerary`, since code works out much of what they say, such as schedule times, drive times with the buffer, and check results.
  - a worker's result, as the coordinator received it.
  - the user's own words.
  - the coordinator's own knowledge, but only where its instructions allow it, or as a general, guidebook-level description of a well-known place, such as "the Ferry Building is known for its food hall."

  Specific facts that can be checked always need a tool result: hours, prices, distances, drive times, addresses, whether a business exists, and current closures. The judge checks where a fact came from, not whether it's true. A made-up opening time fails even if it happens to be right.
- **Where the instructions allow the coordinator's own knowledge.** The rubric copies these two sentences from the coordinator's instructions, in `src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`, rather than giving the judge the whole system prompt:
  - From the trip sketches step: "Sketches come from your own knowledge, not from research. … Seasonal closures and hazards also come from your own knowledge at this stage."
  - From the waypoints rule: "No tool shows the road a route takes, so judge that from your own knowledge of the roads, such as UT-24 running through Capitol Reef."

  Trade-off: the rubric holds a copy. If the instructions change what the coordinator may say from its own knowledge, the judge keeps grading against the old rule until the rubric is updated by hand. Both sentences last changed on 2026-10-26, before the oldest corpus session (2026-10-30), so the copy holds for the whole corpus.
- **What the judge reads for a turn,** built by code from the turn's spans and the earlier turns in the same session:
  - each user message and reply in the session so far, including the date line.
  - each of the coordinator's tool results, labeled with the tool's name. For the 8 tools whose result doesn't say what it changed, the call's input too: `add_memory_item`, `update_memory_item`, `forget_memory_item`, `update_trip_brief`, `update_itinerary`, `update_day`, `update_stop`, and `update_stay`. Example: `add_memory_item` replies only "Added mem_x to this trip's memory.", so without the input the judge can't check "I've noted that you don't want to see the same thing twice." The input isn't a source for facts. It only shows what a successful change did. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, after the first set.
  - each worker shown only by its result, the `Agent` span's output. The worker's own searches are left out, since the coordinator never saw them.
  - the reply being judged.

  Left out: the system prompt, the other tools' inputs, and the coordinator's thinking. A tool call's input is the coordinator's own writing, so it isn't a source, and those tools' results already say what they did. Earlier sessions on the same trip are left out too, since the coordinator doesn't see them.
- **Every tool result counts as a source,** including text the coordinator wrote into the trip that a tool repeats back, such as a stop's purpose. Trade-off: a fact the coordinator made up, saved into the trip, and then repeated would pass. On 2026-11-05, every write to the trip in the live project since 2026-10-30 was checked, about 1,700 calls. The coordinator's writes held settings, such as a day's start time, the user's own words, and purposes. None held a made-up hour, price, or distance. The hours and distances in stop notes came from the workers' searches. If this starts to happen, code can mark the coordinator's own text in the results from the calls' inputs, so the judge doesn't have to tell them apart.
- **Only the coordinator is checked.** If a worker made a fact up, the coordinator passes for repeating it. Checking workers would be a separate evaluator.
- **TypeScript,** in `src/`, so `npm run check` covers it. It uses `@arizeai/phoenix-client` to read spans, write annotations, and run the experiments. The judge calls Haiku through the Anthropic SDK the app already has, with structured output in the labelers' JSON, and code works out the label the same way. Changed by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, from `phoenix-evals`' classifier, which can only return a label. Haiku through Claude Code on the 60 golden turns, listing every fact, matched 51 labels and found 92 of the 103 facts both labelers flagged. Listing only the ungrounded facts also matched 51, but found 87, and got more of Joe's close calls wrong.
- **The judge's prompt is a Phoenix prompt,** `grounded-judge`. The repo's `evals/grounded/rubric.md` stays the source. A command pushes each committed version to Phoenix, tagged with its commit, along with the model, `claude-haiku-5-5`, and high effort. The experiment fetches the prompt from Phoenix, so each experiment links to the prompt version it used. The judge uses `JUDGE_API_KEY` from `.env`. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat.
- **Install `@arizeai/phoenix-client` with an `overrides` entry in `package.json`,** so it uses the app's `@anthropic-ai/sdk`. Its optional peer range, `^0.35.0`, doesn't fit the app's 0.135.0, and `npm install` fails without it. The other fix, `--legacy-peer-deps`, would have to be passed on every install, including the server's builds, and turns off the peer check for every package. The #132 spike tested the `overrides` entry (research/agent-evaluations.md, section 3). `phoenix-client` doesn't use the Anthropic SDK for anything this evaluator calls.
- **The labels are span annotations** on each turn's `coordinator.turn` span, all named `grounded`. Phoenix keeps one annotation per name and identifier on a span, so each labeler gets its own identifier, and writing again under the same identifier replaces only that one:
  - `sonnet-5.5` and `gpt-sol-6.1`, annotator kind `LLM`, for the labelers. The calibration sets also have `opus-5.5`, and the labelers tried there: `gpt-terra-6.1`, plus the medium-effort runs, with `-medium` on the end.
  - `joe`, annotator kind `HUMAN`, for Joe's calls.
  - `haiku-5.5`, annotator kind `LLM`, for the judge's corpus run. Its annotations are named `grounded-haiku`, not `grounded`. Phoenix's project page sums up annotations by name only, not by identifier, so under `grounded` the judge's rate would be mixed with the labelers' labels and Joe's calls on the 60 sampled turns. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-08, in chat.

  Each has the label `grounded`, `not_grounded`, or `no_facts`. `grounded` scores 1 and `not_grounded` scores 0. `no_facts` has no score, so Phoenix's average leaves those turns out, and the label still shows the turn was judged. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat. Each also has the ungrounded facts as its explanation, and the rubric's version in its metadata, with every fact the annotator listed. The version is the commit that last changed `evals/grounded/rubric.md`, such as `{"rubric": "abdae9d"}`, so `git show` gives the exact text. The labeling command refuses to run while the rubric has uncommitted changes. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat. The first set's v1 labels say `v1`.
- **The golden set is a Phoenix dataset,** `grounded-golden`. Each example holds a turn's judge input and span ID, and its settled label. For the 15 turns Joe called, it also holds his ungrounded facts. Its metadata holds the set, where the label came from, and both labelers' ungrounded facts. Sol's list isn't treated as the truth, since Joe's calls on the 5 label splits all went against it. When Joe changes a call, the golden set command updates only the changed turns, as a new version of the dataset. Replacing the dataset would delete the experiments run on it. Each experiment is scored against the labels at the time it ran, so comparing versions across a label change means scoring them again against the current labels.
- **Each rubric version is a Phoenix experiment.** The judge runs with that version over the golden set, and a code check marks whether its label matches the settled one. Phoenix keeps each experiment, so versions can be compared turn by turn. Each experiment judges every turn 3 times, since a run's score moves by about 2 turns from one run to the next. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-07, in chat. The experiment's description is the rubric commit's subject line, so that subject says what the version changed. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-08, in chat.

**The steps, in order:**

1. **Pick the sample.** Code picks about 60 turns from the corpus, about one in five, with at least one from every session, and the same turns for both labelers. The pick is repeatable, such as from a fixed seed, and it's done in sets of 5.
2. **Build each sampled turn's judge input** as its own file, ending with that turn's reply, so a labeler can't see anything that came later in the session.
3. **Draft rubric v1** from the decisions above. Joe reviews its wording.
4. **Label a set of 5.** Opus and Sol each label the set alone, and return JSON listing every fact in each turn's reply, with its source and whether it's grounded. Code works out the label from the list: no facts is `no_facts`, any ungrounded fact is `not_grounded`, and otherwise `grounded`. With only the ungrounded facts, there's no telling whether a labeler checked a fact and passed it, or never saw it. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, after the first set. Code checks the JSON and writes the annotations. Each labeler runs from a folder outside the repo, as the simulated users do (`simulated-users/README.md`, "Start a harness"), so it doesn't load the repo's `CLAUDE.md` or Joe's own. Run Sol on high effort, which Codex shows as `GPT-6.1-Sol high`. Codex starts it on a lower effort by default, and Joe has had better results on high. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat. Opus and Sol labeled the calibration sets.
5. **Joe reviews the set.** A review page shows each turn's judge input in a form that's easy for a person to read, since the raw spans in Phoenix are hard to follow. The page shows only the judge input, not the labels. The agent gives both labelers' labels and flagged facts in chat. For the first sets, Joe reviews every turn, agreements included, and looks into each one in chat with the agent's help. He tells the agent his call in chat, and the agent saves it as the `joe` annotation with a command. The review page only reads. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat, and changed on 2026-11-06 to leave the labels off the page.
6. **Refine the rubric,** and repeat steps 4 and 5 with a new set of 5, until Joe says the rubric is good. The hope is two sets.
7. **Label the rest of the 60** with Sonnet 5.5 and Sol 6.1, both on high effort. On the two calibration sets, Sonnet matched Joe as well as Opus did, for less, and a rerun gave the same labels. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat; the comparison is in a comment. The agent tells Joe in chat which turns the labelers disagree on, and Joe reviews only those, the same way.
8. **Build the golden set,** and run the judge on it as an experiment, one for each rubric version. Tune the rubric until Joe says the judge agrees well enough.
9. **Run the judge over the whole corpus,** writing the `haiku-5.5` annotations, named `grounded-haiku`. Report the rate, such as 12 of 301 turns not grounded, with what the ungrounded facts were like, in a comment on this issue.
10. **Write how the evaluator runs** into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.

## Done when

- The `grounded` annotations from both labelers, and Joe's calls, are on the sampled turns.
- The golden set is a dataset in Phoenix, with an experiment for each rubric version tried.
- The judge's `haiku-5.5` annotations, named `grounded-haiku`, from the final rubric version, are on all corpus turns, and the rate is reported in a comment here.
- `npm run check` passes.

Closes #282

## Results

- **The `grounded` annotations from both labelers, and Joe's calls, are on the sampled turns.** All 60 turns have `sonnet-5.5` and `gpt-sol-6.1` labels, and Joe's calls on 16 turns are saved as `joe`.
- **The golden set is a dataset in Phoenix, with an experiment for each rubric version tried.** `grounded-golden`, 60 turns, on dataset version 4 after Joe's three label changes. Experiments for rubrics v3 to v7, each with 3 runs per turn, plus the first single run of v3. v7 matched 167 of 180 runs.
- **The judge's `haiku-5.5` annotations, named `grounded-haiku`, from the final rubric version, are on all corpus turns, and the rate is reported in a comment here.** All 301 turns, on rubric v7 (`b66b866`): 221 not grounded, 80 grounded. The results are in a comment on #282.
- **`npm run check` passes.**

Checked by hand: each command against the live Phoenix project through the tunnel. `golden` updated only the changed turn each time, and `push-prompt` skipped a commit already pushed.

**Decisions**

- **The judge is Haiku 5.5 through the Anthropic API, listing every fact**, on `JUDGE_API_KEY`. Joe chose it after the A/B run of both rubrics through Claude Code. Written into #282's "Do".
- **Each experiment runs every golden turn 3 times**, and its description is the rubric commit's subject line. Written into #282's "Do" and DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.
- **The golden set changes in place,** as a new dataset version, since deleting a dataset deletes its experiments. Written into #282's "Do" and DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.
- **The judge's annotations are named `grounded-haiku`,** not `grounded`, since Phoenix's project page sums up annotations by name only. Written into #282's "Do" and DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.
- **Rubric v4 to v7**, from the judge's misses on the golden set. Each change is in `evals/grounded/rubric.md`, and its commit says what changed. v4 was replaced by v5.
- **Joe changed golden labels:** the Hungry Horse arrival (set 5) went to not_grounded and then back to grounded, and the Salt Lake City arrival (set 12) went to grounded. Both times can be worked out from the record. The calls are saved as `joe` annotations.
- **The goodbye reply in set 12 stays no_facts,** though the judge calls it grounded. Both mean nothing ungrounded was found, so the rate is the same either way.
- **No confusion table or macro F1 in the experiment output.** Joe walked through them in chat, and didn't need them added.

**Set aside**

- **Scoring the judge on facts, not just labels.** The golden set keeps both labelers' ungrounded facts, and Joe's, but the experiments score only the label. No more work on this evaluator is planned, so this isn't in an issue.
- **A check of the judge on turns it wasn't tuned on.** The results comment on #282 says 93% is likely optimistic for that reason.

**Config changes:** none.

**Check (V1 - The label depends on a fact the reviewer can't check from the repo, and that fact decides whether it's a fix)**

The reply the judge grades is the `coordinator.turn` span's `output.value`. `TurnTrace.#recordResult()` sets that from the Agent SDK's `result.result` (src/agent/turn-trace.ts:286). The browser chat shows every text block the coordinator writes in a turn. `web/src/chat-state.test.ts` has a turn that streams "Let me save that.", calls a tool, and then says "Five days it is." If `result.result` holds only the last assistant message's text, the judge never sees text written before a tool call. Example: "The Ferry Building opens at 10 a.m. Let me add it." followed by an `update_itinerary` call. That fact is never judged, and it's also missing from the earlier turns the judge reads as context. Then the 301-turn rate undercounts facts in multi-step turns. To check: in the live Phoenix project, open a corpus turn whose `coordinator.model_call` spans have a text block before a tool call. Compare the turn span's `output.value` with all of the turn's text blocks. If it holds only the last one, build the reply from the coordinator's model-call text blocks instead.

**Why V1:** Whether it's a fix depends on what the SDK puts in `result.result`. The CLI computes that, and nothing in the repo shows it. If it holds only the last message, the judge grades less than the reply the user saw, which is F1/F2. If it holds all the text, the claim is false.
**Not fixed:** below the bar.

**Note (NF4 - Data is lost or corrupted, but not in normal use)**

`saveCall` splits each `"<quote>|<why>"` argument with `text.split("|")` and keeps only the first two parts. A quote taken from a Markdown table row in a reply, such as `| Day 2 | 9:00 a.m. |`, contains `|`. The split then saves an empty or partial quote, and part of the quote becomes the `why`. Whatever comes after the second `|` is dropped. Joe's saved call, and the golden set's `joeUngroundedFacts` built from it, would hold the wrong text. Splitting at the last `|` only, or using a separator that can't appear in a reply, would avoid this.

**Why NF4:** Saved annotation data comes out wrong, which fits F4's kind. But it needs a quote containing `|`, and Joe types these by hand through a dev-only command, so it's outside normal use.
**Not fixed:** below the bar.

**Note (N5 - A code comment is wrong)**

The comment says the data's "each < written as < so no text in it can close the tag". The code actually writes each `<` as the JSON escape `<` (`replaceAll("<", "\\u003c")`). As written, the comment describes a no-op.

**Why N5:** Only a code comment is wrong, and the code next to it is right.
**Not fixed:** below the bar.

body:
Part of #266. Merging this doesn't close it: the baseline, the fix, and the results before and after come later.

## Task

From Joe: create a separate PR for the code that's needed to run the testing for #266, and include what remains to be tested and the details, such as the env vars, needed for it.

From the "Do" of #266:

- Add a way to run one worker from a recorded worker run: its worker brief from the coordinator's recorded Agent call, the trip as the worker found it, and today's worker instructions and tools. Its trace goes to Phoenix, as a turn's does. Write how it runs into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5, next to `npm run run-turn`.
- Write the evaluation as a Phoenix experiment in TypeScript, as the grounded evaluator is (`src/grounded-eval/`).

## Results

- **`npm run run-worker -- <agent session ID> <Agent tool_use ID>`** runs one recorded worker run alone. It copies the turn's trip version into a new local trip, replays the coordinator's calls made before the Agent call, and runs the worker on its recorded worker brief. It prints each tool call, each refused call, and the candidate call counts.
- **`npm run candidate-refusals -- dataset`** saves `evals/candidate-refusals/cases.json` as the `candidate-refusals` Phoenix dataset. **`-- experiment <trial set or all> <runs per case>`** runs a trial set or every case, 3 at a time, and code scores the refusal rate.
- **The cases** are the 32 recorded worker runs in the corpus that had a refused candidate call: 27 stay researcher runs and 5 leg scout runs.
- **DEVELOPMENT.md** sections 2 and 5 say how both run.
- `npm run check` passes: 136 test files, 968 tests.

**Checked by hand:**

- A stay researcher run alone, on a small worker brief and a local trip, started on Sonnet 5.5 with exactly its 8 tools, followed the worker brief, and traced as `stay-researcher.turn` in `road-trip-agent-local`.
- A one-example scratch experiment put the worker's spans under the run's task span, in the experiment's own Phoenix project. The scratch dataset was deleted afterwards.

## What's left to test

1. ~~Run one case with `run-worker`.~~ Done on the first case. The replay showed no checkpoint that differed, and the worker filled the four stops in its worker brief. It was refused once, for `visitTimeInMinutes` on a meal stop.
2. ~~Check the worker sees what it saw as a subagent.~~ The spans don't hold the system prompt or the tool list, so this can't be compared from the trace. Joe accepted the run as it is, since the worker repeated the recorded refusal. Capturing the model request would come only if a run looks off.
3. ~~Settle the cases and the runs.~~ The cases carry trial sets as Phoenix splits: `trial-1` is 3 cases, and `trial-2` is 12, the 3 in `trial-1` among them. Each trial runs its cases once, and the baseline runs all 32 cases 5 times.
4. ~~Run the trials, then the baseline.~~ Done. `trial-1` and `trial-2` were clean, and the baseline ran all 160 runs: 132 of 713 candidate calls refused, 18.5%. The full results are in the comment of 2026-11-09 on #266.
5. ~~Add splits for the fixes.~~ Done. `visit-time` is the 25 cases that sent `visitTimeInMinutes` on a meal stop in a baseline run, and `no-route` is the one case where Google finds no driving route. Both are in `cases.json` and in the saved dataset.

## What the testing needs

**Tunnels**, each in its own terminal:

```sh
ssh -N -L 15432:127.0.0.1:5432 root@projects.jjk3.com   # the live Postgres
ssh -N -L 6006:127.0.0.1:6006 root@projects.jjk3.com    # Phoenix
```

**The local Postgres** up and migrated: `docker compose up -d postgres`, then `npm run migrate`.

**In the local `.env`**, on top of what `npm run dev` already needs:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `LIVE_POSTGRES_PORT` | `15432`, the tunnel's port on this machine |
| `LIVE_POSTGRES_USER` | `POSTGRES_USER` from the server's `.env` |
| `LIVE_POSTGRES_PASSWORD` | `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` from the server's `.env` |
| `LIVE_POSTGRES_DB` | `POSTGRES_DB` from the server's `.env` |

These aren't in `.env.example`, since only the dev tools that read a recorded session use them.

The worker run also uses these, which `npm run dev` already needs:

- `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, for the worker's model calls.
- `GOOGLE_MAPS_SERVER_KEY`, for the worker's tools and the replayed calls.
- `POSTGRES_*`, for the local database.
- `PHOENIX_URL` (`http://127.0.0.1:6006`) and `PHOENIX_PROJECT` (`road-trip-agent-local`).

The tool_use ID for a case not in `cases.json` is the `tool_call.id` on the coordinator's Agent span, in Phoenix.

## Decisions

- **The worker runs as the query's named agent.** `src/agent/solo-worker.ts` passes `agent: <worker type>`, with the worker's own definition from `agentsFor()`. So it gets the same prompt, tools, model, and effort as when the coordinator starts it, from the same code. Written into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.
- **The worker hooks are left out.** They only build the result the coordinator reads, and there is no coordinator here. Written into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.
- **The trip is the turn's version, plus a replay of the coordinator's calls before the Agent call.** The count in #266 found saves before the worker in all 32 cases, so the version alone isn't the trip the worker found. The replay reuses `rebuild-versions`' code (persistence design section 8.9), so `replayTools` and `serversFor` are now exported. Persistence design section 8.9 itself is unchanged: it describes a coordinator turn, and I didn't want to change it without your sign-off.
- **Replays run one at a time.** A replay's IDs come from a hook on `newId()` that lasts the whole replay, so two at once would take each other's IDs. The worker runs themselves can still overlap.
- **Spans are named after the agent,** such as `coordinator.turn` and `stay-researcher.turn`. A coordinator turn's spans keep their old names.
- **Every case, 5 runs each, 3 at a time.** 5 runs tells a change apart from run-to-run differences. 3 at a time keeps inside the Claude plan's limits. Which cases to keep is still open in #266.
- **The experiment refuses to run with uncommitted changes,** since it's named for the commit, and the code that ran wouldn't be that commit.

## Set aside

- Whether a worker run alone gets the same system prompt as a subagent. It needs a recorded run to compare with. It's step 2 of "What's left to test" in the description.
- Which cases, and how many runs of each. Still an open question in #266.

## Config changes

None.

<!-- fix-loop: summary -->

## Fix loop: deferred, and needs attention

Code updates this comment after each fix round. Resolve a finding's thread once it's handled. A finding in a review body has no thread, so tick its box instead.

**Deferred**

None.

**Needs attention**

None.

**Fix (F2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, in normal use)**

Running replays one at a time doesn't keep them apart, because a worker run can overlap another case's replay. `withIds()` sets the chooser that every `newId()` call in the process uses, through `chooseNewIdsWith()`. The workers' tools run in this same process. Each place a stay researcher's `search_near` or `find_place` saves gets `newId("place")` in `places-client.ts`. Here is the case. In `npm run candidate-refusals -- experiment`, with concurrency 3, case A's replay ends and its worker starts searching. Case B's replay is then running a write under `withIds()`. Case A's `newId("place")` calls go through B's chooser. B's `madeIds` leaves out place IDs, so each of A's calls adds "place" to B's `random` list. B's report then says "Kinds today's code made at random: place" for a call that replayed exactly. The `newId("trip")` on line 75 runs outside the queue, so it can land in another case's replay the same way. That replay summary is what Joe reads to judge whether the trip matches what the worker found (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5). So clean cases get flagged at random. The comment's claim that runs of the worker itself can overlap is the part that isn't true.

**Why F2:** The experiment always runs 3 cases at a time, as designed, and the overlap only needs one worker search during another replay. So the dev tool reports wrong replay results in normal use. No design doc settles it, and nothing hands it to another issue.

**Fixed** in 6cdf5c434bc50e34513a0d7c6f09947a4f9204db.

The claim held. `chooseNewIdsWith()` set one chooser for the whole process, so a worker's `newId("place")` during another case's replay went through that replay's chooser. `chooseNewIdsWith()` in `src/ids/new-id.ts` now takes the work and runs it in an `AsyncLocalStorage`. So only the calls made inside `withIds()` see the chooser, and a worker's tools, or the `newId("trip")` in `runRecordedWorker()`, make random IDs. The `replays` queue in `worker-run.ts` stays, as the decisions comment chose. Only its comment changed, to say why worker runs can now overlap a replay. The test is "hands its IDs only to the work's own calls, not to work running alongside it, such as a worker's search" in `src/version-rebuild/recorded-ids.test.ts`. It failed before the fix, since the call alongside took `stop_aaaaaaaa`.

**Fix (F2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, in normal use)**

A worker run that fails gets the best score. `runSoloWorker()` doesn't throw when the SDK's result is an error. `turn-event.ts` notes that a "success" result can carry an error, such as when the Claude API fails. In the experiment, `onMessage` is the no-op default, so nothing sees the failure. Such a run has 0 candidate calls. `refusalRate` then scores it 0, the best score, and `noRefusals` scores it 1. Here is the case. During the 160-run experiment on the Claude plan, the plan's limit is hit, or the API returns an error. Each failed run counts as a perfect run, with no refusals, and pulls the mean refusal rate down. The before-and-after comparison the evaluation exists for would then show an improvement that never happened. A run that fails should fail the task, or be scored apart from a real run that made no candidate calls.

**Why F2:** An outside service failing is a failure the code is meant to handle, so this is normal use, and the evaluation reports a wrong result. No design doc says how a run with no candidate calls is scored, so D2 doesn't fit.

**Fixed** in 6cdf5c434bc50e34513a0d7c6f09947a4f9204db.

The claim held. `CandidateCallCount` now keeps the run's failure from its result message, through `failureOf()` in `turn-event.ts`. That covers an error result, and a "success" with `is_error`. A run with no result message counts as failed too. `WorkerRun` carries it as `failure`. The experiment's task calls `runOutputOf()`, which throws when `failure` isn't null. Phoenix then records the run as an error with a null output. Phoenix's `runExperiment` still runs the evaluators on that run, but `refusalOutputSchema` fails on a null output, so the run gets no score. I checked this in the installed `@arizeai/phoenix-client`. `npm run run-worker` is unchanged, and still prints "The run failed". DEVELOPMENT.md section 5 now says a failed run fails its task and gets no score. The tests are in `src/worker-run/refusals-experiment.test.ts`.

**Note (NF2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, but not in normal use)**

The `refusal rate` evaluator gives a run with no candidate calls a score of 0, which is the best score. A run that refused every call and a run that made no calls at all look the same in the mean. Here is a case. A replayed call is handled differently today, so a stop the worker was sent to fill isn't on the trip. The worker reports the problem and ends without calling `add_stop_candidates`. Its result is a success, so `runOutputOf()` doesn't throw. The run then scores 0, the same as a perfect run, and pulls the case's mean refusal rate down. The `no refusals` evaluator also scores it 1. With no calls, a run has no rate. It should get no score, as a failed run gets none, or it should be scored apart from the others.

**Why NF2:** Every case made candidate calls when it was recorded, so a successful rerun with zero candidate calls is unusual and isn't normal use. No design doc says how to score a run with no calls, so D2 doesn't fit.

**Note (N5 - A code comment is wrong)**

The comment says the worker hooks are left out because they only build the worker's result. DEVELOPMENT.md line 122 says the same. That isn't true. `workerHooks()` also has the `SubagentStop` hook `sendBack()`, which sends a worker back up to `MAX_SEND_BACKS` (2) times when it tries to end without calling `report_result`. So a worker run alone doesn't run the way it runs in the app. A stay researcher that stops without `report_result` gets sent back in the app. Run alone, it simply ends. Anyone who compares a solo run with the recorded one would be misled by these comments.

**Why N5:** The send-back hook only asks the worker to call `report_result`, which isn't a candidate tool, so the evaluation's counts barely change. What's left is a wrong comment that could mislead someone tracing a run. DEVELOPMENT.md isn't one of the design docs, so F6 doesn't fit.

> 1. **Read and note, with no rubric.** Joe reads the turns in sets, and writes a free note on each about what, if anything, went to the wrong place, and why. This is the open-coding step of error analysis, as Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar teach it. Joe reads until new notes stop showing new kinds of mistakes, not necessarily all 105 turns.

## Results

- `npm run saving -- turns` wrote `evals/saving/turns.json`: 103 corpus turns that call `update_trip_brief`, `add_memory_item`, or `update_memory_item`, in sets of 10 (the last set has 3). The 2 other turns of the 105 called only `forget_memory_item`.

## Decisions

- **A turn is matched to its trip version by the user's words, not by its place among the session's traces.** Phoenix is missing one turn's trace in one corpus session, so counting traces put every later turn one behind its trip version. The match takes the first version at or after the trace's place whose message is the same, with the app's lines removed. Written in DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.
- **The turns file is in the repo, and the pages and notes are not.** The turns file fixes which turns are in each set, so a later change to the corpus can't move them. The pages and notes go to `~/tmp/road-trip-evals/saving/`, like the grounded evaluator's files. Rebuilding a page never writes over its notes file.
- **The page doesn't show the coordinator's thinking.** Joe reads it in Phoenix, through each item's span link (2026-11-10, in chat).

## Fix loop: deferred, and needs attention

Code updates this comment after each fix round. Resolve a finding's thread once it's handled. A finding in a review body has no thread, so tick its box instead.

**Deferred**

None.

**Needs attention**

None.

**Fix (F2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, in normal use)**

`earlierTurn()` passes the current turn's `before.memory` to `callView()`, so an earlier turn's `update_memory_item` card says what the item held when the current turn started, not what that earlier call replaced. Example: turn 3 changes mem_a from "likes beaches" to "likes beaches, hates crowds", and set 1 shows turn 7. Under "Earlier turns", turn 3's card says "It replaced (trip memory): likes beaches, hates crowds". That is the text turn 3 wrote, shown as the text it replaced. Joe reads that card to judge where earlier saves went, so he sees a wrong "before" text. The fix is to leave out the "It replaced" line on earlier turns, or to give each earlier turn its own trip version's memory.

**Why F2:** The reading page, which is the tool this PR builds, shows a wrong "replaced" text whenever an earlier turn in the session updated a memory item, and that's an ordinary case. It isn't text a road trip agent reads, so F3 doesn't fit, and the page does still work, so F1 doesn't either.

**Fixed** in 5dbfc40640877bfe4677c314bb8a085c835d549b.

The claim holds. `earlierTurn()` passed the current turn's `before.memory` to `callView()`, so an earlier `update_memory_item` card showed text from the wrong point in time. The page has memory only as it stood before the current turn, so `callView()`, which only earlier turns use, now passes `null` to `saveView()`. When `memoryBefore` is `null`, `saveView()` leaves out the "It replaced" line. The current turn's saves still pass `item.before.memory`, and still show it. No test is committed: the page's script is inline HTML, and the repo's tests have no DOM. To check it, I ran the page's script in Node against a small fake DOM (`scratch/page-check.mjs`, gitignored), with the finding's example. Turn 3 changes mem_a, and the page shows turn 7. Before the fix it rendered two "It replaced (trip memory): likes beaches, hates crowds" lines. After the fix it renders only the current turn's line.

Line 261.

**Note (NF2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, but not in normal use)**

`versionTurnOf()` assumes a span's place in Phoenix is never after its version's turn, and takes the first version at or after that place with the same words. Two cases break this. (1) A turn that fails before its message reaches the transcript still has a `coordinator.turn` span, but the next turn reuses its version number (persistence design 8.9). After that, every later span's place is one past its version's turn. So `turn >= spanPosition` skips the right version, and the lookup either throws "has no trip version with its message" or matches a later turn with the same words. (2) Say versions are 1 "Plan a trip", 2 "yes" (trace missing), 3 "yes", and the spans are [1, 3]. Then the "yes" span at place 2 matches version 2, and the page silently shows the trip as it was before the wrong turn. The comment above the function says neither case can happen. The fix is to match spans to versions in order by time (the span's start against `savedDateTime`), or to refuse any match that isn't unique.

**Why NF2:** Wrong or failing results need a failed turn, or a missing trace that lines up with a later turn using the same words, among the 103 frozen turns. All 11 pages were built without an error, so the throwing case didn't happen, and only the narrow silent case could still be there. That puts it outside normal use. The design doesn't address how to match spans to versions, so D2 doesn't fit.

**Deferred:** #209.
Rare among the 103 turns, and it doesn't stop the reading. Written in #209's Do, to fix before the labels build the golden set.

**Note (NF2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, but not in normal use)**

`saveView()` looks up the replaced text in `before.memory`, which is memory as it stood when the turn started. So when one turn calls `update_memory_item` twice on the same item, the second card shows the wrong text. Example: in one turn, mem_a goes from "likes beaches" to "likes beaches, hates crowds", then to "likes quiet beaches". The second card says "It replaced (trip memory): likes beaches", but that call really replaced "likes beaches, hates crowds". Joe reads that line to judge what each save changed. One fix is to show the replaced text only on the first update of each item in the turn. Another is to show each later update's replaced text as the input of the update before it.

**Why NF2:** The reading page shows a wrong "replaced" text, which is wrong behavior, but only when a single turn updates the same memory item more than once. That's rare among the 103 frozen turns, so it isn't normal use. It's not text a road trip agent reads, and the design doesn't speak to it, so no F or D label fits.

**Deferred:** #209.
Rare among the 103 turns, and it doesn't stop the reading. Written in #209's Do, to fix before the labels build the golden set.

The grounded evaluator's prompt text and folders are unchanged. `npm run saving -- label <labeler> <set> ...` writes the inputs, runs the labeler, and says which answers don't have one entry for each save. No labeler was run on the sets. That's for the next session.
- **Version order:** `npm run saving -- check-versions` printed "15 of 15 sessions match versions that only go up." Those are all the sessions in `evals/saving/turns.json`, with every turn Phoenix has for each one checked.

## Decisions

1. **A turn whose saves were all refused isn't labeled.** It has nothing to judge, since a refused save saved nothing (decision 8 in `evals/saving/decisions.md`). `label` and `inputs` print each one they skip. None of sets 1 to 3 has one. Written into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.
2. **An `inputs` action, besides `label`.** It writes the inputs without running a labeler, so what a labeler gets can be read before paying for a run. `label` writes them too, for every set first, so the live database's tunnel is needed only at the start. Written into DEVELOPMENT.md sections 2 and 5.
3. **The answers are saved as the harness printed them, as the grounded evaluator's are.** That's a `.txt` file per turn, holding JSON: Claude Code's result, with the answer in it, or Codex's answer. `readAnswers` checks them against the schema. Keeping the grounded evaluator's format means one reader for both.
4. **`label` checks each answer has one entry for each save, numbered 1 to N in order** (`answerFitsSaves`), and says which don't. The JSON Schema can't check that, and the comparison in the next session needs it.
5. **The version check covers every turn Phoenix has in each session, not only the save turns.** A wrong match in any turn shows up as a turn that doesn't go up, so this checks more than the 105 save turns alone would.
6. **Earlier turns are numbered by their place among Phoenix's spans.** When Phoenix is missing a trace, that number can differ from the version's turn number. The labeler only uses it to tell the turns apart.
7. **The grounded evaluator's task and folders moved to `src/grounded-eval/grounded-labeling.ts`, and the saving evaluator's to `src/saving-eval/saving-labeling.ts`.** `labeling.ts` keeps only what both share, `readRubric` among it.

- #287's second review note (a second update to the same memory item in one turn shows the wrong "It replaced" text on the reading page) is still in #209's Do. It doesn't touch the labeler input, which shows each save's input, not the text it replaced.

## Fix loop: deferred, and needs attention

Code updates this comment after each fix round. Resolve a finding's thread once it's handled. A finding in a review body has no thread, so tick its box instead.

**Deferred**

None.

**Needs attention**

- The task says to relabel the batch after each rubric change (`evals/saving/rubric.md:107`): [finding](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/291#discussion_r4530503935), [reply](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/291#discussion_r4530530859)

Line 604.

**Note (NF2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, but not in normal use)**

`labeledTurnsOf()` uses `existsSync(inputPathOf(...))` to tell which turns have a labeler input. That check is meant to skip turns whose saves were all refused. It also skips every turn whose input file just isn't in `~/tmp/road-trip-evals/saving/inputs/`. Example: Joe runs `npm run saving -- compare opus-5.5 gpt-sol-6.1 4` before labeling set 4, or after clearing the local inputs folder. `saveRefsOf()` then returns no saves, `labelsOf()` reads no answers, and the report prints "Saves where every check agrees: 0 of 0" with no error. In the same case, `review 4 opus-5.5` writes a page that shows "No answer for this save." under every save. On a calibration set, every save is also marked as a split against Joe's label. Throwing an error when a set has turns but no input files would make the missing step plain.

**Why NF2:** The wrong output only shows when compare or review runs before `label` has written the set's inputs, which is outside the intended order, so it's NF2 rather than F2. The claim is true for the code as it stands, so D1 doesn't fit, and no design doc covers this case, so D2 doesn't either.

**Fix (F1 - The PR doesn't do what its task says)**

The task says to relabel the batch after each rubric change. This PR changes the rubric last in `49b4a5c`, where check 4 now lets any trip brief item hold a named road, not only the must-sees. The PR description says the batch was labeled only on `34eee57` and `1ed994a`. After `49b4a5c`, only Sol was run, 3 times, on set 2 item 9. Opus wasn't rerun, and neither labeler was rerun on the other 29 turns. The check 4 change can change any memory save whose named road is in the focus or the route preference, so the comparison table and the set pages show labels from the rubric before the last one. Also, `labelsOf()` reads answers from the committed rubric's folder (`labeling/49b4a5c/`). So `npm run saving -- compare opus-5.5 gpt-sol-6.1 1 2 3` and `review <set> opus-5.5 gpt-sol-6.1` on this commit fail with ENOENT until the batch is relabeled. Run `npm run saving -- label opus-5.5 1 2 3` and `label gpt-sol-6.1 1 2 3` on `49b4a5c`, then run compare again and update the results.

**Why F1:** The task's "Relabel the batch after a change" isn't done for the last rubric change, so the PR doesn't do what its task says. No other issue takes on this relabel, so D3 doesn't fit, and the claim comes from the PR's own description, so D1 doesn't fit.

**Needs attention.**

The claim holds. `readRubric()` in `src/grounded-eval/labeling.ts` names the rubric version by the last commit that changed `evals/saving/rubric.md`, which is now `49b4a5c`. So `labelsOf()` in `src/saving-eval/label-files.ts` reads answers from `labeling/49b4a5c/`, and only Sol's reruns of set 2 item 9 were made there. The task's "Relabel the batch after a change" isn't done for the check 4 change, so F1 fits, and no open issue other than #209 plans the relabel.

The fix can't be made from the fix loop. The labelers run on Joe's own Claude Code and Codex sign-ins (`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and `harnessEnv()` in `labeling.ts`), and the inputs and answers live in `~/tmp/road-trip-evals/saving/` on Joe's machine, built from the live database through the tunnels. No code change is needed.

What has to be done, on `49b4a5c` or later with the rubric unchanged: run `npm run saving -- label opus-5.5 1 2 3` and `npm run saving -- label gpt-sol-6.1 1 2 3`. Then run `npm run saving -- compare opus-5.5 gpt-sol-6.1 1 2 3`, rebuild the pages with `npm run saving -- review <set> opus-5.5 gpt-sol-6.1` for sets 1 to 3, and update the PR description's comparison table and the check 4 line with the new counts. If the relabel shows the rubric is unclear somewhere new, that's a rubric change for Joe to decide, followed by another relabel.

**Not fixed:** below the bar.
Joe chose not to relabel after the check 4 change (2026-11-10, in chat). It only loosens F4, and Sol, rerun 3 times on the one turn it could change (set 2 item 9), passed it each time.

title: Save the saving evaluation's golden set to Phoenix (#209)

body:
Part of #209: the Haiku judge, tuned on `saving-golden`. The replays come in a later PR.

## Task

From #209's Do:

- **Tuning the Haiku judge on `saving-golden`, on Claude's own.** Settled by Joe on 2026-11-10, in chat. A full run is one Phoenix experiment over all 103 golden turns, each run 3 times, as the grounded evaluator's experiments are (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5). Claude may make up to 5 full runs without Joe. Targeted runs, on a few turns to test one change, don't count toward the 5.
  - **What may change:** the judge's prompt, and the rubric's explanations and made-up examples. Not what a check means, and not Joe's labels in `calibration.json` or `split-calls.json`. If Claude thinks a label is wrong, or a check needs a new meaning, it stops and asks Joe. Otherwise the judge could look better by bending the checks to fit Haiku.
  - **No examples from the golden set,** in the judge's prompt or the rubric, as decision 7 in `evals/saving/decisions.md` says for the rubric. A judge that could copy an example would match Joe's label without judging the turn.
  - **After each full run, report each check's misses and false alarms.** Stop early if two full runs in a row don't improve. Joe decides from the report whether the judge is good enough, so there's no target number.
- Write the evaluation as a Phoenix experiment in TypeScript, as the grounded evaluator is (`src/grounded-eval/`). Code reads what the turn saved from the local database. The judge runs on Haiku, with `JUDGE_API_KEY`, and its prompt lives in the repo and is pushed to Phoenix, as the grounded evaluator's is.

## Done when

- The golden set is in Phoenix, with the judge's false alarms and misses against it recorded in this issue. **Done.** `saving-golden` was saved in #293. Six full runs were made, and each one's misses and false alarms are recorded in #209 (Do, step 6). The judge's version, rubric `4e4d6d7`, got 274 of 309 judgments fully right, and caught 195 of 213 failures (about 92%). F2 is the weak check, with 11 misses and 11 false alarms over 3 runs of every turn.
- `npm run check` passes. **Done.**

The other "Done when" items (the replay results, and the evaluation staying in the set) come with the replays.

## Checked by hand

- `npm run saving -- push-prompt` pushed each rubric version to `saving-judge` in Phoenix, and `experiment` ran all 103 turns 3 times on each, with no failed tasks.
- `npm run saving -- report` rebuilt each run's report from Phoenix, and rescoring against the changed labels matched a separate count from the saved answers.
- `npm run saving -- try-judge` ran the judge on a few turns from an uncommitted rubric.
- `npm run grounded` wasn't rerun after its judge code was shared. Its prompt name, slot, and request are unchanged, and it typechecks.

nodes.body:
## Decisions

- **The judge code is shared with the grounded evaluator.** `judge-prompt.ts` and `judge.ts` now take a `JudgeSpec`: the prompt's name, the rubric path, the slot, and the labeling task with its answer schema. The grounded judge keeps its prompt name and its `{{conversation}}` slot, so its pushed versions still read the same way. Written into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.
- **The judge's prompt is the rubric, as the labelers read it.** Every tuning change went into `evals/saving/rubric.md` itself, so later labelers read the same text. There's no separate judge-only text.
- **A run is scored save by save, on each check.** Phoenix gets one score per check per run, plus "turn matches". The local report counts misses and false alarms per check, and lists each save the judge got wrong with how many of its runs. Written into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.
- **`try-judge` runs a rubric from disk on a few turns, without Phoenix,** for the targeted runs the issue allows. Run 4 showed its limit: a change that fixed the turns it was aimed at moved errors to other turns, so a full run decides. Written into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.
- **A save's number in the answer schema is a plain number, not an integer.** The API's structured output refuses the minimum and maximum Zod writes for an integer. `answerFitsSaves` already checks the numbers.
- **Run 4's F2 change was reverted,** since that run was worse than run 3. Run 5 reran run 3's prompt, to see how much a full run moves on its own: 6 judgments.
- **Three labels changed, from Joe's calls during tuning** (decisions 20 and 21 in `evals/saving/decisions.md`). Two Florida trip items took the label Joe gave another version of the same item. Joe limited check 4 to trip memory, so the lobster roll habit in user memory passes it.

## Set aside

- **Every full run lost its Phoenix connection at the very end,** after all its runs and scores were saved. It's an error inside the Phoenix client that our code doesn't catch, so the experiment's own report wasn't written. `npm run saving -- report` rebuilds it from Phoenix (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5). The cause isn't known. The SSH tunnel stayed up throughout. One guess, not checked: the client reuses an idle connection that Phoenix's server had already closed. Not written into an issue; Joe can decide whether it's worth one.

## Config changes

None.

Line 31.

**Note (N6 - A design doc is unclear, or doesn't match the code, in a way no builder would act on)**

The `npm run saving` row in the section 2 command table still lists only `turns`, `review`, `inputs`, `label`, `compare`, `check-versions`, and `golden`. This PR adds four more actions: `push-prompt`, `experiment`, `report`, and `try-judge` (`JUDGE_ACTIONS` in `src/saving-eval/saving-judge.ts`). So a reader of the table won't see the judge's actions, even though section 5 and the header of `saving.ts` describe them.

**Why N6:** The doc doesn't match the code, but section 5 of the same file and the comment at the top of `saving.ts` already list and explain the new actions, so no builder would get it wrong. It isn't F6, because nothing would be built wrong from this row.

**Not fixed:** below the bar.
Joe, 2026-11-10: the saving commands are listed in the saving.ts header and DEVELOPMENT.md section 5, and the rest of #209 doesn't depend on the section 2 table.

**Note (N6 - A design doc is unclear, or doesn't match the code, in a way no builder would act on)**

The `golden` bullet says `evals/saving/split-calls.json` holds Joe's labels "for the saves he called on the full labeling's splits". This PR adds two turns to that file that weren't splits. Set 6 item 1 and set 9 item 6 are there because the judge showed that the agreed label was wrong (decisions 20 and 21). The labelers agreed on both, so neither was a split. The comment on `goldenSavesOf` in `src/saving-eval/label-files.ts` was updated to say this, but the DEVELOPMENT.md bullet wasn't. Someone reading only the doc would think every entry in the file is a call on a split.

**Why N6:** The doc no longer matches the data. But `goldenSavesOf` reads every entry in the file the same way, and its comment and decisions 20 and 21 explain the new entries, so no builder would build anything wrong from this. That makes it N6, not F6. The labels above F6 don't fit, because the claim is true and no issue takes over this work.

title: Add the saving evaluation's Haiku judge, tuned on saving-golden (#209)

body:
Part of #209, "Saving to the right place: trip brief, itinerary, or trip memory, checked with an evaluation".

## Task

From #209's Do:

- **The cases, and how many runs.** Settled by Joe on 2026-11-10, in chat. The cases are the `saving-golden` turns that fail a check: 46 of the 103, from 13 sessions. Nothing outside the golden set is a case: the Austin terminal run and the Natick (Finger Lakes) session are dropped, since neither can be replayed in full, and the golden set has the same kinds of mistakes. Each round runs all 46, not only the ones a change is aimed at, so a mistake that moves to another check shows up. Each case runs 5 times, 230 turns a round, as the candidate refusals evaluation's baseline did. The total across the cases is what tells a change apart from run-to-run differences. Before the baseline, a trial runs a few cases once each, to check the setup. A case whose own result matters later, such as the Bar Harbor must-sees, can be rerun more times on its own.
- **How a case runs, and what the judge reads.** Settled by Joe on 2026-11-10, in chat. Nothing replays the old calls. `run-turn` sets the trip up in the local database as it stood before the turn, with the conversation before it, sends the user's recorded message, and the coordinator makes its own calls and saves on today's instructions. The judge reads the same `<before>` and `<earlier_turns>` as the golden turn's labeler input, since a run starts from the same trip version and conversation, and a `<turn>` built from this run's calls and saves. Those come from the run's trace in the `road-trip-agent-local` project in Phoenix, found by the turn span ID `run-turn` prints, built with the same code that builds `<turn>` for the golden set (`src/saving-eval/labeler-input.ts`). The local database holds only the trip after the run, not the calls, so it isn't the judge's source.
- **The baseline runs on its own, overnight.** Settled by Joe on 2026-11-10, in chat. A run that fails, such as on the Claude plan's limit, gets no score and is reported as failed, as in the candidate refusals evaluation. Rerun the failed runs later, rather than scoring them. The baseline ends with its results recorded in this issue and a PR for its code. Don't merge it, and don't start the change to the coordinator's instructions: Joe reviews that wording in the PR (see below).
- Run each case as one turn with `npm run run-turn -- <agent session ID> <turn> --recorded-message` (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5). Every full judge run in #294 lost its Phoenix connection at the very end, after its runs and scores were saved, with an error inside the Phoenix client that the code can't catch. The cause isn't known; the SSH tunnel stayed up. So the replay experiment's report should be one that can be built again from what Phoenix saved, as `npm run saving -- report` does for the judge (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5), and not only written at the end of the run.
- Write the evaluation as a Phoenix experiment in TypeScript, as the grounded evaluator is (`src/grounded-eval/`). The judge runs on Haiku, with `JUDGE_API_KEY`, and its prompt lives in the repo and is pushed to Phoenix, as the grounded evaluator's is.
- Run it on the coordinator's instructions as they are when this starts. Record the results in this issue. As of 2026-11-08, `src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts` has neither of the two tests below.

Changed by Joe on 2026-11-11, in chat, after the first baseline run hit the Claude plan's limit: the 7 cases whose turns start many workers aren't run, the rest are split into `dev` (14 cases, run after each change to the instructions) and `holdout` (35 cases, run when `dev` looks good), and 10 golden turns that saved and passed every check join the cases, to catch a change that breaks saving that works.

## Done when

- **The results are recorded:** in #209, under the Do bullet on running the evaluation. On today's instructions, the 39 light failing cases passed 61 of 195 runs, and passed the checks their golden turn failed in 73. The 10 passing cases passed 35 of 50 runs. Experiments `RXhwZXJpbWVudDoyMQ==` and `RXhwZXJpbWVudDoyMg==` on `saving-replays` in Phoenix, and `npm run saving -- replay-report <experiment ID> [split]` builds each report again.
- **The evaluation stays in the set:** `npm run saving -- replay dev 3` runs it again, as DEVELOPMENT.md section 5 says.
- **`npm run check` passes.**

nodes.body:
## Decisions

Calls I made where the issue and the design docs didn't settle it.

1. **run-turn became a library (`src/turn-run/turn-run.ts`).** The experiment runs each turn inside its own process, through the same code `npm run run-turn` uses, rather than starting the script once for each run. `run-turn.ts` is now a thin script over it.
2. **Each run's turn is its own root trace in `road-trip-agent-local`,** not a child of the experiment's task span. That's how a `run-turn` turn looks, so `traceTurnOf` reads it the same way. The task flushes tracing, then reads the turn by its span ID until Phoenix has it.
3. **A case's judge context is built again from the live data,** with `labelerContextOf`, and the dataset refuses a case whose context doesn't match the start of its golden labeler input. So a run is judged on the same `<before>` and `<earlier_turns>` as its golden turn.
4. **No cases file in the repo.** The `saving-replays` dataset in Phoenix is the record, so no trip content goes in the public repo.
5. **A case's golden checks are every check any of its golden saves fails,** since a run's saves don't line up one to one with the golden turn's.
6. **A run that saved nothing isn't sent to the judge.** Its answer is no saves, so it passes, and the `saved nothing` count shows it.
7. **The judge is asked up to 3 times** when its answer doesn't have one entry for each save. After that the run fails, rather than being scored on a wrong answer.
8. **Each run's output keeps its `<turn>`,** so a run can be judged again, such as on a new judge prompt, without running the turn again.
9. **3 turns at a time,** as the candidate refusals evaluation runs. The plan's limit counts tokens, so this sets the speed, not the cost.
10. **The trial was the first case of each of the first 3 sessions,** `trial-1`: 1.1, 1.2, and 1.4.
11. **The report is built from Phoenix, never only at the end of a run.** Every run writes it in a `finally` block, and `replay-report` builds it again. That covered the end-of-run Phoenix disconnect, which happened again on the first baseline run.
12. **`replay-resume` takes a split and a most-runs limit.** A run it leaves out fails at once without starting a turn, so it stays failed for the next resume. This is how the baseline was finished in batches that Joe could watch on the usage meter.
13. **Splits match cases by set and item, not example ID,** because the resume and the dataset name examples by different IDs.
14. **The whale cutoff is 4 or more workers,** in the golden session or in a replay. 6.10 is out on its replays, since its golden turn started none but every replay started 4.
15. **The baseline's code commits differ:** the failing cases ran on `51f2aab` and later resumes on `9c1f6dd` and `d2c1122`, and the passing cases on `0358441`. The changes between them only touch how runs are picked, not the turn, the judge, or the coordinator's instructions.

Joe's own decisions from the session (the splits, the passing cases, and the cost) are in #209's Do.

<!-- fix-loop: summary -->

## Fix loop: deferred, and needs attention

Code updates this comment after each fix round. Resolve a finding's thread once it's handled. A finding in a review body has no thread, so tick its box instead.

**Deferred**

None.

**Needs attention**

None.

**Fix (F2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, in normal use)**

After a run, `withReplayGiven` writes the report with `writeReplayReport(phoenixUrl, null, split)`. With a null ID, `experimentOf` takes the most recently created experiment on saving-replays, not the one that just ran. That's right after `replay`, but `replay-resume` resumes the experiment ID it was given, which may not be the newest. Example: experiments `RXhwZXJpbWVudDoyMQ==` and `RXhwZXJpbWVudDoyMg==` both exist, and `npm run saving -- replay-resume RXhwZXJpbWVudDoyMQ== all` reruns 21's failed runs. It then prints 22's report and rewrites 22's folder, and 21's report is never updated. Joe reads the wrong experiment's numbers as the result of the resume. `resumeAction` should pass its `experimentId` through to the report.

**Why F2:** Resuming an older experiment while a newer one exists is normal use, and this PR's own results already have two experiments, so the tool shows the wrong result (F2). The task asks for a report that can be rebuilt, which `replay-report` provides, so this is not F1.

**Fixed** in 0faeb4e45aea117336e64fe031420626a9b54195.

`withReplayGiven` now takes an `experimentId`, and passes it to `writeReplayReport` in its `finally` block. `resumeAction` passes the ID it resumes. `replayAction` passes null, so a new run still reports the latest experiment, since its ID isn't known when the run fails partway. I added no test. The path goes through `judgeFor`, both Postgres pools, and Phoenix, and the repo has no fakes for that setup, while tests in `npm run check` make no outside calls (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5). The change is one value passed through. `npm run check` passes.

**Note (NF2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, but not in normal use)**

`replay-resume` runs the remaining runs on whatever commit is checked out. `cleanCommit` only refuses uncommitted changes. It doesn't check that HEAD is the commit in the experiment's metadata. The experiment keeps its first `commit` and `description`, and the report's title names that commit. Example: a baseline stops on the Claude plan's limit, Joe commits a change to `coordinator-prompt.ts`, then resumes the baseline. The remaining runs use the new instructions, but are counted and titled as the old baseline, and nothing shows the mix.

**Why NF2:** This needs an instructions change committed between a run and its resume. The intended flow is to resume right after hitting the limit, and commits in between that only touch eval code are fine, so it's outside normal use (NF2). No design doc says whether a resume must match the experiment's commit, so this isn't D2.

**Note (NF2 - The app does the wrong thing, crashes, or hangs, but not in normal use)**

After `npm run saving -- replay`, the `finally` in `withReplayGiven` always writes a report, even when `runExperiment` threw before it created an experiment. For `replay`, `experimentId` is null, so `writeReplayReport` picks the newest older experiment on saving-replays. It prints that experiment's report and rewrites its folder, as if it were the result of this run. Example: `npm run saving -- replay dev 3` fails at the start, such as on a dataset or split lookup in Phoenix. The output ends with the report of an earlier experiment, such as `RXhwZXJpbWVudDoyMg==`, and nothing says it's not from this run. One fix is to write the report after a new run only when the run got as far as creating its experiment. Another is to name the experiment's ID in the printed line.

**Why NF2:** The usual failure the report is there to handle is losing the Phoenix connection at the end of a run, after the experiment exists. Then the latest experiment is the right one. A failure before the experiment is created is a narrow case, so this is outside normal use (NF2). No design doc says which experiment the report should cover after a failed start, so D2 doesn't fit.

title: Saving replays: run the failing saving-golden turns again on today's instructions, judged on rubric 4e4d6d7, with dev and holdout splits (#209)

body:
Closes #209.

## Task

#209's next step after the baseline (#295): one big change to the coordinator's instructions, aimed at the six saving checks at once, then the dev cases run again. Running it showed that no replay had run on the code's instructions, so this also fixes the replays.

- `src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts` and `src/agent/coordinator-trip-brief-prompt.ts`: one thing in each memory item; who reads memory; user or trip, with a one-time approval not saved as a habit; no copy of the plan or of the trip brief in memory; a named road and food and lodging wishes in the trip brief; and a message sorted into the trip brief items, with the must-see test, so a hedged wish stays out of the must-sees.
- `src/tools/trip-brief-input.schema.ts`: the four text inputs say "In the user's words. Leave out the parts of their message that belong in other items."
- `src/turn-run/recorded-turn.ts`: a run from a recorded turn leaves out Claude Code's `prompt_snapshot` lines. A resumed session sends that saved copy of the system prompt and tools again, so every replay, the baseline's too, ran on the instructions its session was recorded with.
- Technical spec 5.2 and persistence design 8.9 say the same.

## Done when

- **The results before and after are recorded in #209.** On the dev cases, 3 runs each, experiment `RXhwZXJpbWVudDoyNA==` on `51ed6dc`, rubric `4e4d6d7`:

  | Cases | Baseline, runs passed | After, runs passed |
  |---|---|---|
  | `dev`, 10 failing | 9 of 50 | 13 of 30 |
  | `dev`, 4 passing | 16 of 20 | 10 of 12 |

  Runs failing each check went from F1 28 of 70 to 8 of 42, F2 9 to 3, F3 11 to 4, F4 14 to 5, F5 10 to 2, and F6 8 to 4. The holdout wasn't run.
- **A run gets today's instructions.** A run of case 4.10 wrote a new `prompt_snapshot` with the new instructions, and every dev case's first model call has a different input size than before the fix.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Decisions

- **A dislike goes to memory, not the interests.** Decided by Joe on 2026-11-11, in chat: `interestsText` is what the user enjoys. Memory reaches the workers under the worker brief's "Avoid" heading.
- **A day the user asked for stays in trip memory once the itinerary has it,** such as "the Grand Canyon sunset on the second night." The itinerary can't show that the user asked for that night, and the rubric passes a day the user named. Agreed by Joe on 2026-11-11, in chat.
- **`mustSeesText` keeps its name.** None of the failures came from the name, and "must include" would invite plan choices, such as two nights in a town, which F5 fails. Agreed by Joe on 2026-11-11, in chat.
- **Something can go in more than one trip brief item,** such as a hotel the user has to stay at, in the must-sees and the lodging preferences. The rubric passes any overlap between trip brief items.
- **The baseline stays,** though it ran on each session's recorded instructions. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-11: they changed little between the recordings and #295.
- **The holdout isn't run, and #209 closes with this PR.** Decided by Joe on 2026-11-11: the evaluation showed the change working, and more tuning would optimize a design he'd change, the trip brief's text items plus trip memory.

## Set aside

- **7.7 fails F4 in 2 of 3 runs, for "doesn't care about shopping" in trip memory.** The coordinator follows the dislike rule above. The judge reads a trip-wide dislike as the interests' to hold. The fix would be a sentence in F4 saying a dislike isn't what the interests are for, which means a new rubric version and checking the judge against the golden set again. Not done, since #209 ends here.
- **A live session keeps its first turn's instructions and tools,** the same snapshot problem in the app: #296, in Triage.

None.

**Fixed** in 58cde574c58e0318999470f6b0ac08456703680c.

> On `design/functional-spec.md:120`, in [the review](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/297#pullrequestreview-5864791180):
>
> Functional spec 5.2 still says "A lodging wish that comes up later in the chat, after discovery, goes in trip memory, or in user memory when it's a standing preference." This PR changes that rule in technical spec 5.2 ("A preference about food or places to stay goes in the meal or lodging preferences whenever it comes up, for the whole trip or for one stay"). It also changes it in the coordinator's trip brief instructions (src/agent/coordinator-trip-brief-prompt.ts), where the old line sending a later lodging wish such as "let's do something special in Santa Fe" to trip memory was replaced. Here is a concrete case. A builder changing the trip brief instructions or the saving rubric reads functional spec 5.2. They send "let's do something special in Santa Fe" to trip memory. The coordinator's instructions would then save it to lodgingPreferencesText, so the two disagree. The design docs now contradict each other on where this wish goes.

Functional spec 5.2 no longer sends a lodging wish that comes up after discovery to trip memory. It now says a preference about food or places to stay goes in the meal or lodging preferences whenever it comes up, even after discovery, for the whole trip or for one stay, such as "let's do something special in Santa Fe", and that a standing preference also goes in user memory (10.3). That's the rule in technical spec 5.2 and in the trip brief instructions (`src/agent/coordinator-trip-brief-prompt.ts`). It's a doc change only, so there's no test. I left functional spec 10.2's "wants one nice dinner in Austin" example alone, since the finding doesn't name it and the coordinator prompt uses the same example for trip memory.

To reply, post a comment that names `review-5864791180-1`.

<!-- fix-loop: review-5864791180-1 -->

Line 61.

**Fix (F6 - A design doc is wrong, so an agent building from it would build the wrong thing)**

The PR adds a new rule in technical spec 5.2 and the coordinator prompt: each memory item holds one thing, and several things are never gathered into one item. To fit it, the prompt changed "When a memory is full, merge or forget items first" to "forget items that no longer apply first" (src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts:394). Technical spec 3.1 (line 61) still says "When memory is full, the coordinator merges or forgets items first." Tool design 2.x (design/tools.md:245) says the error lets the coordinator "merge or forget items". The add_memory_item refusal the coordinator reads still says "Merge or forget items first." (src/persistence/memory-writer.ts:112). So the design now contradicts itself. Here is a concrete case: a trip's memory is at its maximum and the user says two new things. add_memory_item is refused with "Merge or forget items first." The coordinator follows the error, merges two existing items into one, and breaks the one-thing-per-item rule this PR is tuning for. A builder working from 3.1 or tools.md would also keep the merge advice.

**Why F6:** The doc contradicts itself: 3.1 and tools.md say merge, and 5.2's new one-thing rule rules it out. That leads to a wrong error text and wrong coordinator behavior when memory is full. The claim is checkable from the repo, it isn't handed to another issue, and the design isn't settled in favor of merging, so V1 and D1 to D3 don't fit. F1 to F5 don't fit because the task doesn't name this text.

**Fixed** in aada8c9bf09afe07875e5a7ddc444ae48468ecfe.

The refusal in `MemoryWriter.#refuseIfFull()` (src/persistence/memory-writer.ts) now ends "Forget items that no longer apply first.", the same as the coordinator prompt. Technical spec 3.1 and tool design 2.x (design/tools.md, add_memory_item's refusals) now say the coordinator forgets items that no longer apply, and doesn't merge items, since each holds one thing (5.2). The expected text changed in the tests that go through the refusal: `memory-writer.test.ts` ("refuses an add to full user memory" and "refuses an add to a full trip memory") and `memory-tools.test.ts` ("refuses an add over the maximum items", which calls add_memory_item as the agent does). They failed on the old text, and pass on the new.

**Note (N3 - Text a road trip agent reads is unclear, or says something twice, or is an error message with the wrong reason for a failure)**

Two rules in the same Memory section pull against each other on dates. Line 392 says "Write each item as something to act on, naming places, towns, and dates in words." The new line 416 says "Name a day by what happens on it ... not by its weekday or date", unless the user named the day or something outside the plan fixes it. Line 392 reads as a push to put dates in items, while line 416 says to leave them out by default. A coordinator saving a wish for a day it planned itself could read either rule as the one to follow.

**Why N3:** This is text the agent reads, and it's unclear rather than false: line 392 is about how to write a date, and line 416 about whether to write one. So it's N3, not F3.

Line 197.

**Fix (F6 - A design doc is wrong, so an agent building from it would build the wrong thing)**

Technical spec 5.2 now gives two different homes for a meal wish. The Meals rule (line 197) still says a meal wish such as "we'll picnic on the drive" or pie at Gifford Homestead "is saved to trip memory when it's for this trip". The new rule this PR adds to the same section (line 141, "Sort the user's words into the items") says "A preference about food or places to stay goes in the meal or lodging preferences whenever it comes up, for the whole trip or for one stay." This PR already fixed the same conflict for lodging in functional spec 5.2, but not this one for food. A concrete case: the user says "we'll picnic on the drive on the Moab day." A builder who follows the Meals rule saves it to trip memory. A builder who follows the new rule saves it to mealPreferencesText. The saving rubric and the replays would then score one of those as a wrong place.

**Why F6:** The design doc contradicts itself on a point a builder of the instructions or the saving rubric would act on, so F6 fits. The claim checks out against the repo, and no other issue holds the work, so V1 and D1 to D3 don't fit. The design isn't settled in favor of either rule, since this PR adds the new one.

Line 228.

**Note (N3 - Text a road trip agent reads is unclear, or says something twice, or is an error message with the wrong reason for a failure)**

The coordinator's instructions give two different homes for a food wish. The Laying out days rule (line 228) says a meal wish, such as "we'll picnic on the drive" or pie at a bakery they love, goes in trip memory when it's for this trip. The Memory section's opening (line 383) also names "wants one nice dinner in Austin" as a trip memory note. But the new trip brief rule (coordinator-trip-brief-prompt.ts line 49) says "A preference about food or places to stay goes in mealPreferencesText or lodgingPreferencesText whenever it comes up, whether it's for the whole trip ... or for one stay". The new Memory rule at line 419 says to check for a food preference before saving to trip memory. A concrete case: the user says "we want one nice dinner in Austin." One run saves it to trip memory, as lines 228 and 383 say. Another saves it to mealPreferencesText, as the trip brief rule says. So the saving replays would score them differently from one run to the next.

**Why N3:** This is text a road trip agent reads, and two rules in it pull different ways. Each can be read as true on its own, so it's unclear text (N3), not false text (F3). The design doc half of the same problem is the F6 finding on technical spec 5.2.

These findings are on files this PR doesn't change, so they can't be inline comments.

### `design/functional-spec.md:120`

**Fix (F6 - A design doc is wrong, so an agent building from it would build the wrong thing)**

Functional spec 5.2 still says "A lodging wish that comes up later in the chat, after discovery, goes in trip memory, or in user memory when it's a standing preference." This PR changes that rule in technical spec 5.2 ("A preference about food or places to stay goes in the meal or lodging preferences whenever it comes up, for the whole trip or for one stay"). It also changes it in the coordinator's trip brief instructions (src/agent/coordinator-trip-brief-prompt.ts), where the old line sending a later lodging wish such as "let's do something special in Santa Fe" to trip memory was replaced. Here is a concrete case. A builder changing the trip brief instructions or the saving rubric reads functional spec 5.2. They send "let's do something special in Santa Fe" to trip memory. The coordinator's instructions would then save it to lodgingPreferencesText, so the two disagree. The design docs now contradict each other on where this wish goes.

**Why F6:** The design docs contradict each other on a point a builder would act on, so F6 fits. The claim is checkable from the repo, and no other issue holds the work. The design isn't settled in favour of the old wording, since this PR's own technical spec change replaces it, so D1 to D3 don't fit.

### `src/agent/coordinator-choices-prompt.ts:45`

**Note (N3 - Text a road trip agent reads is unclear, or says something twice, or is an error message with the wrong reason for a failure)**

The coordinator's instructions now give two different homes for the party's pace. coordinator-choices-prompt.ts line 45, and coordinator-prompt.ts line 383 ("Trip memory holds ... the party's pace"), say to save "we're slow" to trip memory. The new User or trip rule in the Memory section says "User memory holds what describes the user on any trip: a habit or trait, such as 'early risers' ... It goes there even when it comes up while planning this trip." "We're slow" reads as a trait just like "early risers". So a coordinator that hears it could save it to either memory, and the saving replays would score it differently from one run to the next.

**Why N3:** This is text a road trip agent reads, and two rules in it pull different ways. Each rule can be read as true on its own, so this is unclear text (N3), not false text (F3). It isn't a design doc problem, since technical spec 5.2 still names pace for trip memory.
